  • More protocols: WARP with free account registration, an endpoint scanner and noise and MASQUE; AmneziaWG; Psiphon; Mieru; Sudoku; TrustTunnel; GooseRelay; Bond; a reverse tunnel; an SSH inbound; and the legacy WireGuard outbound that upstream removed.
  • DNS tunnels that find working public resolvers by themselves: DNSTT, MasterDNS and Soar, with a shared smart resolver pool.
  • Anti-censorship tricks: TLS fragment, TLS tricks (mixed-case SNI, padding) and REALITY additions.
  • Groups and monitoring: a balancer with several strategies, a fallback group, URL test additions, background monitoring of delay and exit IP, and a unified delay that compares across protocols.
  • DNS: a DNS group, bypass_if_failed, DNSCrypt stamps, sslip.io names and IPv6 by outbound.
  • Bug fixes on top of sing-box 1.15, each with its commit.

docs.title: Compared with Xray
docs.text: hiddify-core has Xray's XHTTP, mKCP, finalmask, XDRIVE, raw transport and VLESS encryption written into sing-box. An Xray-style VLESS outbound can therefore run next to Hysteria2, TUIC, WireGuard, WARP and the DNS tunnels in one config, under sing-box's TUN, routing, rule sets and proxy groups. hiddify-core reads Xray JSON configs and Xray share links (including the extra field of XHTTP), and HiddifyCli parse --xray converts share links to Xray JSON.

docs.title: Compared with mihomo
docs.text: hiddify-core reads the proxies of a Clash or mihomo YAML config and converts them to sing-box, so a Clash subscription works with run without changes. Its groups cover what mihomo users expect (select, URL test, fallback, load balancing) and add the monitoring and failover described above. Configs are written in sing-box JSON, not YAML.

docs.title: Read more
docs.text:
• Command-line reference: every command and flag of HiddifyCli.
  • Hiddify sing-box features: one page per feature, in English and Persian.
  • App considerations: what app and core developers need to know about the v5 core.
  • Using HiddifyCli on OpenWrt.

docs.title: HiddifyCli command-line reference
docs.text:
HiddifyCli (installed as hiddify-core by the Linux installer) is the command line of Hiddify Core. This page lists every command and flag. HiddifyCli help and HiddifyCli <command> --help print the same list from the program itself.

HiddifyCli [global flags] <command> [flags]

docs.title: Global flags
docs.text:
These work with every command.

Flag Default Meaning -D, --directory <dir> current folder Working folder. It is created if missing, and relative paths (configs, data/, tmp/) are read from it. --disable-color off Print logs without colors. -h, --help Help for any command.

docs.title: Commands at a glance
docs.text: Command What it does run Run share links, a subscription or the proxies of a config, with a client config built around them srun Run a complete sing-box config as it is parse Convert links or any config format to sing-box outbounds (or to Xray JSON) build Build the full client config that run would use, without running it instance Start a small test instance with a SOCKS port and ping through it health Test DNS, HTTP or QUIC through a proxy speedtest Measure download, upload, ping and jitter through a proxy warp Register a free WARP account and print its WireGuard outbound vlessenc Make a VLESS encryption key pair version Print the versions and build details admin_bgservice Manage the background service the desktop app uses for VPN mode grpcweb A small web page to start and control the core from a browser extension A test server for Hiddify extensions ezytel A viewer for public Telegram channels gen-cert Make TLS certificates for the core's gRPC server Developer commands gen, profile, command completion Print a shell completion script (bash, zsh, fish, powershell)

docs.title: run
docs.text:
HiddifyCli run -c <file or URL> [flags]

Reads proxies from the input, builds a complete client config from the Hiddify settings, and runs it until you press Ctrl+C. See Run a config for when to use run and when to use srun.

The input can be:

  • a file of share links (one per line, plain or base64), which may also hold subscription links;
  • an http:// or https:// subscription link. When the server sends a profile-update-interval header (or the body has a #profile-update-interval: line), the subscription is fetched again every that many hours and the core restarts if it changed;
  • a sing-box JSON config, a list of outbounds or one outbound. Only outbounds and endpoints are taken, unless --full-config is given;
  • a Clash or mihomo YAML config, an Xray JSON config, or a WireGuard .conf file.

While it runs, the core's gRPC server listens on 127.0.0.1:17078 and the Clash API on 127.0.0.1:16756 (0.0.0.0:16756 when allow-connection-from-lan is set in the settings file).

docs.title: Flags of run, build and instance
docs.text:
Flag Default Meaning -c, --config <path or URL> required The proxies: a file, or a subscription URL (run only). -d, --hiddify <file> A Hiddify settings JSON file (see below). When given, the file decides every setting and the flags below are ignored. --full-config off Keep the inbounds, DNS and route rules of a sing-box input, next to the ones hiddify-core builds. --tun off Capture all traffic of the system with a TUN (a system-wide VPN). Needs root or administrator. --tun-service off Use the Hiddify background service for the TUN, as the desktop app does. --system-proxy off Set the system proxy of the desktop to the local proxy. --in-proxy-port <port> 12334 Port of the local mixed (HTTP and SOCKS5) proxy. --dns-remote <server> 1.1.1.1 DNS server used through the proxy: 1.1.1.1, tcp://…, tls://…, https://…/dns-query. --dns-direct <server> 1.1.1.1 DNS server used for direct connections. --fragment off Turn on TLS fragment. --fragment-size <range> 2-4 Size of each fragment in bytes. --fragment-sleep <range> 2-4 Pause between fragments in milliseconds. --padding off Add a TLS padding extension (TLS tricks). --padding-size <range> 1300-1400 Size of the padding. --mixed-sni-case off Send the server name in mixed upper and lower case. --log, --log-level <level> warn trace, debug, info, warn, error, fatal or panic. --web-port <port> 6756 Clash API port written by build. run always uses 16756. --web-secret <secret> Clash API secret written by build.

Examples:

HiddifyCli run -c links.txt
HiddifyCli run -c https://example.com/sub/abc --in-proxy-port 1080 --log info
sudo HiddifyCli run -c links.txt --tun --dns-remote https://1.1.1.1/dns-query
HiddifyCli run -c links.txt --fragment --fragment-size 10-100 --fragment-sleep 50-200
HiddifyCli run -c sing-box.json --full-config
HiddifyCli -D /var/lib/hiddify-core run -c /etc/hiddify-core/config.json -d settings.json

docs.title: The Hiddify settings file
docs.text:
-d takes the settings of the Hiddify app as JSON. In the app, open Settings, tap the ⋮ menu and choose Export → "Export all options to file" ("Export anonymous options to file" leaves out private values). Settings missing from the file are not filled from the defaults, so start from an exported file. The main keys:

Key Meaning log-level Log level. enable-full-config Same as --full-config. mixed-port, tproxy-port, redirect-port, direct-port Local ports; enable-mixed-port and the like turn each on or off. enable-tun, enable-tun-service, set-system-proxy VPN and system proxy, as the flags. tun-implementation, mtu, strict-route, auto-redirect TUN stack and options. allow-connection-from-lan, lan-sharing-port, lan-sharing-password Share the connection with the local network. remote-dns-address, direct-dns-address, remote-dns-domain-strategy, direct-dns-domain-strategy, enable-fake-dns, independent-dns-cache DNS. ipv6-mode, bypass-lan, block-quic, resolve-destination, region, block-ads, route-rule Routing. connection-test-url, connection-test-urls, url-test-interval, ipinfo-url Proxy tests. balancer-strategy, default-proxy, keep-top, keep-tags Which proxy is used and how many run. tls-tricks enable-fragment, fragment-size, fragment-sleep, mixed-sni-case, enable-padding, padding-size. mux enable, padding, max-streams, protocol. warp, warp2 WARP settings. extra-security, unblocker, chain-status Chain a proxy through WARP, Psiphon or another profile. enable-clash-api, clash-api-port, web-secret Clash API.

docs.title: srun
docs.text:
HiddifyCli srun -c <file> [-c <file>…] [-C <folder>…]

Runs a complete sing-box config without changing it, like sing-box run. Every Hiddify addition to sing-box is available (features).

Flag Meaning -c, --config <path> A config file. Repeat it to merge several files; they are merged in the order of their paths. stdin reads the config from standard input. -C, --config-directory <dir> Read every .json file of a folder. Can be repeated.

Signals: SIGHUP checks the config and reloads it without stopping (a broken config is reported and the running one stays); SIGINT and SIGTERM stop it.

HiddifyCli srun -c config.json
HiddifyCli srun -c base.json -c outbounds.json
HiddifyCli srun -C /etc/hiddify-core/conf.d
HiddifyCli -D /var/lib/hiddify-core srun -c /etc/hiddify-core/server.json

docs.title: parse
docs.text:
HiddifyCli parse <file> [-o <file>] [--xray]

Reads a file in any format run understands and prints the proxies as sing-box JSON (outbounds and endpoints), then checks the result. Subscription links inside the file are fetched. Use it to see how a link is understood, or as the first step of a hand-made config.

Flag Meaning -o, --output <file> Write the result to a file (relative to -D) instead of the screen. --xray Convert share links to Xray JSON instead, with libxray. 
HiddifyCli parse links.txt
HiddifyCli parse clash.yaml -o outbounds.json
HiddifyCli parse links.txt --xray -o xray.json

docs.title: build
docs.text:
HiddifyCli build -c <sing-box json> [-d <settings>] [flags] [-o <file>]

Builds the full client config, the one run would start, from sing-box outbounds and the Hiddify settings, and prints it. The input must be sing-box JSON; convert other formats with parse first. It takes the flags of run and:

Flag Meaning -o, --output <file> Write the result to a file (relative to -D) instead of the screen. 
HiddifyCli parse links.txt -o outbounds.json
HiddifyCli build -c outbounds.json --tun -o config.json
HiddifyCli srun -c config.json

docs.title: instance
docs.text:
HiddifyCli instance -c <file> [flags]

Starts a small instance of the given proxies with a SOCKS5 port, pings Cloudflare through it a few times, prints the SOCKS address and waits for Ctrl+C. Useful to test a config quickly. Takes the flags of run.

docs.title: health
docs.text:
HiddifyCli health [target] [flags]

Checks connectivity to a target (default google.com), directly or through a SOCKS proxy. With none of --dns, --http, --quic, it tests HTTP.

Flag Default Meaning --proxy <url> direct Proxy to test through: socks://[user:pass@]host:port. --dns off Resolve the target. --http off Fetch the target over HTTP on TCP. --quic off Open a QUIC connection over UDP. --dns-server <addr> 1.1.1.1:53 DNS server: host:port, udp://host:port or tcp://host:port. --timeout <duration> 15s Time limit of each check. -v, --verbose Debug logs; -vv for more. 
HiddifyCli health --proxy socks://127.0.0.1:12334 --dns --http --quic cloudflare.com

docs.title: speedtest
docs.text:
HiddifyCli speedtest [flags]

Runs a speedtest.net test, directly or through a SOCKS proxy.

Flag Default Meaning --proxy <url> direct socks://[user:pass@]host:port, or just host:port. --distance <km> 2000 Distance of the test server to pick. --no-download off Skip the download test. --no-upload off Skip the upload test. --no-ping off Skip the ping test (and jitter). --no-jitter off Do not print jitter. -v, --verbose Debug logs; -vv for more. 
HiddifyCli speedtest --proxy 127.0.0.1:12334

docs.title: warp
docs.text:
HiddifyCli warp

Registers a new free Cloudflare WARP account and prints a sing-box WireGuard outbound for it. The Hiddify way to use WARP in a config is the warp endpoint, which registers by itself.

docs.title: vlessenc
docs.text:
HiddifyCli vlessenc [--json]

Makes a new key pair for VLESS encryption (mlkem768x25519plus): the decryption value for the server and the encryption value for the client. --json prints them as JSON.

docs.title: version
docs.text:
HiddifyCli version [-n]

Prints the hiddify-core and hiddify-sing-box versions, Go version, system, build tags, commit and whether CGO is on. -n, --name prints only the sing-box version name.

docs.title: admin_bgservice
docs.text:
HiddifyCli admin_bgservice <action> [argument]

Also called tunnel. The desktop app (Windows, macOS, Linux) runs VPN mode through a background service with administrator rights; this command manages it. You do not need it to run a config yourself.

Action Meaning install [owner] Install the service. On Linux the owning user can be given. uninstall Remove the service. start, stop Start or stop the service. run Run the service in the foreground. activate, deactivate Turn the service's VPN on (with IPv6, mixed port 12334) or force it off. connect <request.json> Ask the service to connect with a request file. disconnect Ask the service to disconnect. exit Ask the service to exit. build-id Print the build ID, which the app compares with the running service.

docs.title: grpcweb
docs.text:
HiddifyCli grpcweb [flags]

Starts a core and serves a small HTML page and the core's gRPC API on the same port, to start, stop and choose proxies from a browser. Open http://127.0.0.1:18088.

Flag Default Meaning --listen <addr> 0.0.0.0:18088 Address of the page and of the gRPC API. --workdir <dir> a temporary folder Working folder of the core. --config <path> Config path shown in the page. --mixed-port <port> 12334 Local proxy port of the core it starts. --connect off Start no core; control the one at --grpc. --grpc <addr> gRPC address of the core to control, with --connect.

docs.title: extension
docs.text:
HiddifyCli extension

Starts a test server for Hiddify extensions, so you can try an extension's interface in a browser at https://127.0.0.1:12346.

docs.title: ezytel
docs.text:
HiddifyCli ezytel <command> [flags]

Reads public Telegram channels through their web preview, as the app's channel viewer does.

Command Flags Meaning info --channel <id>, --last-read <post id>, --disable-inline-images, --json The channel's details, with the unread count after --last-read. messages --channel <id>, --before <post id>, --disable-inline-images, --html-only, --json The channel's messages as HTML, page by page. proxy-image --hex <url>, -o <file>, --json Download an image of a post. parse-channels --raw <text>, -f <file>, --json Read a list of channels, one per line. serve --listen <addr> (default 127.0.0.1:17079) Run the viewer's gRPC server.

All of them take --cache-dir <dir> (default: a folder in the system's temporary folder).

HiddifyCli ezytel messages --channel hiddify --html-only

docs.title: gen-cert
docs.text:
HiddifyCli gen-cert

Makes a server and a client certificate for the core's gRPC server in data/cert/ (server-cert.pem, server-key.pem, client-cert.pem, client-key.pem).

docs.title: Developer commands
docs.text:
These are for developing hiddify-core and may change:

  • gen <file>: build a config the way the app does and log it at debug level.
  • profile <url>: add a profile from a URL, as the app does, and print the result.
  • command: connect to a running core's gRPC API (127.0.0.1:17078) and print its status, outbounds and logs.

docs.title: Hiddify sing-box
docs.text: Features and fixes in the Hiddify fork that upstream sing-box does not have. Each feature page has an English and a Persian version.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
• TLS fragment: split the ClientHello into small pieces with pauses, so DPI cannot read the server name.
  • TLS tricks: a mixed-case server name and a padding extension in the ClientHello.
  • REALITY in Hiddify: the post-quantum key share, the key_share option, and fragmentation on REALITY.
  • PROXY protocol: inbounds read the PROXY protocol header and the direct outbound sends it.

docs.title: Protocols
docs.text:
• WARP: Cloudflare WARP over WireGuard, AmneziaWG or MASQUE, with free account registration, noise packets and an endpoint scanner that fails over per network.
  • WARP scanner and noise: how the endpoint scanner, the noise modes and presets (DNS, QUIC, SIP, random), the noise search and auto mode find a way through.
  • WARP over MASQUE: the standalone masque outbound for WARP over HTTP/3, HTTP/2 or both, with a device enrolled elsewhere; to register one, use the warp endpoint with mode masque; for a self-hosted MASQUE server, use upstream masque-client.
  • AmneziaWG: WireGuard with junk packets, padded handshakes and custom message types that defeat WireGuard fingerprinting.
  • WireGuard: Hiddify additions: noise packets before handshakes, per-peer user names, socket recovery and UDP fragmentation on by default.
  • WireGuard outbound (legacy format): the old WireGuard outbound that upstream removed, kept so old configs still load.
  • VLESS encryption: Xray's post-quantum VLESS encryption, with Vision over it even without TLS.
  • Sudoku: an encrypted TCP proxy that sends its bytes as sudoku clues, so traffic looks like text or has low randomness, with optional HTTP tunnels (build tag with_sudoku).
  • Mieru: a fully encrypted, padded proxy over TCP or UDP port ranges with no fixed pattern.
  • TrustTunnel: proxy traffic as HTTP CONNECT streams over HTTP/2 or HTTP/3.
  • SSH: an SSH server inbound for port forwarding, plus UDP over TCP and a background connection for the SSH outbound.
  • Psiphon: connect through the Psiphon network with no server of your own, and pick the exit country.
  • DNSTT: carry traffic inside DNS queries through public resolvers, which it finds by itself.
  • MasterDNS: the MasterDnsVPN tunnel over public resolvers, with a small header, packet duplication over several resolvers and MTU tests; the server connects to the destination itself.
  • Soar: Lantern's DNS tunnel, every resolver a path of its own with fast loss recovery and resolver discovery, through the smart pool by default; soar:// links.
  • GooseRelay: send traffic through Google Apps Script to your own server, so the network sees only HTTPS to Google.
  • Call tunnel: carry proxy traffic inside a video call on VK, Telemost, Dion, WB Stream or Bitrix24, so it looks like a call to an allowed domestic service; not tested end to end (build tag with_call).
  • Tunnel: a reverse tunnel that reaches machines behind NAT through a public server.
  • Bond: split each connection over several outbounds at once and join it on the server, to add up throttled connections (build tag with_bond).

docs.title: Transports
docs.text:
• XHTTP: Xray's XHTTP transport with its modes, padding, placements, XMUX and split download.
  • mKCP: Xray 26's mKCP over UDP for lossy or TCP-throttled networks, hidden by finalmask UDP masks (build tag with_kcp).
  • XDRIVE: Xray's storage transport, a VLESS connection carried in files on Google Drive, S3 or another storage service, so the client never contacts the server (build tag with_xdrive).
  • Raw transport: the raw transport, so configs converted from Xray load.
  • Custom gRPC paths: Xray-style multi-segment gRPC paths in service_name.
  • finalmask: Xray's finalmask masks (fragment, noise, header-custom, xdns over UDP, TCP or DoH, udphop, merge, oob and more) on every connection an outbound dials.
  • Shadowsocks simple-obfs server: a simple-obfs server on Shadowsocks inbounds, with a decoy when obfs or login fails.
  • rmux: one more multiplex protocol for many connections in one, next to smux, yamux and h2mux.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
• DNS group: ask several DNS servers at once, in turn, or stick to the one that works, and drop poisoned answers.
  • DNS rules: bypass_if_failed: when a DNS rule's server fails, the query goes on to the next matching rule.
  • Smart resolver pool: the resolver pool each DNS tunnel outbound runs for itself with smart_pool, shared by DNSTT, MasterDNS and Soar, with auto resolvers, saved scores and DoT/DoH.
  • DNSCrypt (SDNS stamps): the sdns server, which sends encrypted queries to a DNSCrypt resolver given by its stamp.
  • sslip.io names: the hosts server answers sslip.io names with the address written in the name.
  • IPv6 by outbound: IPv6 only through outbounds known to carry it, verified at the URL test and learned from the connections; a connection an outbound cannot carry is carried over IPv4 inside, so no app sees it die.

docs.title: Groups and monitoring
docs.text:
• Balancer: spread connections over members by round robin, lowest delay, consistent hashing, sticky sessions or a sticky pool.
  • Fallback: try members in order and skip one that failed for a while.
  • URL test: Hiddify additions: more test URLs, a failover mode, and a move to another member on the first failed connection.
  • Monitoring: background tests of every outbound for delay and exit IP, which feed the groups.
  • Unified delay: URL tests time one HTTP round trip on an open connection, so delays compare across protocols.

docs.title: For app developers
docs.text: • App considerations: what hiddify-app and hiddify-core need to change or know because of the v5 work.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text: • v5 bug fixes: bugs fixed on top of sing-box v1.15, newest first, each with its commit.

docs.title: App considerations
docs.text: What hiddify-app and hiddify-core need to change or know because of the v5 work in hiddify-sing-box. Each item says what changed in the core, and what the app or hiddify-core should do about it. Items marked Required break or misbehave until they are handled.

docs.title: Build
docs.text:
• Submodules. The core now uses six forks under replace/, each a git submodule on its own branch: wireguard-go (v5), sing-tun (dev), gvisor (go), amneziawg-go (v5), sing-mux (v5), plus the existing ones. go.mod and test/go.mod point at them with replace. Required: hiddify-core and every CI or gomobile build must check out submodules recursively (git submodule update --init --recursive), or the build fails on missing modules.
  • MasterDnsVPN fork. replace/MasterDnsVPN (module masterdnsvpn-go, fork github.com/hiddify/MasterDnsVPN, branch hiddify) is the client of the masterdns outbound, with a library API in lib/. Required: hiddify-core's go.mod (and ray2sing's) need replace masterdnsvpn-go => ./hiddify-sing-box/replace/MasterDnsVPN, like the other replace/ forks. No build tag.
  • Build tags. with_masque is now in the core Makefile and in hiddify-core's Makefile (hiddify-core commit 6bea470). Four new features are behind tags that are off by default: with_kcp (mKCP), with_sudoku (Sudoku), with_bond (Bond) and with_call (call tunnel). A config using one of them fails with "… is not included in this build" unless the tag is set. Decide per platform whether to ship them; with_call pulls in a large WebRTC stack. rmux needs no tag.
  • XDRIVE and the default tags. The core Makefile's default tags meant to include with_sudoku, with_call, with_bond and with_kcp but joined them with /, so none of the four was built; they are now separated by commas, and with_xdrive (the XDRIVE transport) is added. hiddify-core's PROTOCOL_TAGS has with_xdrive too. A profile with "transport": {"type": "xdrive"} fails with "XDRIVE is not included in this build" without it.
  • Go 1.27 required. Xray-core v26.10.31, which finalmask and XDRIVE use, needs Go 1.27, so go.mod and test/go.mod now say go 1.27. Every CI and gomobile build must use Go 1.27.3 or newer. (Binaries with Psiphon crashed at start when built with Go 1.27; fixed in bb18926a9.)
  • uTLS fork. github.com/metacubex/utls is replaced by github.com/Leadaxe/utls-lx in go.mod and test/go.mod. The firefox fingerprint is now Firefox 148 and safari is Safari 26.3; chrome stays Chrome 133. Nothing to change in configs.
  • Tailscale. The core Makefile no longer lists with_tailscale (573719dd5), so tailscale configs fail to load in the default build; keep the app from generating them, or build with the tag.

docs.title: Configuration the app generates
docs.text:
• Required — WARP by id and auth_token. A warp profile given by id and auth_token now needs private_key (the device's own key); without it the endpoint fails at start. Before, it started without a key and never worked.
  • Required — AmneziaWG on a wireguard endpoint. A wireguard endpoint with an awg block now fails to load ("use type awg"); before, the block was ignored and the connection was plain WireGuard. Generate "type": "awg" for AmneziaWG, or a warp endpoint with an awg block.
  • Required — sdns stamps. The sdns server accepts only DNSCrypt stamps, and now refuses a DoH, DoT or plain stamp when the config loads. Convert those stamps to https, tls or udp servers.
  • SSH and UDP. The SSH outbound offers UDP only with udp_over_tcp; without it, UDP goes to another outbound. Set udp_over_tcp if UDP should go through SSH. On the SSH inbound, host_key_algorithms and network now take effect.
  • XHTTP mode. An empty or auto mode now behaves as Xray's client: stream-one over REALITY, stream-up over REALITY with a separate download, packet-up otherwise. Before, the client always used packet-up, and an empty mode was an error. Configs that relied on packet-up over REALITY should set it explicitly.
  • tls_fragment in the tls block. The core now moves a tls_fragment written inside an outbound's tls block to the dialer (unless the dialer has its own). hiddify-core's config patching that does the same can stay or be removed.
  • REALITY and fragmentation. tls.fragment and tls.record_fragment now work with REALITY. hiddify-core skips fragmentation for REALITY nodes; that skip can be removed. The new tls.reality.key_share ("", hybrid, classical) is available; classical is refused by Xray 26.9.8 and newer servers.
  • TLS tricks. tls.tls_tricks (mixed-case SNI, padding extension) now works for uTLS clients; padding with a random fingerprint is a config error.
  • Balancer. delay_acceptable_ratio now defaults to 2 when unset or 0 (the app sends 2 already). With interrupt_exist_connections, the hashing strategies interrupt only when the set of usable members changes, not on every test round.
  • Balancer connections are stable. lowest-delay now honours tolerance (50 ms when unset; hiddify-core sends 20, with tolerance_ratio 0.3, so the rule is mostly relative) and tolerance_ratio (a tenth of the selected member's delay when unset), and keeps its member until one is faster by more than the larger of the two or it fails a test. Connections are closed only for a member that died (its own connections) and once, 30 seconds after start, for the members the first tests left out. A faster member takes new connections only, so interrupt_exist_connections: true no longer cuts calls or downloads on every test round. The balancer starts from the cached results, and the first cycle tests the cached fastest member first.
  • Balancer pool strategy. strategy: "pool" with pool and sticky_hash gives a fixed set of slots with sticky keys that do not move when another member dies (lx's round_robin). tolerance and tolerance_ratio let a faster member outside take a slot, as for lowest-delay; unset, the first working members keep their slots, so hiddify-core sends them to the lowest-delay group only. sticky_hash is sticky-sessions' key too.
  • URL test failover. A failover member that is more than 2 times slower than the fastest other one, twice in a row, is now left for one more than 1.5 times faster.
  • A tapped or selected proxy answers at once. The outbound a group's selection leads to is tested before the first cycle and again when the selection moves; a test asked for runs at once beside the cycle, in stages (experimental.monitoring.on_demand_timeouts, 1 s, 3 s, 10 s by default): the app sees the proxy as unavailable after the first mark with no answer, then the answer, however late. A proxy is pinged once; only a failed attempt is tried again, at the next mark. A tap while the proxy is being tested joins that test instead of a second ping, and a selection measured in the last 15 s is not tested again. A ping cached from the previous run decides nothing and is not shown: it orders the members until the real pings arrive, and the app's proxy list sorts by sort_delay, which carries it, while url_test_delay stays 0 for it. hiddify-core sets the lowest-delay groups' tolerance to 20 ms and tolerance_ratio to 0.3: an absolute 100 ms kept a 59 ms member over a 25 ms one. The MONITORING and LOWEST log lines say why each test ran and what the group decided. hiddify-core keeps a profile's proxy tags stable across its updates (an unchanged proxy keeps the tag it had, whatever its new position in the list), so a hot reload after a subscription update keeps the unchanged proxies and their pings and tests only what changed; keep top keeps its pick while every kept proxy is unchanged and none timed out. A proxy that worked in this run skips the first mark: it keeps its ping through a slow answer rather than flicker to unavailable after one second. The delay is published before the IP lookup, so the IP arrives after the ping. Nothing to set; the core's defaults are these.
  • IPv6 for the apps is off by default, and verified per proxy when on. hiddify-core answers the apps with ipv4_only DNS rules and rejects every IPv6 destination before the sniff rule (so before the handshake) unless the IPv6 mode turns IPv6 on; the app's routing page says why (most exits have no IPv6, and a connection the proxy cannot carry dies after it opened, which browsers never retry). When on, the core sets verify_ipv6 (each proxy's URL test is followed once per run by the same URL over IPv6, cached per proxy), route.ipv6_fallback (an IPv6 connection through a proxy not known yet is carried over IPv4 inside the connection and teaches the proxy's IPv6), ipv6_by_outbound on the DNS rules answering the apps and an ipv6_unavailable_via reject rule on the main selector, both fail-open. A subscription turns IPv6 on for its profile with an ipv6-mode: prefer_ipv4 header (the app's override list), and a share link declares its proxy with ipv6=1 or ipv6=0 (ray2sing, ipv6_declared). No probe of a public address is made (ipv6_probe is retired): the verification uses the user's own test URL. See IPv6 by outbound.
  • MasterDNS outbound. "type": "masterdns" (display name MasterDNS) is a new outbound type for MasterDnsVPN servers: domains, resolvers, encryption, key, mode and tuning fields, see MasterDNS. TCP only; in socks5 mode it needs no outbound behind it, in tcp mode the app chains a socks or ssh outbound with detour as for DNSTT. Its status is CONNECTING until the resolvers are tested and the session is open, which can take several seconds; the app should show that rather than an error. ray2sing reads masterdns:// links, slipnet:// links (SlipNet profiles for DNSTT, NoizDNS and VayDNS) as dnstt outbounds with a socks or ssh outbound in front, and dnst:// links (the dnst URL spec, github.com/net2share/dnst-url-spec) for the dnstt, vaydns and masterdns transports.
  • Soar outbound. "type": "soar" (display name Soar) is a new outbound type for Soar servers (github.com/getlantern/soar): domain, public_key, resolvers and tuning fields, see Soar. TCP only, no outbound behind it. The resolvers written go through its smart pool, on by default; auto or no resolvers runs Soar's own discovery. The session opens at the first connection, so the status is CONNECTING until then. ray2sing reads soar:// links: WhiteDNS's profile link (base64url JSON, schema whitedns.profile) and a URL form. The JSON editor offers a soar template.
  • Links turn the masterdns smart pool on. ray2sing gives a masterdns:// or dnst:// masterdns outbound smart_pool unless the link says smart_pool=0 or lists an address range, and a link without resolvers gets auto. It also reads WhiteDNS's masterdns:// profile link.
  • Shared resolver discovery. smart_pool.discovery (country, sample_ranges, want, concurrency, pace) is the same block for dnstt, masterdns and soar: their auto starts with the candidates of Soar's discovery (device resolvers, the country's bundled list, global resolvers), then the built-in list. hiddify-core fills discovery.country from the app's region when it is empty. Links take country, sample_ranges, discovery_want, discovery_concurrency and discovery_pace.
  • Soar fork. replace/soar (module github.com/getlantern/soar, to be forked as github.com/hiddify/soar, branch hiddify) adds Discovery.List(), so the pool takes Soar's discovery candidates from Soar's own code. hiddify-core's go.mod needs replace github.com/getlantern/soar => ./hiddify-sing-box/replace/soar, like the other forks.
  • Smart resolver pool, per outbound. dnstt, masterdns and soar take smart_pool, true or an object (load_balance, deadline, per_attempt, probe_interval, down_after); the resolver list, scores, probe and pool of every DNS tunnel are one shared package, common/dnspool, and each outbound runs its own pool. With it, auto, DoT and DoH resolvers work for both tunnels. See Smart resolver pool. Required: the smart_dns_pool service is removed; a config with it fails to load. Set smart_pool on the outbound instead.
  • New options worth exposing:
  • DNS group: mode stable and fastest, error_ttl, win_ttl.
  • URL test: urls (more test URLs) and mode: "failover".
  • WARP: scanner (endpoint scanner with per-network scores) with search_noise (it also looks for a noise preset that gets through, see the WARP page) and noise_presets; noise.fake_packet.mode "quic" and "raw", noise.fake_packet.packets (AmneziaWG-style templates, for the "WG Mimic" DNS, QUIC and SIP configs); the awg block with AmneziaWG 3.x settings and the QUIC masquerade (ip, id, ib).
  • MASQUE: vhttp (h3, h2, auto), server_name, scanner, mtu, unique_identifier.
  • AmneziaWG: 3.x settings (header_protection_key, content_padding_addition, the timers, random_trailers, disable_cookies), s3/s4 and h1–h4 ranges now work.
  • Multiplex: protocol: "rmux".
  • New types (build-tagged): mkcp transport, sudoku, bond, call; new fallback group.
  • WARP mode. A warp endpoint takes mode: wg, awg, masque or auto. auto races one handshake per tunnel and runs the fastest; it needs with_masque for the MASQUE leg. The app can offer auto as the default WARP choice. Its display type is WARP · Auto until it chose, then the chosen tunnel's.
  • WARP behind a detour. Searching for a way in through a detour only measures the detour, so for every warp endpoint with a detour (the extra security hop, WARP in WARP) hiddify-core sets rotate_ports: false, turns the scanner off and gives an IPv6 WARP address as fallback_address: the endpoint tries the profile's IPv4 address, then that IPv6 one. It also turns off the scanner of a masque outbound with a detour. MTU discovery is on for every WireGuard and AmneziaWG tunnel; a config can turn it off with "mtu_discovery": false.
  • WARP devices are kept, in a pool. Registered devices are kept in one pool in the cache file (key warp-profiles), shared by every warp endpoint; each endpoint leases devices of its own, so several warp endpoints in one config never share one. A device is only replaced when Cloudflare says it is gone, disabled or out of quota, not when the network blocks it. Keep store_warp_config on, and a stable unique_identifier per endpoint (it takes its own device back first), or every start registers again (and Cloudflare limits registrations).
  • Status in OutboundInfo. OutboundInfo.status (field 18, enum Status: READY, CONNECTING, RECONNECTING, SEARCHING, FAILED, REGISTERING) mirrors adapter.Status, so the app can show the state without parsing the label (in hiddify-core, uncommitted at the time of writing).
  • IP information from the cache. At start every outbound shows the exit IP and country of the last run, from the cache, until a working test of this run looks them up again (a failed test leaves them as they are). The exit IP of WARP, Psiphon or a rotating proxy can change between runs, so URLTestHistory.IpInfoFromCache says which they are, and hiddify-core sends it as IpInfo.from_cache. Show such an IP as not confirmed yet (dimmed, or with a mark).
  • Core STARTED and a single proxy. hiddify-core moves WAITING → STARTED from the ping of the lowest (lowest-delay) balancer when the profile has 2+ proxies. With only one proxy, lowest is not built; connectivity then uses that proxy's own ping (the select leaf) so the core does not stay WAITING ("Connecting") forever.
  • MASQUE devices from links. The masque outbound never registers a WARP device: it needs device, and a config without one fails to load ("use the warp endpoint with mode masque"). A device needs no endpoint_public_key: the edge's fixed key is built in. The port of an endpoint written as ip:port is used. A masque:// link to WARP (an endpoint in WARP's ranges or under cloudflareclient.com, or Cloudflare's server name, or none) is a warp endpoint with mode masque (ray2sing): the link's key goes to masque.device, and a link without a key gets a saved or registered device from the WARP pool. When Cloudflare refuses masque.device, WARP remembers it in the cache file (<unique_identifier>/refused-masque-device) and takes a pool device, so the cache file matters for such configs too. ray2sing sets unique_identifier from the link's device id, else a hash of its key or endpoints, so renaming the profile keeps its devices. Only a link to another MASQUE server stays a masque outbound, and needs its key.
  • WARP over MASQUE in the warp endpoint. A warp endpoint can now run MASQUE instead of WireGuard: "masque": {"enabled": true}, or any MASQUE setting (vhttp, server_name, use_ipv6, tls, …). Prefer this to a separate masque outbound: one endpoint handles registration, the scanner and failover for all three tunnels. An empty "masque": {} is dropped by the config parser and gives WireGuard, so always write enabled or a setting. awg and masque together fail the config. MASQUE needs the with_masque tag. The MASQUE device is saved apart from the WireGuard one (<unique_identifier>/masque), so switching an endpoint between the two does not break either.
  • Enrolled MASQUE devices (device). A masque outbound can use a device enrolled elsewhere, as masque:// share links carry it, instead of registering one through Cloudflare's API (often blocked). ray2sing writes masque:// links to this option, and their inner= link as a second outbound whose detour is the first.
  • Self-hosted MASQUE. Use upstream's masque-client (and masque-server). The Hiddify masque type is WARP only.
  • Display types. WARP shows WARP · WG, WARP · AWG or WARP · MASQUE; the masque outbound shows WARP · MASQUE. After them comes the endpoint the scanner chose (· 🔍 <address:port>, or · 🔍 Not found). If the app maps display types to icons or labels, match on the prefix.
  • Status, for every outbound and endpoint. IsReady() bool is replaced by Status() adapter.Status: StatusReady, StatusConnecting, StatusReconnecting, StatusSearching, StatusFailed and StatusRegistering; adapter.IsReady(o) is the yes/no. adapter.DisplayType(o) is the type and what the status cannot say, nothing more: the resolvers a DNS tunnel uses (MasterDNS · 3 resolvers), the endpoint the WARP scanner chose. It has no status mark (no ⏳ Connecting..., no ✔️): hiddify-core sends the status on its own (OutboundInfo.status) and the app shows it. A failed outbound adds why it failed, adapter.StatusError(o): Invalid: bad uuid, WARP · WG: <error>. While it is only connecting, the error of its last attempt goes to OutboundInfo.error and not to the type (SSH's last connection error, for example). The app's typeWithoutStatus still strips the marks an older core sends.
  • WARP registration fallback. When registration through profile.detour fails, WARP (all three tunnels) tries again through every other outbound, direct included. That was already so for WireGuard and is kept; it lets a cold detour group not block registration, but it means Cloudflare's API can be reached outside the detour. If the app must never do that, it should not rely on profile.detour alone, or ask for an option to turn the fallback off. The masque outbound only uses its profile.detour.
  • MASQUE profile key. The saved MASQUE profile is still keyed by the tag unless unique_identifier is set. If the app renames outbounds, set unique_identifier so the device is not registered again.
  • Schema. docs/schema.json is generated again (make schema) and now covers the Hiddify options. Editors or validators that use it should take the new file.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: • MPTCP is off unless asked. Inbounds and outbounds use Multipath TCP only with tcp_multi_path: true; the Go default (on, for listeners, since Go 1.24) is overridden in the code and by godebug multipathtcp=0 in go.mod. A main module that builds sing-box into its own binary needs the same godebug line in its go.mod, as hiddify-core has, or -X runtime.godebugDefault=multipathtcp=0 in its link flags; internal/godebug.defaultGODEBUG is not a symbol and does nothing. Keep inbounds on 127.0.0.1 unless the LAN really needs them, and keep the Linux kernel updated.

docs.title: Network changes and caches
docs.text:
• Network change callbacks. WARP and MASQUE now react to network changes: they check the current endpoint and only rescan when it fails, and they name the network by asking cloudflare.com/cdn-cgi/trace (or speedtest.net), not by SSID, so no location permission is needed. The DNS group clears its record of failed servers. All of this relies on the platform reporting interface changes as it does today; keep that working.
  • Cache file. Scanner scores, the WARP config and the MASQUE profile are kept in the cache file. Keep experimental.cache_file enabled, with store_warp_config and store_masque_config where wanted; without the cache file, every start registers a new WARP/MASQUE device and scans from scratch.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text: • Crash, OOM and power reports are not encrypted. The encrypt request is accepted and ignored, and archives are always named .zip (no more .age). Instead the archive leaves out the configuration and the list of open connections, and scrubs logs and other text of IP addresses, proxy links and DNS stamps, URL paths and queries, UUIDs, emails and key=value secrets. The app's "include configuration" option no longer adds the configuration. The app should stop showing an "encrypted" state for reports.

docs.title: Behaviour the app should know about
docs.text:
• finalmask follows Xray v26.10. xdns takes domains as {"names": [...]} and resolvers as {"addrs": [...]}, with DoH resolvers (https://… plus tlsConfig); the older string forms still load. New masks: udphop, noise type: "exp" and script. Masks are now dialed through: xdns and udphop open their own sockets with the outbound's dialer. Links carry finalmask as JSON (fm=), which ray2sing passes through unchanged, so nothing to change in link parsing for the new masks.

  • XDRIVE. The xdrive transport needs VLESS with encryption for an Xray server. The outbound's server and server_port are required but unused; the app may show them as meaningless for such a profile. Each proxy connection is its own storage session, since the client has no Mux.Cool: a profile on Google Drive is slow and spends API quota, so a URL test every few minutes costs a session each time.

  • URL test. A dial that fails because the path is dead moves the group to another member immediately, without closing live connections, so the selected member can change between tests. failover keeps a member until it fails. A URL test or balancer that moves now signals monitoring at once, as a selector does, so the proxy list stream updates without waiting for the next test.

  • WARP behind a group. WARP (and the masque outbound) moves at once when the user changes a selector in its detour, but follows a URL test or balancer at most every 30 seconds, through a new tunnel that replaces the old one only once it connects. hiddify-core's chain mode selectable relies on this: in Extra Security its WARP hops dial through select, and the user can move both select and the hop selector on the fly. The app offers selectable as a mode of both hops; the proxy list then has a selectable group named after the hop (🔒 Extra Security · Selectable or 🔓 Unblocker · Selectable; its tag ends in §hide§ like every chain hop, so do not hide it) whose items are Lowest → <hop> (the default, a lowest-delay balancer) and each WARP tunnel and Psiphon, moved with SelectOutbound.
  • Why a proxy failed. The URL test history keeps the error of a failed test (Error), and an outbound that is not ready says why through adapter.StatusError (WARP and MASQUE: a refused registration, a tunnel that does not connect, with the tunnel's last connect error). hiddify-core passes either to the app as OutboundInfo.error, for the proxy's details. A result loaded from the cache keeps its error only until the next test. See Monitoring.
  • Fake DNS rule. The DNS rules hiddify-core generates set strategy, which keeps sing-box in legacy DNS mode. A query_type (or ip_version) matcher in any DNS rule then makes the router refuse to start, with "Legacy strategy DNS rule action option is deprecated", and the app stays on Connecting. The fake IP rule therefore matches every query with bypass_if_failed; queries other than A and AAAA fail at the fake IP server, at debug level only, and go on to the remote rule. See bypass_if_failed.
  • DNS predefined answers. In legacy DNS mode, A/AAAA records in 10.0.0.0/8 and 2001:4188:2:600::/64 are removed from predefined answers (dns/blocked_checker.go). This is deliberate and tested, but a predefined answer in those ranges returns nothing; keep it in mind when generating predefined rules.
  • Rule sets. A remote rule set without a cached copy starts empty and is downloaded once the service is up; a failed download is retried after 1 s, 10 s, 30 s, 1 min, 5 min, 10 min, then every 30 min. Rules that depend on it apply only once it arrives.
  • Reverse tunnel. tunnel_server / tunnel_client now carry traffic: route rules must set override_tunnel_destination on the server.

docs.title: Call tunnel (if shipped)
docs.text:
• The call link is the tunnel's only key: anyone with it can read the tunnel or use the server as a proxy. Treat join links as secrets in the UI, in shared configs and in logs. The server logs the link of a call it creates, which is how the user learns it.
  • Account cookies and the Dion password are stored in the config in plain text; store configs that contain them with the same care as other credentials.
  • Only the server side (inbound) needs an account; the client joins as a guest. Bitrix24 has no server side in this build.
  • Not tested end to end in Hiddify.

docs.title: Deferred, needs the app
docs.text: • Android auto-redirect rework (from reF1nd 74f12fb8) is not ported: it changes the gomobile PlatformInterface, so it needs matching changes in hiddify-app's Android code.

docs.title: Repositories
docs.text: All forks have GitHub repos under github.com/hiddify/ (sing-tun, gvisor, wireguard-go, amneziawg-go, sing-mux, and the older ones). Nothing has been pushed yet: push each fork's branch before pushing hiddify-sing-box, or the submodule commits cannot be fetched.

docs.title: Bug fixes
docs.text: Choose a page from the menu, or see the list of every feature.

docs.title: Bug fixes in Hiddify sing-box v5
docs.text:
Bugs fixed in the Hiddify fork on top of sing-box v1.15. The newest fix is at the top. Each entry names the commit that fixes it.

All Hiddify features

docs.title: A proxy was pinged several times at once, and lowest-delay moved to a slower one
docs.text:
Commit: 635d533ac

What happened: a tap on a proxy, or a group moving its selection to it, started a test while the cycle's test of it was running, and a staged test started a second and a third attempt beside a slow first one: the proxy was pinged two or three times, and whichever test ended last wrote the result, so a late failure replaced a fresh answer and the groups left the member. After a start or a hot reload, when every result is cached, the first member to answer took the lowest-delay selection at 91 ms over a 17 ms one still being tested, and lost it a moment later; each move tested the new pick again, seconds after it was measured, and under load that second ping read 2549 ms for a 59 ms member. A member chosen while the fast one did not answer was held for the whole cycle, long after the fast one answered again. hiddify-core sent an absolute tolerance of 100 ms, which kept a 59 ms member over a 25 ms one.

Fix: one URL test per outbound at a time: a test asked for while one runs joins it and takes its result. A staged test retries only a failed attempt, at the next mark, and skips the first mark for an outbound that worked in this run. Lowest-delay holds during a cycle only until the cycle has tested the member in use. A selection measured in the last 15 s is not tested again. The MONITORING and LOWEST log lines say why every test runs and what the group decides. hiddify-core sends a tolerance of 20 ms with a ratio of 0.3, and keeps a profile's proxy tags stable across its updates, so a hot reload keeps the unchanged proxies and their pings. Then (a85a71b1a): the first cycle's results arrive one by one and the selection still hopped at each faster one, 439 ms to 170 to 112 to 41 to 18 in forty seconds. A member that took the selection with a real ping stays for 30 s while it answers, then the best known takes it. A ping cached from the previous run decides nothing and is not shown: it only orders the members until the real pings arrive, and the app's list sorts by it (sort_delay) without showing it.

docs.title: With a large subscription, the pings changed every few seconds
docs.text:
Commit: 635d533ac

What happened: with a free subscription of a hundred or more configs, the ping the app showed changed every few seconds, up and down (29, 44, 33 ms). Three things tested the same proxies again and again. A round robin balancer told monitoring of a new selection whenever the members it rotates through changed, which is almost every result of a cycle, and each telling tested its parents (the Extra Security hop) and its next pick. A member that started working retested everything measured through each group it is in, the hop behind the selector too, whether the group used it or not. And each regular cycle moved the selection result by result. In the first minutes on an unstable network, the home screen said the selected proxy was not responding while others worked: lowest-delay stayed on the member it had cached from the last run, since a staged test's miss was hidden from the groups behind the last confirmed result, which for that member was the cached one, and was even marked as fresh.

Fix: only a balancer that sends every connection through one member (lowest-delay) tells monitoring of a new selection. A member that starts working retests what goes through a group only when the group uses it. During a regular cycle of the schedule, lowest-delay and round robin keep the members they use while these answer, and choose with all the results when it ends (monitoring tells every group); the first cycle and one after a network change take results as they come. A miss of a member with no result of this run but the cached one is seen by the groups, so lowest-delay leaves it for a member that answers. The app shows a round robin group by a member that another replaces only when faster by more than the lowest-delay tolerance. On the Android emulator with a 160-config subscription and Extra Security, the hop's priority tests in three minutes went from 65 to 0, and the ping shown stayed the same after the first seconds.

docs.title: WARP crashed the packet tunnel when it restarted during a network change
docs.text:
Commit: 00f7b6e63

What happened: after a network change, a WARP endpoint with the scanner checks its endpoint in the background, and scans for another when it does not answer. When WARP restarted meanwhile (a refused device, a change of tunnel), the restart cleared the endpoint's scanner state while the check of the start that ended still ran. The scan read that state again to save its scores and hit a nil pointer, which ended the whole process: on iOS, the packet tunnel. The first scan at connect did the same, its probe reading the state again (h_failover.go:258 in 5.5.1): on Windows, right after connecting on a filtered network, when a refused registration restarted WARP ("register WARP masque device: context canceled").

Fix: a check reads the scanner state of its start once and works on it to the end; the scan, the probes, the noise candidates and the scores take it from the check instead of reading the endpoint again, and the state is read and written under the endpoint's lock. A test clears the state in the middle of a scan, as a restart does; it crashed before the fix.

docs.title: A DNS rule with bypass_if_failed logged an error for every query it passed on
docs.text:
Commit: b1ec924c5

What happened: when the server of a rule with bypass_if_failed failed, the next rule answered the query, but the failure was still logged at error level. hiddify-core's Fake DNS rule uses bypass_if_failed to pass every query other than A and AAAA (HTTPS, TXT, ...) from the fake IP server to the remote rule, so a browser filled the log with "only IP queries are supported by fakeip" errors.

Fix: a failure that the next rule takes over is logged at debug level. A failure with no bypass is still an error. Two tests check both cases.

docs.title: A masterdns outbound used one of several resolvers on the same IP
docs.text:
Commit: 0e8ed7f69

What happened: with smart_pool off, the outbound gives its resolvers to the MasterDnsVPN client, whose library entry point kept one resolver per IP. Resolvers on one IP with different ports (127.0.0.1:5301, 127.0.0.1:5302, or a server answering on more than one port) became a single resolver, so the client's balancer and packet duplication had nothing to spread over.

Fix: MasterDnsVPN (the Hiddify fork, 62e94f1) keeps each IP and port as a resolver of its own; the resolver file loader keeps its old behaviour. A test checks one IP with three ports.

docs.title: The default build left out mKCP, Sudoku, Bond and the call tunnel
docs.text:
Commit: 1c6b0ec6f

What happened: the Makefile's default tags were meant to add with_sudoku, with_call, with_bond and with_kcp, but they were joined with / instead of ,. Go read the four as one unknown tag, so make builds and the test runs that use the Makefile tags had none of them, and a profile with mKCP failed with "mKCP is not included in this build".

Fix: the tags are separated by commas. The full test suite passes with them on.

docs.title: Links with Xray's merge mask, dialMode or hellochrome_120 were dropped or failed
docs.text:
Commit: 502f16cfa

What happened: patterniha's Xray-core links (and the subscriptions built from them) use three things this fork did not know. A finalmask merge mask made the whole link fail to load, so the link was left out of the profile. dialMode=oob.0 was ignored. Xray's versioned fingerprint names such as fp=hellochrome_120 failed the outbound with "unknown uTLS fingerprint".

Fix: finalmask has the merge mask and an oob mask, Xray's oob. dialMode, which sends the first writes with an extra byte as TCP urgent data (ported from patterniha/Xray-core, MPL 2.0). uTLS takes every fingerprint name of Xray's lists, in any case, after sing-box's own names.

docs.title: Monitoring: proxies stayed "waiting" after a hot reload, and stopped being tested when idle
docs.text:
Commit: pending

What happened: Three things kept rows of the proxies page on the waiting animation for good. A hot reload (a profile update, a changed setting) replaces the outbounds whose options changed; each replaced one started over with no result, and Reload could only start a test cycle when none was running. In a profile of hundreds of proxies a cycle runs for minutes, so the replaced ones waited for the next interval tick. The ticks themselves stop once the core has routed nothing for the idle time (three intervals, 30 minutes with Hiddify's defaults), and the app watching the list did not count as activity, so with little traffic nothing was tested again at all; a tap on a row still tested that one row, which made it look as if only the clicked proxy got a ping. And the Touch that restarts the stopped workers left the old activity time in place, so the next tick stopped them again.

Fix: A replaced outbound keeps its last result as a cached one, due for a test, the way a result loaded at start is: the groups can fall back on it and the app shows it as waiting. A reload then tests the outbounds it created or replaced, and only those, at once and whether or not a cycle is running; the others keep their result until their regular time. Restarting the workers counts as activity. hiddify-core touches the monitoring while the app's proxies stream is open.

docs.title: IPv6 by outbound: IPv6-first sites still died through a proxy without IPv6
docs.text:
Commit: d992de248

What happened: The IPv6 probe that 5.4.0 added opened a connection to a public resolver's IPv6 address through the outbound and took an open connection as IPv6 carried. A VLESS, Trojan, VMess or Shadowsocks dial returns before the proxy's server has connected anywhere, so the probe said yes for every such proxy, AAAA answers went out, Chrome, Samsung Internet and the YouTube app reached Google over IPv6, the proxy closed the connection and the page showed ERR_CONNECTION_CLOSED, while Telegram and Instagram, on IPv4, worked (hiddify-app 5.3 and 5.4 on Android 16 and 17, #2420). The probe was also traffic of its own to Google and Cloudflare addresses, which a filtered exit breaks, and a reset after the proxy's attempt would not have helped: an app falls back to IPv4 only when the connect itself fails, and through a TUN the connect succeeds locally before the proxy has tried anything.

Fix: The probe is gone (ipv6_probe is retired). An outbound's IPv6 is verified at its URL test, with the user's own test URL fetched once more over the host's IPv6 address (verify_ipv6), once per run and cached per outbound; a share link may declare it (ipv6=1, ipv6=0, ipv6_declared); and a TCP connection to an IPv6 address through an outbound not known yet is watched by the router (route.ipv6_fallback): when the outbound gives nothing, the same outbound is dialed with the sniffed domain, the app's bytes are said again and the connection goes on, the app seeing no failure, and the outcome teaches the outbound's IPv6. ipv6_by_outbound and ipv6_unavailable_via are fail-open again: an outbound not known yet is let through, and one known to have no IPv6 gets no AAAA answers and has its IPv6 connections refused before the handshake. hiddify-core turns IPv6 for the apps off by default and all of this on when the IPv6 mode turns it on. See IPv6 by outbound.

docs.title: Naive: App Review rejected macOS builds for a non-public API
docs.text:
Commit: pending

What happened: App Review rejected the macOS app because hiddify-core.dylib and the packet tunnel referenced _kCFBundleNumericVersionKey, which Apple counts as a non-public API. The reference comes from Chromium's base::mac::OuterBundleCachedInfoPlistData() (info_plist_data.o) in the macOS libcronet.a that with_naive_outbound links. The iOS and tvOS libraries do not have it.

Fix: protocol/naive/h_cronet_info_plist_darwin.go defines that function itself, returning empty data, so the linker no longer takes info_plist_data.o from the archive. Only Chromium's multi-process code (Mach port rendezvous, child-process code signature checks) calls it, and Cronet runs inside the process, so naive works as before.

docs.title: MASQUE: masque:// links from MahsaNG failed to load
docs.text:
Commit: pending

What happened: MahsaNG writes the device's key before the @ and the endpoint, with its port, after it, and leaves the endpoint's key out. ray2sing only read a key parameter, so the device had no key and the config failed with "private_key is not an ECDSA key"; and even with the key, a device without endpoint_public_key was refused, and a port other than 443 was dropped.

Fix: ray2sing reads that shape of link (key, endpoint and port, address, mtu, keepalive, transport, sni, insecure, pin, ech, packets). The device's endpoint_public_key defaults to the key of the fixed certificate Cloudflare's MASQUE edge presents on every endpoint, the port of an endpoint written as ip:port is used, and tls.certificate_public_key_sha256 pins the endpoint by the hash of its key, as the links do. A link to WARP is a WARP config: when Cloudflare refuses the link's device (its key was never enrolled, or the device was deleted), the outbound registers a device as the profile does, saves it as the replacement and runs the tunnel with it.

docs.title: DNS and routing: IPv6-first sites failed through a proxy without IPv6
docs.text:
Commit: bc0447ad8

What happened: Sites that publish AAAA records (Google, YouTube, most big CDNs) were reached over IPv6 whenever the device had it, through a proxy whose exit has no IPv6. The connection died on the server side, the browser never fell back in time, and the site did not open, while IPv4-only sites through the same proxy worked. Routing IPv6 away was no answer: traffic that is not routed leaks past the proxy.

Fix: Monitoring probes each outbound and endpoint, on its own, for IPv6 reachability and keeps the answer in its URL-test history. A DNS rule with ipv6_by_outbound hands out no AAAA answers while that outbound lacks IPv6, and a route rule with ipv6_unavailable_via matches the IPv6 destinations that would die there so they can be rejected at once. One proxy can carry IPv6 while the next one does not; a proxy that gains IPv6 is used for it on the next run. See IPv6 by outbound.

docs.title: DNS: a hanging server in a sequential group failed every query
docs.text:
Commit: 900d60c40

What happened: A sequential group walked its servers from the first on every query and gave each one the rest of the query's time. A first server whose port the proxy's exit dropped hung for the whole DNS timeout, the query failed, and the servers behind it were never asked. With hiddify-core's remote group, where the chosen TCP server comes first, configs through such a proxy never resolved a name, while the same configs worked with a plain UDP address.

Fix: A server that fails is asked after the others for error_ttl, still asked when they all fail, and forgotten when the network changes. Each server is waited for at most member_timeout, or, unset, the query's time left shared among the servers still to ask, at least 2 s each.

docs.title: Monitoring: the selected proxy's ping arrived late
docs.text:
Commit: f7d6695cb

What happened: The first test cycle took the members fastest-first by last run's result, so the proxy the user had selected waited behind every member sorted before it. Moving a selector to another member tested only the outbounds routed through the selector, never the new selection, so its ping waited for the next cycle. A test asked for (a tap, a selection) went through the worker pool, behind a cycle of timeouts that holds every workers for up to url_test_timeout each; its delay was stored only after the IP lookup that follows the URL test, which takes as long again; and a proxy that did not answer showed nothing until the whole timeout had passed.

Fix: Before the first cycle, the outbound each group's selection leads to (a selector's pick, a balancer's member, through nested groups) is tested ahead of everything else, and a selection change tests the new selection with priority. A test asked for runs at once, beside the cycle's tests, in stages (on_demand_timeouts, 1 s, 3 s and 10 s unless set): the proxy shows as unavailable for now at the first mark with no answer, or as soon as the first attempt fails, and the first answer from any attempt replaces it at once, however late. Groups keep the last confirmed result through such a miss. The delay is published as soon as the URL test answers, the IP information when its lookup is done, and a priority result reaches the groups' subscribers past debounce_window.

docs.title: Monitoring: after a while nothing was tested any more
docs.text:
Commit: f7d6695cb

What happened: A URL test dials the outbound with a deadline in its context. An outbound whose dial ignores that deadline, as a dial into a native library may (cronet's naive dial, by the logs), never returned, so its worker waited for good, and so did the cycle waiting for that result. A few such tests, and every worker was held: no cycle, no priority test, no ping for any outbound, until the core was restarted.

Fix: A worker waits for one test at most twice its deadline plus url_test_timeout and two seconds: the URL test, the IP lookup and one more test after a network reset, each with its own deadline. Past that the test counts as failed, its late result is dropped if it ever comes, and the worker goes on to the next test.

docs.title: Security: every inbound listened on MPTCP
docs.text:
Commit: 9aca6c8c1

What happened: Go 1.24 and newer listen on Multipath TCP by default on Linux, and the Linux kernel let a remote root listen on IPv4 MPTCP. The TCP listener and the dialer set MPTCP only when tcp_multi_path is true and left the Go default otherwise, so every inbound of a build without the multipathtcp=0 setting was an MPTCP listener. The sing-box binary had the setting in its link flags; hiddify-core's Makefile had none, and its CI set a symbol that does not exist (internal/godebug.defaultGODEBUG), so the app's cores listened on MPTCP.

Fix: The listener and the dialer set MPTCP off unless tcp_multi_path asks for it, and both main modules carry godebug multipathtcp=0 in go.mod, which every build of them gets without link flags, as go version -m of the binaries shows. A Linux-only test checks that an inbound with the defaults accepts a plain TCP connection, not an MPTCP one. Update the Linux kernel as well: the kernel bug is not fixed by this, and an inbound listening on all addresses (0.0.0.0) is reachable from the network in any case.

docs.title: Balancer: every test round moved the selection and cut every connection
docs.text:
Commit: d23f1250b

What happened: The lowest-delay strategy took the new minimum at every monitoring update, with no tolerance (the option was accepted and ignored), and the balancer then closed every connection through it, inbound ones included with interrupt_exist_connections. Two servers with close delays swapped at every round, and during a ping of all servers the results arrived one by one, so the selection moved and the connections were closed again every half second. A voice call or a video dropped, and an app update being downloaded failed, while the previous server was fine. The first cycle also sorted untested members (delay 0) ahead of the cached ones, so the member that was fastest last run was tested last, and the group started on the first member of the list instead of the cached best.

Fix: lowest-delay keeps its member while it answers, and moves only to a member faster by more than tolerance (50 ms when unset), or when its member fails a test. Connections are tracked per member; a member that becomes faster takes new connections only, a member that dies has only its own connections closed, and 30 seconds after start the connections on the members the group no longer uses are moved once, when a result of this run exists. The balancer starts from the cached results, and the first cycle tests the cached fastest member first. Tested with unit tests of the strategy, the per-member interrupt, the settle, the start from the cache and the cycle order.

docs.title: WireGuard noise: the reserved bytes were written into the noise packets
docs.text:
Commit: wireguard-go@3b861c636

What happened: A wireguard endpoint with no detour sends through the standard bind, whose SendWithoutModify called Send, and Send writes the peer's reserved bytes (WARP's client id) into bytes 1–3 of every packet. Noise packets are sent with SendWithoutModify to stay as they are, but got the reserved bytes too: a QUIC template or <qi> Initial went out as ce 57 3d 35 01 08 … instead of ce 00 00 00 01 08 …, a broken QUIC version, and every random packet carried the same three bytes as the tunnel's own packets, an easy fingerprint. AmneziaWG (awg) endpoints and endpoints behind a detour were not affected.

Fix: The standard bind writes the reserved bytes in Send only. Tested with a packet capture of WARP configs using wnoise links, Clash amnezia-wg-option and sing-box jc/id/ip/ib: the templates now go out byte for byte and the tunnels still connect.

docs.title: XHTTP: the server leaked goroutines and connections
docs.text:
Commit: 0f0f6966e

What happened: On an XHTTP inbound, the download (GET) request hands its connection to the inbound, which reads the request header from the upload queue. Only closing the connection ends that read, and it was closed only after the inbound returned; the session cleanup is off once the download has started. A client that went away before uploading anything kept the handler, its connection and its session forever: servers grew to about 11,000 goroutines and 1,500 sockets in a week (hiddify-core#163). A full upload queue that nobody read could also stop the session's cleanup for good.

Fix: The connection is closed as soon as the download request ends, and a pending upload gives up when the queue closes. Tested with a client that leaves before uploading and with a full queue, which both hung without the fix, and against Xray 26.10.29 and 26.3.27.

docs.title: AmneziaWG: an endpoint behind a detour that was not ready failed to start
docs.text:
Commit: df246df56

What happened: An awg endpoint with a single peer opens its connection to the peer when it starts. When its detour was not ready yet, such as another WireGuard endpoint still starting, that dial failed, and with it the start of the endpoint and of the whole config ("WireGuard is not ready yet"). The warp endpoint's awg mode retried; a plain awg endpoint did not.

Fix: The endpoint starts without the connection and dials it again each second until the detour lets it, then works as before. Tested with a dialer that fails its first dials, which failed the start without the fix, and live with an awg endpoint through a WARP wireguard endpoint.

docs.title: Monitoring: an outbound behind a detour was tested before its detour
docs.text:
Commit: 79c0e9c00

What happened: An outbound that dials through another was tested once that one was merely connected; a selector detour passed when any member had a ping, even a cached one, or when every member was connected, which a selector over one SOCKS proxy always is. The Extra Security hop (Psiphon, WARP) was tested before the proxy it goes through had a result, so its ping and IP measured nothing. The check also stopped applying after the tenth test cycle.

Fix: It is tested once the outbound its detour leads to (the selected member, for a group) has a result of this run and is not being tested again, waiting at most 10 times 3 seconds. When that outbound works after failing, those tested through it are tested again. Tested with an outbound behind a selector, which was tested too early without the fix.

docs.title: Monitoring: a cached IP was never looked up again
docs.text:
Commit: 9b7726a00

What happened: At start each outbound shows the last run's exit IP from the cache file. It was looked up again only while the outbound's result came from the cache, and the first test of the run, even a failed one, cleared that. The cached IP then stayed for the whole run, though the exit IP of WARP or Psiphon can change between runs.

Fix: URLTestHistory.IpInfoFromCache marks cached IP information, and each working test looks it up until a lookup of this run succeeds. The app can show a cached IP as not confirmed. Tested with a saved IP, a failed test, then a working one, which kept the old IP without the fix.

docs.title: Monitoring: URL test did nothing for an outbound that was connecting
docs.text:
Commit: 8239116da

What happened: A URL test asked for while the outbound was still connecting (Psiphon) was skipped and queued again, but the outbound stayed marked as having a test queued, so the retry and every later URL test of it were dropped until the core restarted.

Fix: The retry clears the mark first. Tested with a URL test asked for while the outbound connects, then another, which never ran without the fix.

docs.title: Psiphon: never connected, "domain not resolved"
docs.text:
Commit: 1a9f0b4f7

What happened: Psiphon (alone, or in the chain modes) never connected, on every platform. Since its own connections go through a SOCKS bridge on the outbound's dialer (c82d7d86b), that dialer did not resolve domains. On its first start Psiphon has no servers and fetches its server list from s3.amazonaws.com; each fetch failed with "domain not resolved", so it never found a server ("no active tunnels").

Fix: The dialer resolves domains, or leaves them to the detour. Psiphon now connects in seconds. Tested that the outbound's dialer resolves domains, which it did not without the fix.

docs.title: MASQUE: MASQUE in MASQUE never connected
docs.text:
Commit: 11a8c9737

What happened: With a MASQUE outbound behind another one, the inner tunnel dials its HTTP/2 endpoint as an IPv4-mapped address ([::ffff:162.159.198.2]:443). The outer tunnel took it as IPv6 and, having only an IPv4 address, refused it with "missing IPv6 local address".

Fix: The tunnel's stack unmaps the destination before choosing the address family. Tested with an IPv4-only tunnel dialing an IPv4-mapped address, which it refused without the fix.

docs.title: HTTP transport (HTTP/1.1): Trojan behind Xray's raw HTTP header answered 400
docs.text:
Commit: e29388e76

What happened: A Trojan outbound with the http transport over HTTP/1.1 (Xray's "raw TCP with HTTP header", rawhttp in Hiddify Manager) failed about half the time with "v2ray-http: unexpected status: 400 Bad Request" against an Xray server behind HAProxy. With the PROXY protocol, Xray's first read holds at most 256 bytes with that header, so 200 to 228 bytes of the request. Xray parses the HTTP header from it and fails when the read ends in a header name; when the whole request fits in it, its Trojan inbound reads its request from what is left of that read only and rejects a piece shorter than its 58-byte header. The headers are sent in random order, so a short request from Hiddify fell in either case depending on the connection.

Fix: The request starts with a Cookie header (unless the configuration has one) whose value covers the bytes where that first read can end, so the request is longer than it and the read always ends inside a value. Tested with a short request, which fits in the first read without the fix.

docs.title: AmneziaWG: the core could not stop behind a stalled detour
docs.text:
Commit: 96652cba6

What happened: Stopping the core hung for minutes with WARP in AmneziaWG mode behind a proxy (VMess over XHTTP here) whose stream had stalled. Each AmneziaWG send holds the device's network lock while it writes to the detour; the write never returned, and closing the device, which takes that lock to close the socket, waited for it. WARP's search for a port that answers hung the same way when it replaced the tunnel.

Fix: The device closes its detour connections before it closes, so the stuck write fails and the lock is released. Tested with a detour whose writes block, which fails without the fix.

docs.title: WARP behind a URL test or balancer: torn down on every move
docs.text:
Commit: ce1ed43e8

What happened: When WARP's detour was a URL test or a balancer, every move of the group closed the tunnel and opened a new one, just as a selector change does. A group that flips between two close members (the lowest-delay one changes every few tests) cut WARP each time, and in auto mode started a new race each time, though the old tunnel still worked.

Fix: A move the user made in a selector still applies at once. A move the group made by itself applies at most every 30 seconds (at once when the member left had failed, or WARP is not connected), through a new tunnel opened next to the one in use, which replaces it only once it connects. Tested with a URL test whose member fails, for every tunnel, live.

docs.title: URL test and balancer: their moves reached monitoring late
docs.text:
Commit: 4b866b5d9

What happened: A URL test that moved to another member did not tell monitoring, so whatever followed the group (a tunnel through it, the app's proxy list) only saw the move at the next monitoring test. A balancer told only its own subscribers, and a follower of all groups could read the old member first.

Fix: Both signal monitoring when they move, as a selector does. Tested with a test that fails without the fix.

docs.title: WARP auto mode: stuck on a tunnel that never connected
docs.text:
Commits: ae3ec6c67, 8db9e7ba2

What happened: Behind Extra Security, WARP in auto mode showed WARP · AWG ⏳ Connecting... for good. The race picked the tunnel whose handshake answered first, here AmneziaWG, and kept it although the tunnel itself never started: the AmneziaWG socket asked the detour for UDP to any address (0.0.0.0), which a proxy whose UDP needs a destination refuses (400 Bad Request), while the probe asked for UDP to the peer and got through. Changing the proxy in the selector only reconnected the same tunnel.

Fix: With a single peer, AmneziaWG opens its UDP to that peer, as WireGuard does. Auto mode gives the chosen tunnel 20 seconds to connect and otherwise races again without it, and races again when the detour moves to another proxy (one without UDP then gets MASQUE over HTTP/2). Tested live through an HTTP proxy for every tunnel, and with a move to SOCKS4, which has no UDP.

docs.title: Psiphon: dead after its tunnel core stopped, and only one at a time
docs.text:
Commit: 3c5e93945

What happened: When Psiphon's tunnel core gave up (after establish_tunnel_timeout, for example on a network where Psiphon was blocked for a while) or failed, the outbound stayed dead until the app restarted. A second Psiphon outbound could not start next to the first, and two would have written the same server list files.

Fix: A stopped tunnel core is started again, after 5 seconds and up to every 5 minutes. Several Psiphon outbounds run at once: each has its own data folder, and each checks its own tunnel before it shows as connected, since the tunnel core's notices do not say which outbound they are about.

docs.title: Psiphon: shown as connecting with a working tunnel
docs.text:
Commit: df13d433d

What happened: Psiphon showed "Connecting..." while traffic and URL tests went through it. Its connected state came only from the Tunnels notices, through the single notice writer that psiphon-tunnel-core has for the whole process. Each Psiphon set its own writer and reset it when it closed, so one started while another was closing (an app reload) lost the writer and never saw its notice; a second one could not set a writer at all.

Fix: One notice writer is installed for the process and passes every notice to each running Psiphon; it is reset only when the last one stops.
