A connection through the tunnel counts too: the Psiphon controller only dials while a tunnel is up, and its "no active tunnels" error marks it as not connected.

docs.title: WARP scanner: probes did not send what the device sends
docs.text:
Commit: 28ff47e9b

What happened: The scanner judges an endpoint by a handshake made after the same noise the device sends. But in the default noise mode the probe left out the short header the device puts before each fake packet, and with awg it sent the WireGuard noise instead of the AmneziaWG junk and special packets. An endpoint could then answer the probe and not the device, or the other way round.

Fix: The device and the probe build the fake packets with the same code, and with awg the probe sends i1–i5 and the jc junk packets. Tested with every noise preset against Cloudflare.

docs.title: Shadowsocks: QUIC protocols never connected through it
docs.text:
Commit: 1e2ddd7fd

What happened: Hysteria2, and any other QUIC protocol, through a Shadowsocks detour never connected. QUIC reads each packet into a buffer of about one packet, the Shadowsocks client decrypts in place in that buffer, and a full packet with its salt and tag did not fit. It failed with "cipher: message authentication failed", and the QUIC connection ended.

Fix: The Shadowsocks client reads each packet whole and copies it. Tested with Hysteria2 through Shadowsocks, VLESS and Trojan; only Shadowsocks failed before.

docs.title: WARP: background work outlived the box, and AmneziaWG through a cold detour never started
docs.text:
Commit: 79d187b08

What happened: The box closes each endpoint's scope, not the endpoint, so WARP's port rotation, failover and their goroutines kept running after the box closed, and tried to start replacements that failed with "context canceled". Separately, AmneziaWG opens its socket when it starts, and fails when the detour does not work yet (a group still on a dead member); WARP then gave up and stayed "endpoint not initialized" for good, even after the detour recovered.

Fix: WARP's background work stops when its scope closes. The first start of the tunnel is retried with a backoff (1 s, doubling, up to 30 s), like the registration. Tested live through a selector that moves from a dead member to a working one, and with a unit test that fails without the fix.

docs.title: MASQUE: a tunnel set up while the outbound closed stayed open
docs.text:
Commit: ff42383d6

What happened: Closing a masque outbound whose tunnel was still being set up returned "tunnel not initialized", and the tunnel, once set up, was never closed. The profile's endpoint addresses were also cut out of ip:port by fixed offsets, which breaks on any other port.

Fix: Close ends a registration in progress, and a tunnel set up meanwhile is closed when its setup ends. The endpoints are parsed as addresses with a port.

docs.title: masque-client: shown as connected before it reached the server
docs.text:
Commit: 85cff7f36

What happened: The upstream masque-client endpoint used the default ready state, so it showed as connected while it had no session with the server.

Fix: It is ready only while a session with the server is up. An on_demand endpoint, which connects when it is used, is always ready.

docs.title: Psiphon: connected state raced, and a notice could crash the process
docs.text:
Commit: 7a85e7be9

What happened: The connected flag was written from a new goroutine for each notice and read without a lock. It was only ever set, never cleared when the tunnel count dropped to zero. A Tunnels notice whose count was not a JSON number panicked on a type assertion.

Fix: Notices are handled in order, the state is atomic and follows the tunnel count, and a count of any other type is ignored.

docs.title: Monitoring: a selection reached the app late, and chained outbounds were tested too early
docs.text:
Commit: af68dde0a

What happened: A selection change waited for the debounce meant for bursts of test results before the group's subscribers saw it, and a subscriber busy with the last update could miss it. An outbound behind a group detour was tested before any member of that group worked, so a chained WARP was marked dead at start.

Fix: A selection is published at once, to the group, its parents and the catch-all group, with room for 8 pending events. An outbound whose detour is not ready is not tested yet, for the first 10 cycles.

docs.title: Sudoku: a large transfer to a slow reader reset the stream
docs.text:
Commit: 16096efa2

What happened: The Sudoku mux had no flow control. Once a stream held 4 MiB its reader had not read, the next frame reset the stream with "mux receive queue full". The mux's own test failed in 61 of 900 runs.

Fix: The mux waits for the reader to make room, which holds the session and so the sender. 900 of 900 runs pass.

docs.title: MASQUE: HTTP/3 never connected through Shadowsocks, VLESS or Trojan
docs.text:
Commit: 1f44631b9

What happened: WARP over MASQUE with HTTP/3 worked through a SOCKS detour only. QUIC reads each packet into a buffer of about one packet, but a proxy that decrypts in place needs room for its own header and tag too. A full packet was cut off, failed to decrypt ("cipher: message authentication failed"), and the read error ended the QUIC connection.

Fix: Each packet is read whole from a proxy's packet connection and then copied, in the tunnel and in the scanner's probes. Tested live through SOCKS, Shadowsocks, VLESS and Trojan.

docs.title: Psiphon: every binary crashed at start when built with Go 1.27
docs.text:
Commit: bb18926a9

What happened: Go 1.27 added a field to tls.ConnectionState. The psiphon-tls fork checks at start that its own copy has the same layout, and panicked, so any program with Psiphon crashed before doing anything.

Fix: The fork keeps one copy of the struct per Go version. Built and tested with Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.3.

docs.title: Shadowsocks simple-obfs: obfs_host was not checked
docs.text:
Commit: 357a0ec54

What happened: The Shadowsocks inbound accepted obfs_host but never compared it with the host the client sent, so any host passed the simple-obfs handshake.

Fix: When obfs_host is set (one host or a comma-separated list), a client whose HTTP Host or TLS server name is not listed is treated as not simple-obfs. It goes to obfs_fallback, or is closed. Tested over HTTP and TLS obfs, with a listed and an unlisted host.

docs.title: DNS: bypass_if_failed ignored an empty answer in legacy mode
docs.text:
Commit: 0e67074d9

What happened: In legacy DNS mode, a rule with bypass_if_failed moved on to the next rule only when the query failed. An A or AAAA query that came back with no address stopped there, although a lookup already treated the same empty answer as a failure.

Fix: An address query with no address in the answer now counts as failed and moves on to the next rule, as it does for lookups.

docs.title: WARP: WireGuard through a detour often never connected
docs.text:
Commit: ce64e6017

What happened: WARP over WireGuard behind a detour (for example Extra Security) often never connected. WireGuard sent the handshake to the profile's IPv4 and IPv6 addresses through one UDP association, and a detour without IPv6 closed it. Without the scanner, a profile port that did not answer was also used for good. WARP and MASQUE showed as connected as soon as they were set up, even when nothing got through.

Fix: WARP uses the profile's IPv4 peer address and moves to the next port when one completes no handshake within 10 seconds. WARP counts as connected only while a handshake is less than 3 minutes old, kept fresh by a 25-second keepalive; MASQUE only while it has a connection to the server. Tested live through a working and a dead detour, for WireGuard, AmneziaWG, and MASQUE over HTTP/3 and HTTP/2.

docs.title: WireGuard legacy outbound: network was ignored
docs.text:
Commit: 2ab7b4351

What happened: The wireguard_legacy outbound accepted network, but always offered TCP and UDP.

Fix: The outbound offers the networks in network, as upstream's old outbound did. Ping is always offered.

docs.title: Sudoku: fallback did nothing
docs.text:
Commit: d53e3c37f

What happened: The Sudoku inbound accepted fallback but did not use it. A connection that was not Sudoku was closed.

Fix: A connection whose handshake fails is passed to the fallback address with the bytes it already sent, so a prober sees the site there. A connection that sends more than 64 KiB before its handshake fails is closed.

docs.title: Call: an unknown wbstream mode never connected
docs.text:
Commit: 7d6d0ef26, 88d4af4c2

What happened: With "platform": "wbstream", a mode other than dc or video was accepted, but the tunnel never connected.

Fix: The config fails to load with "call: unknown wbstream mode …, use dc or video".

docs.title: Call: route rules stopped after a reconnect, and a failed connect was final
docs.text:
Commit: 3f48fb169

What happened: On vk, telemost and dion, after the call reconnected, the server side opened connections itself, past the router, so route rules no longer applied. The inbound and outbound connected once, and after a failure did not try again until sing-box restarted. On dion, email and password without cookies failed with "empty cookie string". The bridge and Telemost's active bridge were read and written by several goroutines without a lock.

Fix: After a reconnect, connections go to the router again. Both sides try again after 5 seconds, 10 seconds, 30 seconds, then every minute until sing-box stops. On dion, email and password alone log in. The bridges are read and written safely.

docs.title: TLS: a tls_fragment in the tls block did nothing
docs.text:
Commit: a29c81702

What happened: Old editor templates put tls_fragment inside the outbound's tls block. sing-box accepted it there and did not apply it.

Fix: An enabled tls_fragment in the tls block is moved to the outbound's dial fields, where it applies. When the dial fields have their own enabled tls_fragment, that one is used.

docs.title: WARP MASQUE: renaming the outbound registered a new device
docs.text:
Commit: a6ca1672a

What happened: The MASQUE profile and scanner scores were saved under the outbound's tag, so renaming the outbound registered a new device with Cloudflare. With profile.detour set and no outbound manager available, the outbound crashed on a nil pointer.

Fix: The new unique_identifier field names the saved profile and scores. When it is empty, the tag is used, as for warp. A missing outbound manager is reported as an error.

docs.title: DNSTT: DNS queries could loop back into the VPN
docs.text:
Commit: 8f5156c41

What happened: The DNSTT client opens its resolver sockets itself, and they did not get sing-box's socket settings. bind_interface, routing_mark and the platform's socket protection were not applied, so on a VPN the DNS queries could loop back into the tunnel.

Fix: The resolver sockets get the outbound's socket settings. detour, which the DNSTT client cannot use, logs a warning.

docs.title: DNSTT: record-type did not change the tunnel
docs.text:
Commit: 474f382e5

What happened: record-type only named the saved resolver list. The tunnel always asked for TXT records.

Fix: record-type selects the record type of the data the server sends back: txt, cname, a, aaaa, mx, ns or srv. The server must use the same type.

docs.title: DNSCrypt: a stamp of another type failed only at the first query
docs.text:
Commit: 219cd3dcc

What happened: The sdns server takes only DNSCrypt stamps, but a DoH, DoT or plain DNS stamp loaded and failed only at its first query.

Fix: Such a stamp fails when the config loads, and the error says to use the https, tls or udp server type.

docs.title: SSH inbound: host_key_algorithms, network and deadlines were ignored
docs.text:
Commit: 0ebdf81b7

What happened: The SSH inbound read host_key_algorithms and network but used neither. Forwarded connections ignored read and write deadlines.

Fix: host_key_algorithms limits the host keys. An RSA key signs only with the listed rsa-sha2-512, rsa-sha2-256 or ssh-rsa. Another key is used only when its type is listed. If no host key is left, the config fails to load. A network without udp turns UDP over TCP off. Deadlines work on forwarded connections.

docs.title: Balancer: an unset delay_acceptable_ratio left no usable member
docs.text:
Commit: 3943213db

What happened: Unset, delay_acceptable_ratio was 0, so no member was within the acceptable delay. round-robin used only the fastest member, and consistent-hashing and sticky-sessions treated every member as dead.

Fix: Unset or 0 means 2, the value the Hiddify app sends.

docs.title: AmneziaWG: the first packet after setting s4 was dropped
docs.text:
Commit: 40dfde705

What happened: After s4 was set, the first data packet went out with the old padding, and the server dropped it.

Fix: The bundled amneziawg-go is updated with the fix.

docs.title: Reports: archives held sensitive data
docs.text:
Commit: 37d5006d1

What happened: Report archives are not encrypted, but when the app asked for encryption they were named .age. They held the configuration, the open connections of OOM reports, and logs with addresses, links and secrets. The metadata held the full process path, which can contain the user name.

Fix: Archives are always named .zip. They leave out the configuration and the open connections. Logs and other text files are scrubbed of IP addresses, proxy links and DNS stamps, URL paths and queries, UUIDs, emails and key=value secrets. The metadata keeps only the process name.

docs.title: Call: a Telemost relay failure stopped the app, and VK logged the join token
docs.text:
Commit: e727940f5

What happened: When the Telemost relay failed to start, the whole process exited. On vk, joining an existing call wrote the call's join token, part of the tunnel key, to the log.

Fix: The Telemost error is logged and the process keeps running. The join token is no longer logged.

docs.title: WireGuard: an awg block was silently ignored
docs.text:
Commit: 3fa692844

What happened: A wireguard endpoint accepted an awg block but never used it. The endpoint ran plain WireGuard while the config looked obfuscated.

Fix: Such a config fails to start and says to use "type": "awg".

docs.title: AmneziaWG: s3, s4 and h ranges stopped the endpoint
docs.text:
Commit: ee5e66490

What happened: The bundled amneziawg-go was older than AmneziaWG 2.0. A config with s3, s4 or a range in h1–h4, as AmneziaWG 2.0 servers give out, failed to start with "invalid UAPI device key: s3".

Fix: The endpoint uses amneziawg-go 3.1, which accepts these values and adds the 3.x settings.

docs.title: DNSCrypt: each query fetched the resolver certificate again
docs.text:
Commit: 3e475bb96

What happened: The sdns server fetched the resolver certificate before every query, so each lookup took two round trips.

Fix: The certificate is kept until it expires, a query fails, or the network changes.

docs.title: XHTTP: auto mode did not match Xray's client
docs.text:
Commit: a4310256e

What happened: With mode set to auto, the client always used packet-up. Xray's client uses stream-one over REALITY, so a server that allows only stream-one refused a Hiddify client left on auto, while an Xray client got through.

Fix: auto picks the mode as Xray's client does: stream-one over REALITY, stream-up over REALITY with a separate download, and packet-up otherwise. Tested against Xray 26.10.21 and 26.3.27.

docs.title: URL test: a canceled unified delay test kept running
docs.text:
Commit: 48dd50df5

What happened: With unified delay, a test makes two requests. The second one did not stop when the test was canceled, so it could run on for 15 seconds. A cancel between the two requests was reported as a success.

Fix: The second request stops on cancel, and a canceled test reports an error.

docs.title: SSH: UDP was sent to an outbound that cannot carry it
docs.text:
Commit: a4afbdedf

What happened: The SSH outbound offered UDP by default, but SSH carries UDP only with udp_over_tcp. Without it, the router sent UDP to the outbound and every UDP connection failed.

Fix: The outbound offers UDP only when udp_over_tcp is on, so UDP goes to another outbound.

docs.title: SSH: one bad forward request closed the whole connection
docs.text:
Commit: ea5c6b5be

What happened: When the SSH inbound got a port-forward request it could not read, it closed the whole SSH connection, with every other forward on it.

Fix: Only that request is refused; the connection and its other forwards go on.

docs.title: Balancer: connections closed on every test round
docs.text:
Commit: 0e4c6636e

What happened: With consistent-hashing or sticky-sessions and interrupt_exist_connections, the balancer closed all its connections after every monitoring update, even when nothing changed.

Fix: Connections are closed only when the set of usable members changes.

docs.title: Rule sets: a failed download was retried only after a day
docs.text:
Commit: d918f8167

What happened: A remote rule set with no cached copy starts empty and is downloaded once the service is up. When that download failed, for example because the proxy was still connecting, the next try came only after update_interval, a day by default. Until then the rules in it did not apply.

Fix: A failed download is retried after 1 s, 10 s, 30 s, 1 min, 5 min and 10 min, then every 30 min until it succeeds. A cached copy stays in use meanwhile.

docs.title: XHTTP: seq in the path was lost when the session was elsewhere
docs.text:
Commit: a22fe417c

What happened: The XHTTP server read the path only when both session_placement and seq_placement were path. With the session in the query, a header or a cookie and the seq in the path, every packet-up request lost its seq, so the upload did not work.

Fix: As in Xray, the session and the seq each take the next path segment when they are placed in the path, so seq in the path works wherever the session is.

docs.title: XHTTP: the padding generator could loop forever
docs.text:
Commit: ee39f4889

What happened: The random padding string never finished for a character set whose size divides 256, because every random byte was rejected. The padding uses a 62-character set, so no current config hit this.

Fix: The limit no longer wraps around, so the generator ends for any character set.

docs.title: Shadowsocks obfs: the HTTP server's Date header looked fake
docs.text:
Commit: 4aef1b3ca

What happened: The HTTP obfs server wrote the Date header in the server's local time zone. A real nginx always sends GMT, so the response was easy to tell from a real web server.

Fix: The Date header is sent in GMT, in the standard HTTP format.

docs.title: MASQUE: an IPv6 bind address in a port mapping was rejected
docs.text:
Commit: 9e374aaf0

What happened: A port mapping in the documented [::1]:8080:host:port form was always rejected, because the colons inside the IPv6 address were treated as separators. No Hiddify option uses port mappings yet, so no config was affected.

Fix: A bracketed IPv6 bind address is read as one part, and it resolves correctly.

docs.title: MASQUE: UDP to IPv6 addresses failed
docs.text:
Commit: db20461ff

What happened: UDP to an IPv6 destination through MASQUE was sent from the tunnel's IPv4 address, so it failed.

Fix: UDP to an IPv6 destination uses the tunnel's IPv6 address.

docs.title: VLESS: the Vision wrapper could skip a layer below it
docs.text:
Commit: f9eca8b90

What happened: The Vision wrapper told the copy loop it could read and write the TLS connection directly, even when an encryption layer or a transport sat between them. That could have sent data past that layer. The Vision connection above it already prevents this, so no traffic was affected.

Fix: The wrapper allows the shortcut only when the connection below it does.

docs.title: VLESS: padding rules in encryption were read as keys
docs.text:
Commit: dcbc72095

What happened: A padding rule such as 100-111-1111 in a VLESS encryption or decryption string is also valid base64. It was decoded as a key and rejected with an invalid key length, so the node did not start.

Fix: In the padding part of the string, a segment of digits and dashes is read as a padding rule.

docs.title: SSH: a UDP-over-TCP session never closed when idle
docs.text:
Commit: a1f14b533

What happened: With udp_over_tcp, each UDP connection was counted twice on the SSH session, and one count was never released. The session always looked busy, so it stayed open after it went idle.

Fix: A UDP-over-TCP connection is counted once, and an idle session closes as expected.

docs.title: SSH: the inbound ignored server_version
docs.text:
Commit: 97539d44c

What happened: The SSH inbound read server_version but never used it, so it always announced the Go library's default version.

Fix: The server announces server_version. A bare name such as OpenSSH_9.6 gets the required SSH-2.0- prefix.

docs.title: DNSTT: resolver tests left connections open
docs.text:
Commit: f3b9ea0b3

What happened: Each test of a DoH, DoT or TCP resolver opened a connection and never closed it. A resolver that never answered could also hold the test forever.

Fix: Each test closes its connection and gives up after 10 seconds.

docs.title: DNSTT: a failed resolver connection crashed the test
docs.text:
Commit: 2048c1b84

What happened: When the connection to a DoH, DoT or TCP resolver could not be opened, the resolver test ignored the error and crashed.

Fix: The test returns the connection error.

docs.title: AmneziaWG: an IPv6 peer address was rejected
docs.text:
Commit: c59c8eb37

What happened: A peer at an IPv6 address was passed to the device as 2001:db8::1:51820, without brackets. The device rejected it, so the endpoint could not reach that peer.

Fix: An IPv6 peer address is written in brackets, as [2001:db8::1]:51820.

docs.title: Clash API: a balancer's connection showed the wrong chain
docs.text:
Commit: 6bf0372a9

What happened: For a connection through a balancer, the connections list built a chain with the outbound the balancer chose, but then showed the original chain. The chosen outbound did not appear.

Fix: The connections list shows the chain with the outbound the balancer chose.

docs.title: DNS hosts: sslip.io names did not resolve
docs.text:
Commit: 68a7c5d30

What happened: The hosts DNS server never resolved sslip.io names, because the name in a DNS query ends with a dot. An IPv6 name such as 2001-db8-0-0-0-0-0-1.sslip.io could also be read as the IPv4 address 0.0.0.1.

Fix: The trailing dot is removed before matching. IPv6 is tried first, and each pattern starts at the beginning of a label.

docs.title: SDNS: the server had no tag or type
docs.text:
Commit: 8affe038b

What happened: An sdns DNS server was created without its tag and type. Its detour outbound was also not marked as something it needs, so it was not sure to start first.

Fix: The sdns server gets its tag and type, and its detour is started before it.

docs.title: Xray helpers: a range number too large was changed silently
docs.text:
Commit: 164930d71

What happened: A range field such as x_padding_bytes, given as a number too large for it, was silently cut down to a different value. For example, 9999999999 became 1410065407. The same value as a string was rejected.

Fix: A number out of range is rejected, as in the string form.

docs.title: Xray helpers: a UUID of the wrong length could crash
docs.text:
Commit: b291486b7

What happened: Reading a UUID from 16 raw bytes crashed when the length was wrong, instead of returning an error. Nothing in Hiddify uses this yet, so no config was affected.

Fix: A wrong length returns an error that gives the length.

docs.title: Xray helpers: the buffered writer stopped when its buffer filled
docs.text:
Commit: 8e2f9b3e5

What happened: The Xray buffered writer stopped with a "buffer full" error when the data was larger than its free space, instead of sending the buffer and writing the rest. Nothing in Hiddify uses this writer yet, so no traffic was affected.

Fix: A full buffer is sent and the writer goes on with the rest of the data.

docs.title: URL test: a canceled test was reported as 0 ms
docs.text:
Commit: b160c990b

What happened: When a URL test was canceled after its connection opened, it returned no delay and no error. It was recorded as a successful test with a 0 ms delay.

Fix: A canceled test is reported as an error.

docs.title: WARP: a bad device id crashed license registration
docs.text:
Commit: 9b503de83

What happened: Adding a WARP license to a new device built the request before checking that it was valid. A device id with a control character in it crashed the app instead of returning an error.

Fix: The request error is checked first and returned.

docs.title: WARP: a device given by id and auth_token could not start
docs.text:
Commit: 0b03e9f80

What happened: A warp profile with id and auth_token fetched the existing device from Cloudflare, but the API does not return the private key, so the endpoint had no key and did not start.

Fix: That path now takes the device's key from profile.private_key, checks it against the device's public key, and refuses to start without it.

docs.title: Tunnel: override_tunnel_destination did nothing
docs.text:
Commit: 3f3c7eece

What happened: The override_tunnel_destination route option was read but never set on the connection. Nothing else sets a tunnel destination, so the tunnel_server endpoint refused every connection and the reverse tunnel could not carry traffic.

Fix: The option now sets the connection's tunnel destination.

docs.title: Tunnel: an unknown user froze the server
docs.text:
Commit: 641b3fc9e

What happened: When a connection was for a user the tunnel_server endpoint did not know, the endpoint returned an error but kept its lock held. Every later connection through it then hung. The error also named the sender instead of the unknown user.

Fix: The lock is released on that path, and the error names the unknown user.

docs.title: MASQUE: use_ipv6 stopped the outbound from starting
docs.text:
Commit: 8fe3e948b

What happened: The profile has no IPv6 HTTP/2 endpoint. Since vhttp auto became the default, a MASQUE outbound with use_ipv6 looked one up, failed and never started.

Fix: auto uses the scanner's IPv6 HTTP/2 endpoint when it finds one, and otherwise stays on HTTP/3.

docs.title: DNS group: a poisoned CNAME or a server failure could win
docs.text:
Commit: 46df8123e

What happened: A DNS group accepted the first response that still had records after ignore_ranges. A poisoned answer made of a CNAME and a blocked address kept its CNAME, so it won with no address in it. A SERVFAIL or REFUSED response was kept as the fallback answer, so when no server had an address the group could return it instead of another server's NXDOMAIN.

Fix: An A or AAAA query needs an address in the answer, so a CNAME left alone is not enough. SERVFAIL and REFUSED count as failures, and the group goes on to the next server. NXDOMAIN is still returned when no server has an answer.

docs.title: MASQUE: closing the tunnel did not stop it
docs.text:
Commit: 130720144

What happened: Closing the WARP MASQUE outbound (on a reload or shutdown) did not stop its tunnel. While it was connecting, closing blocked for good. After closing, it kept reading the closed device in a tight loop, filling the log with "failed to read from TUN device" and using CPU until the service stopped.

Fix: Closing the tunnel stops a connect in progress and both of its loops.

docs.title: REALITY: fragment and record_fragment did nothing
docs.text:
Commit: 59a414925

What happened: tls.fragment and tls.record_fragment were accepted on REALITY nodes but never applied, so the ClientHello always went out whole. With the post-quantum key share it is about 1.7 KB, two TCP segments, which some networks drop.

Fix: Both options now apply to REALITY as to the other TLS clients. Tested against Xray 26.10.21 and 26.3.27.

docs.title: WARP: network changes were not passed on
docs.text:
Commit: ab47a78e6

What happened: The warp endpoint did not pass network changes to the WireGuard endpoint inside it, so after moving between networks it kept its old socket.

Fix: Network changes reach the inner endpoint, which rebinds its socket.

docs.title: XHTTP: obfs mode padding outside the Referer was rejected
docs.text:
Commit: 17c771dd4

What happened: The XHTTP server read the padding only from the Referer header or the query. With x_padding_obfs_mode and another placement (a header, a cookie, or a custom header), every request was rejected with 400, so an Xray or sing-box client using those settings could not connect.

Fix: The server reads and checks the padding where the configured placement puts it, as Xray does. Tested against Xray 26.10.21 and 26.3.27.

docs.title: XHTTP: data races
docs.text:
Commit: 0493e3f8d

What happened: Four pieces of XHTTP state were shared between goroutines without synchronization: the download stream's reader, a buffer's length read after it was handed off, the upload queue's closed flag and reader, and the connection addresses. Under load these could corrupt data or crash the process.

Fix: Each is now guarded or passed atomically.

docs.title: gVisor: a failed TCP handshake could crash the process
docs.text:
Commit: 31947f874 (gVisor fork d811af3)

What happened: In the gVisor network stack, a TCP segment that arrived just after a handshake failed, while the connection was being closed, used state that had already been cleared. The whole process crashed. The gVisor TUN stack and the MASQUE and AmneziaWG endpoints use this stack.

Fix: Such a segment is ignored, and closing the connection cleans up. gVisor is now forked under replace/gvisor.

docs.title: TUN: new TCP connections refused after a listener error
docs.text:
Commit: de0aae2c2 (sing-tun fork abfac68)

What happened: The system TUN stack hands each new TCP connection to a local listener. Any error while accepting, even a short-lived one such as running out of file descriptors, stopped the listener's loop for good. Every new TCP connection was then refused until the VPN restarted, while UDP kept working.

Fix: Short-lived errors are waited out, and a listener that died is recreated. sing-tun is now forked under replace/sing-tun.

docs.title: WireGuard: recovery after the network goes bad
docs.text:
Commits: 386158d33 and 31c0f5732 (wireguard-go fork f191d67, b46c414, a7a59c8, 6f870fd, 5e21bd6, a6fcdc9)

What happened:

  • After the device slept, or when DPI flagged a connection, handshakes kept failing from the same source port, and WireGuard and WARP did not recover until the network changed.
  • A receive routine that met a lasting socket error stopped, and nothing restarted it.
  • WireGuard did not start at all on a host or interface without IPv6.
  • Noise (fake) packets: only the first one was sent, the start of each was cut off, and the top of every configured range (count, size and delay) was never used.

Fix:

  • After failed handshakes, the socket is reopened on a new port. This happens once the handshake cycle gives up, or after 3 unanswered attempts when the session is already dead, at most once every 90 seconds. A configured listen_port is kept.
  • A receive routine that stops reopens the socket.
  • IPv4 is kept when IPv6 cannot be opened.
  • All noise packets are sent whole, and ranges include their upper bound.

docs.title: Local DNS on Linux: no fallback when systemd-resolved is incompatible
docs.text:
Commit: 53aa823c9

What happened: On Linux, the local DNS server failed outright when the systemd-resolved service lacked a method it needs.

Fix: It falls back to /etc/resolv.conf, and returns to systemd-resolved once it works.

docs.title: MASQUE: no fallback from HTTP/3 when UDP is blocked
docs.text:
Commit: 787f27a51

What happened: When UDP was blocked, the HTTP/3 attempt used up the whole connection timeout, so there was no time left to fall back to HTTP/2. A session that failed on HTTP/3 also kept retrying HTTP/3.

Fix: The HTTP/3 attempt gets at most 5 seconds (or half the time left), and a failed HTTP/3 session makes the next attempt fall back.

docs.title: Tailscale: control connection over port 80
docs.text:
Commit: a210bd114

What happened: Tailscale's control connection first tried a plaintext HTTP upgrade on port 80, which filtered networks intercept or recognize, and moved to port 443 only after a delay.

Fix: It goes straight to port 443. Set TS_FORCE_NOISE_443=false to restore the old behavior.

docs.title: Crash reports: unbounded, and they carried the configuration
docs.text:
Commit: 1017225d5

What happened: Every crash added a report that was never removed. Each report also carried a copy of the configuration, including server addresses, keys and passwords, although reports are made to be shared.

Fix: The newest 32 reports of each kind are kept, up to 64 MiB. Reports no longer include the configuration, and an old copy is removed.

docs.title: SOCKS: UDP never reached servers that answer with 0.0.0.0
docs.text:
Commit: 70d6601fd

What happened: Many SOCKS5 servers answer a UDP request with the address 0.0.0.0, meaning "the address you reached me on". sing-box sent UDP to that address, which is the local machine.

Fix: It sends UDP to the server's address instead.

docs.title: WireGuard: packets larger than the path were dropped
docs.text:
Commit: 1ed324a7b

What happened: sing-box marks outgoing UDP as "do not fragment". A WireGuard packet larger than the network path allows, as in a tunnel inside another tunnel, was dropped, and large transfers stalled.

Fix: The system may fragment WireGuard packets, as official WireGuard allows. udp_fragment still overrides it.

docs.title: WireGuard: a stuck detour froze the tunnel
docs.text:
Commits: 304bde1fd, dd032dfd7

What happened: WireGuard's connection through a detour was dialed while holding the lock that sending and receiving wait on, with no time limit. A detour that hung froze the whole tunnel. The same code also had a data race.

Fix: That dial gives up after 15 seconds and is retried, and the race is fixed.

docs.title: WireGuard, AmneziaWG, MASQUE: slow failure for unreachable hosts
docs.text:
Commit: b1d063442

What happened: A TCP connection through these tunnels to a host that never answers waited one to two minutes before failing, against 15 seconds for a direct connection.

Fix: It fails after 15 seconds.

docs.title: Clash API: FakeIP flush did nothing
docs.text:
Commit: 3949d2479

What happened: The Clash API's FakeIP flush cleared only the cache file. With the default settings, FakeIP mappings live in memory, so nothing was cleared.

Fix: The flush clears the FakeIP store in use and restarts address allocation.

docs.title: HTTP transport: client cancellations logged as errors
docs.text:
Commit: 0ac410ae9

What happened: On the server side of the HTTP transport, a client that cancelled its stream was logged as a failure.

Fix: It is treated as a closed connection.

docs.title: Shadowsocks 2022: "bad request salt"
docs.text:
Commit: fb981ebba

What happened: With Shadowsocks 2022, a reply could be read before the first upload finished. The connection then failed with "bad request salt", most often when the first upload was large.

Fix: The request header is written while connecting, before the connection is used.

docs.title: Cache file: entries lost when saving failed
docs.text:
Commit: 6927625a1

What happened: When the cache file could not be written (a full disk, a read-only file), the pending DNS cache and FakeIP entries were dropped from memory as well.

Fix: They are kept and saved at the next attempt.

docs.title: DNS: duplicate queries after a failure
docs.text:
Commit: 42acc7903

What happened: Identical DNS queries wait for the one already sent. When that query failed, every waiting query went to the server separately.

Fix: The waiting queries share one new query.

docs.title: DNS outbound: connections never closed
docs.text:
Commit: dfb54ab49

What happened: A DNS session through the dns outbound never reported that it ended. The connection stayed in the connection list and statistics, and some inbounds waited for it until shutdown.

Fix: The end of the session is reported.

docs.title: Routing: UDP sessions leaked after a routing error
docs.text:
Commit: 7ea28f847

What happened: When a UDP session from Shadowsocks, multiplex or UDP-over-TCP could not be routed, the code handling it waited until shutdown.

Fix: It returns after the error.

docs.title: Startup held by a slow multiplex connection
docs.text:
Commit: 0cb109659

What happened: Starting the service could wait up to 15 seconds for a multiplexed connection being opened through a slow or dead server.

Fix: That work happens after startup.

docs.title: XHTTP: deadlines silently ignored
docs.text:
Commits: 6534ce882, 1288cc7c6

What happened: XHTTP connections accepted time limits and ignored them, so a wait on a silent peer never ended. Closing a connection also lost the download side's error.

Fix: XHTTP connections report that they need help with time limits, and the router adds it, as for gRPC and HTTP. The error is returned.

docs.title: VLESS encryption: hang on a silent server
docs.text:
Commit: 3db8eb988

What happened: With VLESS encryption, a server that accepted the connection and never answered held the connection, and any URL test through it, forever.

Fix: The handshake stops when its time limit ends.

docs.title: URL test: tests kept running after a reload
docs.text:
Commit: 6360e3afb

What happened: After a configuration reload, the old URL test group's tests kept running for up to 15 seconds and wrote results for outbounds that might no longer exist.

Fix: Closing the group stops its tests.

docs.title: TUN: DNS stalled the whole tunnel
docs.text:
Commit: d098fded1

What happened: DNS queries caught by the TUN were handled on the tunnel's packet loop. With a DNS server behind a dead proxy, each query held every packet of the tunnel for 10 seconds.

Fix: Each query is handled separately, at most 256 at once.

docs.title: libbox: Connections was not safe for concurrent use
docs.text:
Commit: 767a337ef

What happened: A platform app applies connection events on its command client's thread, and its UI filters, sorts and lists the same Connections object on the main thread. Nothing guarded the map and slices they share, so the connection list could crash the app or show broken entries.

Fix: Every exported method of Connections now takes a lock.

docs.title: Balancer: sticky sessions landed on dead members
docs.text:
Commit: 299f7c824

What happened: When the member remembered for a session was dead, sticky-sessions picked again with a seed that was often identical on every retry. After the last retry it used the pick without checking it, so about half of the new sessions went to a dead member.

Fix: Each retry draws with a new seed. If no retry finds a live member, the first live member is used. A dead member is used only when none is alive.

docs.title: Balancer: untested members counted as the fastest ones
docs.text:
Commit: 26038512b

What happened: consistent-hashing and sticky-sessions read the raw test delay. A member that was never tested has a delay of 0, so it looked like the fastest member and got traffic. A delay restored from the cache was trusted as if it were fresh.

Fix: These strategies now use the same adjusted delay as lowest-delay and round-robin. An untested member counts as timed out, and a cached delay gets a penalty.

docs.title: Balancer: a large delay ratio overflowed
docs.text:
Commit: 9352492aa

What happened: The largest acceptable delay is the smallest delay × delay_acceptable_ratio. It was stored in a 16-bit number, which wraps past 65,535 ms. A cached delay gets a 20,000 ms penalty, so with a ratio of 3 two cached members gave a limit of about 9,000 ms, and round-robin then used only one of them.

Fix: The limit is computed in one place and capped just below the timeout delay. A timed-out member is still never accepted.

docs.title: Balancer: round-robin reported no selected member
docs.text:
Commit: c4c581f38

What happened: A round-robin balancer always reported an empty current member, so the app and the Clash API showed nothing selected.

Fix: It reports the member the next TCP connection goes to.

docs.title: Balancer: closing did not stop the worker
docs.text:
Commit: e3a6b22fa

What happened: Close did nothing, so the worker that follows URL-test results kept running until the whole service stopped. After a configuration reload, the old balancer kept updating itself.

Fix: Close stops the worker.

docs.title: SSH: no background connection after start
docs.text:
Commit: 69fa3a66e

What happened: The SSH outbound connects in the background after start and reconnects when the connection drops, so it is ready and tested before any traffic. After the move to sing-box v1.15's startup stages, this step was never run. The outbound stayed not ready, and the URL test skipped it, until traffic arrived.

Fix: The background connection starts again once the service has started.

docs.title: Startup: some outbounds were never started, and the balancer crashed
docs.text:
Commit: ac35f63e4

What happened: sing-box v1.15 starts components in stages. Outbounds written for the older startup (balancer, psiphon, dnstt and gooserelay) were only closed at shutdown and never started. A balancer that was never started has no strategy, and its first connection crashed the whole process.

Fix: These outbounds go through the startup stages again: preparation, start, and the step after the service has started.

docs.title: WARP: an incomplete profile crashed the process
docs.text:
Commit: 35779caa3

What happened: The WARP endpoint starts in the background, so any crash there takes the whole process down. Three cases crashed it:

  • the profile request failed and there was no outbound to retry through;
  • the profile (cached, written in the config, or from the API) had no peers or no ports;
  • the profile had no interface addresses.

Fix: Each case now reports an error. The peer address and port are picked with checks, in this order: the configured server and server_port, a port listed in the profile, or the port in the host name. A missing address family is skipped.

docs.title: TUIC: a misspelled UDP relay mode was accepted
docs.text:
Commit: 36861907a

What happened: Any udp_relay_mode other than quic, such as quick or Native, silently meant native.

Fix: An empty value or native means native, and quic means QUIC. Any other value fails when the configuration loads.

docs.title: XHTTP: lost dial errors and accepted rejected uploads
docs.text:
Commit: fee26e298

What happened:

  • When the download stream could not connect, the error was lost. The caller got a reader that never returned data, so the connection hung until it timed out.
  • On HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, an upload the server rejected (any status other than 200) counted as sent.
  • The closed flag was read and written from different goroutines without synchronization.

Fix: The dial error reaches the caller. On HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, a status other than 200 is an error, as in Xray. The closed flag is atomic.

docs.title: REALITY: a long short_id crashed the process
docs.text:
Commit: f6f378e81

What happened: A REALITY short_id is at most 8 bytes, which is 16 hex digits. A longer value overflowed the buffer it was decoded into and crashed the process, on both the client and the server.

Fix: A short_id longer than 16 hex digits is a configuration error.

docs.title: VLESS: a failed handshake leaked the connection
docs.text:
Commit: ea3c70fa5

What happened: When the TLS handshake or the VLESS encryption handshake failed, the underlying TCP connection was never closed. A failed encryption handshake also replaced the connection with an empty value, which could crash later code. This applied to both TCP and UDP.

Fix: The original connection is closed on any handshake failure, and it is replaced only after a successful handshake.

docs.title: Trojan: a disabled TLS block crashed the process
docs.text:
Commit: 27c97f0d8

What happened: A Trojan outbound with a tls block where enabled is false built a TLS dialer with no TLS settings, and the first connection crashed the process.

Fix: The TLS dialer is built only when TLS is enabled.

docs.title: Features
docs.text: Choose a page from the menu, or see the list of every feature.

docs.title: PROXY protocol
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

The PROXY protocol is a short header at the start of a TCP connection that says which client address the connection really comes from. Upstream sing-box removed it in version 1.6. Hiddify brings it back in two places: inbounds can read the header (proxy_protocol in the listen fields), and the direct outbound can send it (proxy_protocol of "type": "direct").

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• Inbound: your server sits behind a load balancer, a CDN edge or a relay such as HAProxy or nginx stream. Without the header, every connection seems to come from the relay. With it, logs, stats and route rules on source_ip_cidr see the real client address.
  • Direct outbound: sing-box forwards connections to a backend that expects the header, for example nginx or another proxy server with PROXY protocol turned on, so the backend sees the client address.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: It does not. It only passes the client's address between servers you run.

docs.title: Inbound
docs.text:
• When proxy_protocol is on, the inbound reads a version 1 (text) or version 2 (binary) header at the start of each TCP connection. The source and destination in the header become the connection's addresses.
  • The header must arrive within 10 seconds. A slow client does not hold up the others, because headers are read in parallel.
  • A connection without a valid header is closed. With proxy_protocol_accept_no_header, a connection that does not start with a header is used as it is, with its real addresses. A client that sends nothing until the server speaks is still closed after 10 seconds.
  • A header with the LOCAL command (sent by health checks) keeps the connection's own addresses.
  • It works for every inbound that listens on TCP. UDP is not affected.

docs.title: Direct outbound
docs.text:
• When proxy_protocol is 1 or 2, the outbound writes a header of that version at the start of each new TCP connection, before any data. UDP is not affected.
  • The source in the header is the address of the original client, as the inbound saw it. The destination is the address the outbound connected to.
  • Both addresses must be of the same family. If the client used IPv4 and the destination is IPv6, or the other way round, the outbound's own local address is used as the source. If no pair matches, a LOCAL header is sent, so the backend uses the connection's own addresses.
  • If the header cannot be written, the connection is closed and fails.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Inbound behind a load balancer:

{
"inbounds": [
{
"type": "vless",
"tag": "vless-in",
"listen": "::",
"listen_port": 443,
"proxy_protocol": true,
"users": [{ "uuid": "<uuid>" }]
}
]
}

Direct outbound that sends the header to a backend:

{
"outbounds": [
{
"type": "direct",
"tag": "to-backend",
"proxy_protocol": 2
}
]
}
Field Where Type Default Meaning proxy_protocol inbound listen fields bool false Read a PROXY protocol header on each TCP connection, and close connections without one. proxy_protocol_accept_no_header inbound listen fields bool false Read the header, and also accept connections that do not start with one. Turns the reading on by itself. proxy_protocol direct outbound int 0 0 sends nothing, 1 sends a version 1 header, 2 a version 2 header. Other values are an error.

Turn on proxy_protocol on an inbound only when every client reaches it through a relay that sends the header. Otherwise anyone can send a header and claim any source address.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: • SSH: inbound and Hiddify additions

docs.title: REALITY in Hiddify
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

Hiddify changes how the REALITY client builds its ClientHello so it connects to current Xray servers, and adds one option, key_share, in the reality object of an outbound's tls block. This page covers only those changes; the rest of REALITY works as in sing-box.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text: Xray servers from v26.9.8 reject a REALITY ClientHello without the hybrid post-quantum key share (X25519MLKEM768). Upstream sing-box removes that key share from REALITY ClientHellos, so it cannot connect to those servers. Hiddify sends it, and still connects to older servers.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
REALITY makes the connection look like a TLS 1.3 visit to a real website (the server_name), with the ClientHello of a real browser. Sending the hybrid key share, as current Chrome, Firefox, Safari and Edge do, keeps it close to what those browsers send.

The hybrid key share makes the ClientHello about 1.7 KB, which is two TCP segments. Some networks drop or block such ClientHellos. For those networks, key_share: "classical" or the fragment options can help.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The ClientHello is the uTLS fingerprint's own, changed only where REALITY needs it: TLS 1.3 is offered, and the key shares are X25519MLKEM768 then X25519 (the share REALITY authenticates with), followed by the fingerprint's other shares. Fingerprints that lack TLS 1.3 or an X25519 share (old browsers, Android OkHttp, 360) get them added, so every fingerprint works.
  • With key_share: "classical", X25519MLKEM768 is removed from the groups and key shares. The ClientHello fits one TCP segment, but Xray servers from v26.9.8 refuse it.
  • The client reports itself to the server as Xray 26.10.17. Servers compare this with their minimum client version; the old version sing-box sent (1.8.1) is refused by servers that set one.
  • tls.fragment and tls.record_fragment now apply to REALITY. Upstream accepted them on a REALITY node and did nothing.
  • A short_id longer than 16 hex digits is a configuration error. Before, it crashed the client or server when the config loaded.
  • The unsafe uTLS fingerprint cannot be used: REALITY needs uTLS.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"outbounds": [
{
"type": "vless",
"server": "203.0.113.1",
"server_port": 443,
"uuid": "bf000d23-0752-40b4-affe-68f7707a9661",
"flow": "xtls-rprx-vision",
"tls": {
"enabled": true,
"server_name": "www.example.com",
"utls": { "enabled": true, "fingerprint": "chrome" },
"reality": {
"enabled": true,
"public_key": "jNXHt1yRo0vDuchQlIP6Z0ZvjT3KtzVI-T4E7RoLJS0",
"short_id": "0123abcd",
"key_share": "hybrid"
}
}
}
]
}
Field Type Default Meaning key_share string "" "" or hybrid: send the X25519MLKEM768 and X25519 key shares (works with all Xray versions). classical: X25519 only, a smaller ClientHello; only Xray servers older than v26.9.8 accept it.

Any other key_share value is a configuration error.

Compatibility: tested with the chrome, firefox, safari and edge fingerprints against Xray 26.10.21 and 26.3.27. The default works with both; classical works with 26.3.27 and is refused by 26.10.21. fragment and record_fragment work with both.

docs.text:
• TLS fragment
  • VLESS encryption
  • XHTTP transport

docs.title: TLS fragment (tls_fragment)
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

tls_fragment splits the TLS ClientHello an outbound sends into many small pieces, with an optional pause between them. It is the tls_fragment object in the dial fields of an outbound (next to detour, not inside tls). Hiddify keeps it for existing configs; inside, it is applied as the first finalmask fragment mask.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text: Some filters read the server name (SNI) from the ClientHello and block the connection when they see a blocked name. Splitting the ClientHello can get a connection through such a filter without any change on the server. Use it when a TLS or REALITY node connects only sometimes, or fails right after the ClientHello.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
The ClientHello is cut into TLS records of a few bytes, each written separately, so the SNI is spread over many records and TCP segments. A filter that looks at single packets, or does not reassemble TLS records, cannot read the name. The server's TLS stack puts the pieces back together, so it needs no setting.

It does not help against filters that reassemble the stream, or that block the server's IP. Small pieces and long pauses make the handshake slower.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• method tlsHello (the default) splits only the ClientHello. range splits the writes named in range (such as the first three) into pieces of size bytes, whatever they contain.
  • Each piece is size bytes (a random size from the range), with a pause of sleep milliseconds between pieces.
  • It wraps the outbound's TCP connections under the TLS layer, so it works for every protocol that uses TLS on that outbound, including REALITY.
  • It is added in front of the outbound's own finalmask.tcp masks, so it gets the bytes the TLS stack writes before any other mask.

docs.title: Compared with tls.fragment and tls.record_fragment
docs.text:
Upstream sing-box has two switches inside the tls block:

  • tls.fragment splits the ClientHello into TCP segments at the server name and waits for each segment to be acknowledged (fragment_fallback_delay when it cannot tell).
  • tls.record_fragment splits the ClientHello into several TLS records, also inside the server name.

They take no sizes or delays. In this fork both also work with REALITY (upstream ignored them on REALITY nodes). tls_fragment is Hiddify's own option: it sets the piece size and the pause, and can split writes other than the ClientHello. Use one of them, not several at once.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"outbounds": [
{
"type": "trojan",
"server": "example.com",
"server_port": 443,
"password": "secret",
"tls": { "enabled": true, "server_name": "example.com" },
"tls_fragment": {
"enabled": true,
"size": "10-30",
"sleep": "2-8"
}
}
]
}
Field Type Default Meaning enabled bool false Turn fragmentation on. size string 1-10 Piece size in bytes, a number or a range "from-to". sleep string 0 Pause between pieces in milliseconds, a number or a range. method string tlsHello tlsHello splits the ClientHello; range splits the writes in range. range string — With range, which writes to split, such as "1-3". Required for that method.

Errors: with tcp_fast_open on the same outbound, the config does not load (the first data is sent with the TCP handshake, before it can be split). An unknown method, or range without a range, is also a configuration error.

Old templates put tls_fragment inside the tls block. When the outbound is created, an enabled tls_fragment there is moved to the outbound's dial fields and applied, unless the outbound already has its own enabled tls_fragment. Then the one in the tls block is ignored.

docs.title: TLS tricks (tls_tricks)
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

tls_tricks changes the TLS ClientHello an outbound sends: it can send the server name in a random mix of upper and lower case, and add a padding extension of a chosen size. It is the tls_tricks object inside an outbound's tls block.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text: Some filters match the server name (SNI) exactly, or match the ClientHello by its size. Changing the case of the name, or making the ClientHello bigger, can get past such filters without any change on the server.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
• Mixed-case SNI: DNS names do not depend on case, so ExAmPle.CoM reaches the same site and the certificate still matches. A filter that compares the name byte by byte, in lower case, does not see a match. The case is new for every connection.
  • Padding: a padding extension of padding_size bytes is put right before the SNI extension. It makes the ClientHello larger and pushes the server name further in, often into a later TCP segment, where a filter that reads only the first packet does not look.

It does not help against filters that compare names without case, reassemble the stream, or block the server's IP.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The tricks are made by the TLS client itself, not as finalmask masks. The ClientHello is part of the TLS 1.3 handshake transcript, which both sides hash and check, so a mask that edited it on the wire would break the handshake. Here the TLS library builds the changed ClientHello and uses it in its own transcript.

  • mixedcase_sni works with the standard Go TLS client and with uTLS.
  • Padding needs uTLS with a fixed fingerprint (such as chrome or firefox). It replaces the fingerprint's own padding extension with one of the chosen size, and leaves the rest of the fingerprint as it is. With random or randomized fingerprints the config does not load. Without uTLS, padding is ignored with a warning.
  • REALITY builds its own ClientHello and does not use tls_tricks.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"outbounds": [
{
"type": "vless",
"server": "example.com",
"server_port": 443,
"uuid": "bf000d23-0752-40b4-affe-68f7707a9661",
"tls": {
"enabled": true,
"server_name": "example.com",
"utls": { "enabled": true, "fingerprint": "chrome" },
"tls_tricks": {
"mixedcase_sni": true,
"padding_mode": "random",
"padding_size": "800-1200"
}
}
}
]
}
Field Type Default Meaning mixedcase_sni bool false Send the server name with a random case on each connection. padding_mode string "" random adds the padding extension. Empty also adds it when padding_size is set. padding_size string — Padding length in bytes, a number or a range "from-to" (a random length each connection), from 1 to 16000. Required with random. padding_sni string — Not supported; ignored with a warning.

The padding modes sni and hello_client and the field padding_sni were never implemented. They are ignored with a warning, so configs that carry them still load. A padding_size that is not a number or range, or is out of range, is a configuration error.

docs.title: DNS rules: bypass_if_failed
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

bypass_if_failed is a field of the DNS route action. When the server chosen by the rule fails, the query goes on to the next matching DNS rule instead of failing. Without it, the error of that server is the result.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• You send some names to a special server (a local resolver, a server only reachable through one outbound, a DNSCrypt resolver), and want the normal rules to answer when that server is down or blocked.
  • You want a chain of servers for the same names, tried in rule order.

For trying several servers at once, use a DNS group instead.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: It does not. It only lets the next rule try another server when one is blocked.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The rule's server is asked as usual. If it answers, that answer is used.
  • If it fails, rule matching goes on from the next rule. The next rule that matches picks the server, and if no other rule matches, the final server is used.
  • For an address lookup made by sing-box itself (for example to resolve a server name of an outbound), an empty answer also counts as a failure.
  • If the query is canceled, it stops; the next rule is not tried.
  • Several rules in a row can each have bypass_if_failed.
  • A failure that the next rule takes over is logged at debug level, not as an error.

docs.title: Limit: legacy DNS rule mode only
docs.text:
sing-box 1.15 has two ways to run DNS rules. bypass_if_failed works only in the legacy mode; in the new mode it is ignored and a failed server is the result.

sing-box uses the legacy mode when at least one DNS rule matches on the answer's address (ip_cidr, ip_is_private or ip_accept_any, without match_response) or sets strategy in its action, and no rule needs the new mode (for example match_response, query_type, ip_version, or the evaluate or respond actions). Upstream marks these legacy fields as deprecated, so sing-box logs a warning for them.

A config that mixes the two (a strategy in one rule and a query_type in another, for example) is rejected at startup. In the legacy mode, a fake IP rule therefore cannot match query_type: [A, AAAA]. Give it bypass_if_failed instead: the fake IP server fails every other query type, and the next rule answers it.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"dns": {
"servers": [
{ "type": "udp", "tag": "office", "server": "10.0.0.53" },
{ "type": "https", "tag": "remote", "server": "1.1.1.1" }
],
"rules": [
{
"domain_suffix": ["corp.example"],
"action": "route",
"server": "office",
"strategy": "ipv4_only",
"bypass_if_failed": true
}
],
"final": "remote"
}
}

Here strategy puts the rules in legacy mode. When the office server does not answer, names under corp.example are resolved by remote.

Field Type Default Meaning bypass_if_failed bool false When the rule's server fails, go on to the next matching rule.

docs.title: DNS group
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

A DNS group asks several DNS servers for one query and returns the best answer. It can drop answers that point into blocked ranges, so a poisoned reply from a filtered resolver does not win. It is a DNS server: "type": "group" in the dns.servers list. Upstream sing-box has the group type; Hiddify adds mode, ignore_ranges, error_ttl, win_ttl and member_timeout, and keeps the older multi type as an alias.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• Your resolvers are unreliable or slow, and you want an answer from whichever one works.
  • Your network's resolvers return fake addresses (for example a censor's block page) for some names, and you want those answers thrown away.
  • You want one server used most of the time, with the others taking over only when it fails.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: DNS filtering usually answers a blocked name with a fixed address, such as a block page in a private range. ignore_ranges drops A and AAAA records in those ranges. A response with no address left is not an answer, so the group waits for another server, for example an encrypted one through the proxy. It does not help when the filter drops the query or answers with an address you don't list.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The group has four modes:

Mode What it does parallel (default) Asks every server at once and returns the first good answer. sequential Asks the servers one at a time, in order, until one gives a good answer. A server that failed is asked after the others for error_ttl, and each server gets a bounded share of the query's time. stable Asks only its current server. When that server fails, asks the others at once; the first to answer becomes the current server. fastest Like stable, but keeps the current server only for win_ttl. Then it asks every server at once again and the fastest becomes the current server.

In every mode:

  • A good answer still has records after ignore_ranges. An A or AAAA query needs an address: a CNAME left alone after filtering is not enough.
  • SERVFAIL and REFUSED count as failures.
  • A response without an answer, such as NXDOMAIN, is kept and returned only if no server gives a good answer.

In sequential mode:

  • A server that fails, or whose answer ignore_ranges empties, is asked after the others for error_ttl; it is still asked when they all fail. So a dead first server does not open every query. When the network changes, the group forgets its failures.
  • Each server is waited for at most member_timeout, or, when that is unset, the query's time left shared among the servers still to ask, at least 2 s each. A server that hangs, as a TCP or TLS server behind a port that drops packets does, no longer spends the whole query on its own and leaves the servers behind it unasked.

In stable and fastest mode:

  • The current server gets half of the time left for the query, so the others still have time to answer when it does not.
  • A server that fails, or whose answer ignore_ranges empties, is skipped for error_ttl. When every server failed recently, they are all asked.
  • When the network changes, the group forgets its failures and its current server.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"dns": {
"servers": [
{ "type": "udp", "tag": "local", "server": "192.168.1.1" },
{ "type": "https", "tag": "remote", "server": "1.1.1.1", "detour": "proxy" },
{
"type": "group",
"tag": "dns-group",
"servers": ["local", "remote"],
"mode": "stable",
"ignore_ranges": ["10.10.34.0/24"],
"error_ttl": "1m",
"win_ttl": "10m"
}
]
}
}
Field Type Default Meaning servers list of strings required Tags of the DNS servers in the group, in order. A group cannot hold another group or a fakeip server. mode string parallel parallel, sequential, stable or fastest. ignore_ranges list of IP prefixes A and AAAA records in these ranges are dropped from answers. error_ttl duration 1m sequential: how long a failed server is asked last; stable and fastest: how long it is skipped. member_timeout duration sequential: the longest one server is waited for. Unset shares the query's time left among the servers still to ask, at least 2 s each. win_ttl duration 10m fastest: how long the fastest server stays current.

The deprecated "type": "multi" still loads: "parallel": true means "mode": "parallel", and otherwise "mode": "sequential".

The stable and fastest modes follow sing-box-lx.

docs.title: IPv6 by outbound
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

Gives the apps IPv6 only through an outbound that carries it, and never lets them see an IPv6 connection die. The monitoring learns, for every outbound, whether its exit carries IPv6: from the URL test (verify_ipv6), from the link (ipv6_declared), and from the connections the router carries. A DNS rule with ipv6_by_outbound leaves AAAA questions unanswered while the outbound the traffic goes through is known to have no IPv6; a route rule with ipv6_unavailable_via refuses such an outbound's IPv6 connections before their handshake, so the app falls back to IPv4 at once; and the route option ipv6_fallback carries over IPv4, inside the connection, an IPv6 connection that an outbound not yet known turns out not to carry.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• Google, YouTube and most large sites are IPv6-first: a browser that gets an AAAA answer connects over IPv6. Through a proxy without IPv6 the proxy accepts the connection and then closes it, which Chrome shows as "unexpectedly closed the connection" (ERR_CONNECTION_CLOSED) and never retries over IPv4, while apps that use IPv4 work (hiddify-app #2307, #2420). A reset at that point is no better: an app falls back only when the connect itself fails, and through a TUN the connect succeeds locally before the proxy has tried anything.
  • With this, a proxy that carries IPv6 gives IPv6, a proxy that does not is never asked for it, and the first connections that teach the difference reach their destination anyway, over IPv4.
  • The TUN keeps its IPv6 route, so nothing leaves the device outside the VPN, and a server with only an IPv6 address still routes: no family is ever refused outright.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: It does not; it keeps a working proxy from looking broken.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Verification at the URL test (experimental.monitoring.verify_ipv6): after an outbound answers its URL test, the monitoring fetches the same test URL once more through it, from the IPv6 address of the URL's host (resolved by the box's DNS). An answer says the exit carries IPv6; no connection or no answer says it does not. Once per outbound per run; the answer is cached with the URL test results (URLTestHistory.IPv6) and is known again at the next start, before any test, until verified again. No new destination is contacted: it is the user's own test URL. A test URL whose host has no IPv6 address verifies nothing.
  • Declaration by the link (experimental.monitoring.ipv6_declared, by outbound tag): a share link with ipv6=1 says its exit carries IPv6, ipv6=0 that it does not; ray2sing turns the parameter into this option. A declaration is known from the start.
  • Learning from the connections (route.ipv6_fallback): a TCP connection to an IPv6 address through an outbound not known yet is watched. The router dials the IPv6 address as asked, sends on the app's first bytes (the request header goes at once, so the exit tries the destination even for an app that waits for the server to speak first), and waits up to 10 s for the destination's first byte. Nothing back, or a refused dial, and the same outbound is dialed again with the domain the app named (sniffed from its client hello or request; the proxy resolves it as it can), the bytes the app sent are said again (up to 64 KiB), and the connection goes on; the app never sees the failure. The destination answering over IPv4 after nothing over IPv6 is one failure against the outbound; two in a row with no success between them say the outbound has no IPv6. A destination that answers over neither family says nothing about the outbound. An outbound known not to carry IPv6 is not asked again: its IPv6 connections go straight over the domain. One known to carry IPv6 is watched like the rest, which costs no traffic, so an exit that loses IPv6 is noticed and its connections carried over anyway. Without a domain there is nothing to carry the connection over with, and it ends as it would have.
  • An outbound found without IPv6 stays so for 10 minutes, then is let an IPv6 connection again (carried over IPv4 if it still cannot), since nothing else can tell when its exit gains IPv6.
  • A group answers for the member it leads to; a group with no single selection (a balancer that hashes or rotates) carries IPv6 only when every live member is known to, and lacks it as soon as one is known to.
  • ipv6_by_outbound on a DNS rule: while the named outbound is known to have no IPv6, the query runs with the ipv4_only strategy (AAAA gets an empty answer); otherwise the rule's own strategy applies.
  • ipv6_unavailable_via on a route rule: matches a connection to an IPv6 address while the named outbound is known to have no IPv6. With "action": "reject" the TUN refuses it before the handshake, the client gets a reset and tries IPv4. Put the rule before any sniff rule: the TUN judges a TCP connection before its handshake only up to the first rule that needs the stream.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"dns": {
"rules": [
{ "action": "route", "server": "remote", "strategy": "prefer_ipv4", "ipv6_by_outbound": "select" }
]
},
"route": {
"ipv6_fallback": true,
"rules": [
{ "ip_version": 6, "ipv6_unavailable_via": "select", "action": "reject" },
{ "action": "sniff" }
]
},
"experimental": {
"monitoring": {
"verify_ipv6": true,
"ipv6_declared": { "my-proxy § 0": true }
}
}
}
Field Where Type Default Meaning ipv6_by_outbound DNS rule action route, route_options string An outbound, or a group; while it is known to have no IPv6, AAAA questions get an empty answer. ipv6_unavailable_via route rule string An outbound, or a group; the rule matches an IPv6 destination while it is known to have no IPv6. ipv6_fallback route bool false A TCP connection to an IPv6 address through an outbound not known yet is carried over IPv4 (the sniffed domain) when the outbound gives nothing, and teaches the outbound's IPv6. verify_ipv6 experimental.monitoring bool false After each outbound's URL test, the same URL is fetched over the host's IPv6 address through it, once per run; the answer is cached with the URL test results. ipv6_declared experimental.monitoring object, tag to bool Outbounds whose IPv6 the link declared (ipv6=1, ipv6=0); known from the start. ipv6_probe experimental.monitoring Retired, no effect: the probe of a public address it replaced.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• hiddify-core turns all of this on when the IPv6 mode gives the apps IPv6 at all ("on, IPv4 first" or "on, IPv6 first"); the default, IPv4 only, answers the apps with ipv4_only and refuses every IPv6 destination before the sniff rule, with nothing to verify or carry over.
  • The verification is one more request per outbound per run to the test URL the user already chose; through a proxy, that is one more connection its server sees.
  • The carry-over is one failed round trip through the proxy per IPv6 connection while an outbound is not known yet: at most a couple of connections after a start without a cached answer, since two failures settle it and the verification at the first URL test usually settles it first.

docs.title: DNSCrypt (SDNS stamps)
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

The sdns DNS server sends queries to a DNSCrypt resolver, given by its DNS stamp (a string that starts with sdns://). DNSCrypt encrypts and signs each query and answer. It is a DNS server: "type": "sdns" in the dns.servers list.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• Your network changes or blocks plain DNS answers, and you want encrypted DNS that does not use TLS or HTTPS.
  • A resolver you trust publishes a DNSCrypt stamp, for example from the public DNSCrypt resolver lists.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
A filter cannot read DNSCrypt queries, and cannot change the answers without the change being detected. So DNS poisoning, a common way to block sites, does not work against it.

It does not hide that you use DNSCrypt. The resolver's address is in the stamp and the traffic has a known shape, so a filter can block the resolver or the protocol. When that happens, send the queries through a proxy with detour.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The stamp holds the resolver's address, its provider name and its public key.
  • Before the first query, the server asks the resolver for its current certificate and checks it with the public key from the stamp. Then it sends the encrypted query and decrypts the answer.
  • The server keeps the certificate for later queries, so they take one round trip. It fetches a new one when the certificate expires, when a query fails, or when the network changes.
  • Queries go over UDP. Each step gives up after 10 seconds.
  • Only DNSCrypt stamps work. A stamp for DNS over HTTPS, DNS over TLS or plain DNS is refused when the config loads. Use the https, tls or udp server type for it.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"dns": {
"servers": [
{
"type": "sdns",
"tag": "dnscrypt",
"stamp": "sdns://AQcAAAAAAAAA..."
}
],
"final": "dnscrypt"
}
}
Field Type Default Meaning stamp string required The DNSCrypt stamp of the resolver, starting with sdns://.

The dial fields of other remote DNS servers work here too, for example detour to send the queries through an outbound. The server address comes from the stamp: server and server_port are not used.
