docs.title: Smart resolver pool
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

The smart resolver pool is the resolver handling that every DNS tunnel outbound shares: the DNSTT, MasterDNS and Soar outbounds each run their own pool when their smart_pool field is set (Soar's is on unless set to false). The pool spreads the tunnel's queries over many resolvers, moves to another when one is slow, rate-limited or down, and checks the down ones in the background until they answer again. It is not a separate server or service: it lives inside the outbound, and every outbound has its own.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
A DNS tunnel sends a lot of queries, and public resolvers soon start to limit or refuse them. With the pool, the tunnel client sees one local resolver, and the pool keeps the queries flowing over all the resolvers that work.

The same code also gives every DNS tunnel the same resolver features: auto (the candidates of Soar's resolver discovery, from its own code: the device's resolvers, the bundled list of the country in discovery.country, global public resolvers and, with discovery.sample_ranges, addresses of the country's ranges; then the built-in list of about 58,000 public resolvers), a saved score for each resolver so the ones that worked before are tried first, and a plain-query check before a resolver is used. DoT and DoH resolvers work for every tunnel through the pool, even for a client that only speaks plain UDP.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: It does not hide anything by itself. It keeps a DNS tunnel running when single resolvers are throttled or blocked, by spreading the load and leaving out the ones that stop working.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• At start, the outbound opens a pool on a free local port and gives its client that address as the only resolver. Then it checks the resolvers in resolvers, the ones with the best saved score first, and adds each one that passes; DNSTT also opens a real tunnel through it, MasterDNS and Soar send the plain query of pretest_domain. Checking pauses once ten work, and MasterDNS and Soar check again every 15 seconds: when resolvers in the pool have gone down and fewer than ten work, the next resolvers in the list are checked, like Soar's own discovery does for its paths.
  • The pool relays the tunnel's queries over one long-lived socket per resolver, so it adds almost nothing to a query's time. Toward the pool, DNSTT runs 300 workers (udp-workers sets another number), each keeping one query out on a socket of its own, instead of 100 workers that open a socket per query, which is meant for real resolvers, for random source ports.
  • Each query goes to one of the best resolvers under their rate cap (load_balance: auto). A resolver's cost is its latency, weighed by its loss. Every resolver within 1.2 times the cheapest, plus 5 ms, and within 2 points of the lowest loss, counts as equally good, and those take turns, the least recently used first: equal resolvers get equal shares, a clearly slower or lossier one is left out. The latency is the resolver's fastest answer of the last ten seconds, so a poll the tunnel server held for a second does not sideline the resolver that carried it; queries in flight do not count, since a tunnel keeps hundreds of polls in flight at a resolver that is not loaded at all. Loss is compared with its uncertainty, so a few samples neither shut out a clean resolver nor pass a lossy one as clean. A new resolver gets one query at a time until it has answered eight (refusals included): it may be many times slower, and a share of the queries there would stall the tunnel's ordered stream. A resolver left out is tried again every two seconds.
  • Each resolver's rate cap is learned from what it really answers. When it refuses (REFUSED, SERVFAIL, HTTP 429) its cap becomes 1.2 times its recent answer rate (a refusal is retried at once, so a little overshoot keeps it saturated); when it drops queries while it still answers others, 0.9 times (a drop shows only after a timeout and costs the tunnel a retransmission). The cap grows 10% a second while the resolver keeps answering, and is lifted once it no longer holds queries back. Each resolver is therefore used up to its limit, and the tunnel gets close to the sum of the limits. A resolver in use for less than three seconds is measured over the time it has been in use, and for a second after the pool sent it overflow its refusals do not lower its cap: otherwise a tunnel that keeps hundreds of queries in flight drives the caps far below the limits. A refusal after a quiet spell steps the cap down by at most 30%, a first refusal before ten answers completed assumes ten (a resolver that just refused does at least some tens a second), and answers over two complete seconds at a rate above the cap raise it at once.
  • A refused query is sent again at once to another resolver with capacity, and the refusal empties the pool's token bucket for the resolver that refused: it has no capacity right now, whatever its cap. A query that finds every resolver at its cap, or that every resolver refused, waits for a token, up to 300 ms (about what a tunnel client waits for an answer), and fails only then: a token comes within a few hundredths of a second, while a query sent past the cap is refused after a round trip and waits all the same, and a failure costs the tunnel a retransmission timeout. One waiting query per resolver and 100 ms is still sent past the cap, to find capacity the cap does not know of, unless that resolver refused or lost something lately. DNSTT does not wait: its KCP times its retransmissions by the round trip, and a held query costs it more than a failed one (measured, 82 against 173 kbps on one limited resolver).
  • Past the resolver's mean latency plus four deviations, like TCP's retransmission timeout, a query is also tried on another resolver, but the first try stays open until per_attempt and its answer still counts: a tunnel server holds polls, and dropping a late answer would lose its data. The retry goes to any resolver when the first one really loses queries, and only to one about as fast as the best when it does not, since the query is then most likely held. A resolver that lost packets lately also has its unanswered queries sent to a second resolver sooner; a healthy one is never hedged.
  • With duplicate (DNSTT: 2; MasterDNS: its packet_duplication, else 3), each query is sent up to that many times. The DNSTT server answers each query with the packets it has queued too, and the VayDNS client queues every answer a kept socket reads, so copies carry data there as well (40 Mbit/s against 33 on one resolver 10 ms away). The MasterDNS server answers every query it gets with the next packet it has, so a query sent twice fetches two packets, and the tunnel keeps more in flight than its client does. A copy goes to the resolver without a rate limit whose packet comes back soonest and surest, the lowest latency weighed by loss, which may be the one the first send went to (MasterDnsVPN's own balancer never sends a copy there), and every answer reaches the tunnel. The copies go out a little after the first send, a quarter of the round trip: the client acks each answer with a query, and acks of answers that arrive together are packed into one query while acks of answers that arrive apart each go as one, so the client keeps more queries in flight. The pool sends only as many copies as carry data: while most of the copies' answers are full it sends more, once half come back small (the server has nothing more to send, or the client is bound by its own CPU) it sends fewer, and without copies it tries a few every two seconds. A rate-limited resolver gets no copies and keeps its quota for new data.
  • After down_after timeouts or network errors in a row with no answer at all, a resolver is down. It gets a copy of a live query every second, and is back in use on its first answer. A resolver that still answers some queries is capped, never taken down.
  • Each resolver's score, from -10 to 10, is saved in the cache file, under a key of the outbound's own (dnstt_resolvers<record type>, masterdns_resolvers).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
smart_pool is either true, the pool with every default, or an object:

{
"outbounds": [
{
"type": "dnstt",
"tag": "dnstt-out",
"domain": "t.example.com",
"pubkey": "<server public key, hex>",
"resolvers": ["auto", "8.8.8.8:53", "dot://1.1.1.1:853", "https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query"],
"smart_pool": {
"enabled": true,
"load_balance": "lowest_latency"
}
},
{
"type": "masterdns",
"tag": "masterdns-out",
"domains": ["v.example.com"],
"resolvers": ["auto"],
"key": "<the server's encrypt_key.txt>",
"smart_pool": true
}
]
}
Field Type Default Meaning enabled bool false Run the pool. "smart_pool": true is the same as {"enabled": true}. load_balance string "auto" auto sends each query to the resolver with the most spare capacity, as described above. roundrobin takes turns. weighted picks at random by weight (all equal here). lowest_latency prefers the fastest. deadline duration 5s Longest time for one query, over all tries. per_attempt duration 2s Longest time for one try at one resolver; once its latency is known, a try gets its mean latency plus four deviations, at most this. probe_interval duration 5s How often a down resolver is checked. down_after int 8 Timeouts or network errors in a row before a resolver is down. duplicate int dnstt: 2; masterdns: its packet_duplication, else 3 How many times each query may be sent, copies included; the pool sends as many as carry data. The copies go only to resolvers without a rate limit, and every answer reaches the tunnel. discovery object How "auto" resolvers are found, the same for DNSTT, MasterDNS and Soar: country (ISO code of the device's network; hiddify-core fills it from the app's region), sample_ranges (addresses of the country's ranges to try last, default 0), want (working resolvers to keep: 10 for the pool, 16 for Soar's client), concurrency (tests at once: 100 for the pool, 16 for Soar's client), pace (least gap between two tests: none for the pool, 20ms for Soar's client).

The resolvers themselves are the outbound's resolvers: host:port or host for UDP, tcp://host:port, dot://host:853, https://host/dns-query, and auto.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The pool changes what the tunnel client sees: one resolver. A client that balances resolvers itself (MasterDNS) then balances over the pool as a whole, and measures one MTU for it, so a pool of resolvers with different limits gets the MTU of the smallest.
  • Use the pool with every DNS tunnel; it is also what makes DoT, DoH and auto resolvers work. Measured on the loopback with test/dnstunnel-bench/run.sh, which needs no internet and no root: QUICK=1 checks in about two minutes that the pool behaves (spread, slow and lossy resolvers avoided, limited ones combined), the full run takes about 40 minutes with three rounds. Median download in kbps (kilobits a second) of three rounds: 128 KiB through rate-limited resolvers, 5 seconds otherwise. The resolvers: one or three unlimited; one unlimited 10 ms away; one limited to 30 queries a second; three limited to 20, 30 and 40 (the last dropping instead of refusing); 30 and 40 with a third one dead; three unlimited answering after 10, 60 and 250 ms; three unlimited losing 0%, 10% and 30%. "First resolver" is the setup's first one alone, which is the fastest and the lossless one in the last two setups.
Setup DNSTT, first resolver DNSTT, pool MasterDNS, first resolver MasterDNS, own balancer MasterDNS, own, no duplication MasterDNS, pool one-unlimited 23365 41468 22941 24754 22734 30334 one-10ms 22203 38378 725 545 567 29084 one-limited 150 158 79 78 80 86 three-unlimited 25003 42300 22120 18467 29569 30486 three-limited 87 563 34 337 327 295 three-limited-one-dead 156 212 79 211 275 232 three-uneven-latency 20707 36280 644 17694 896 26833 three-lossy 23328 41464 23041 23652 74 29703

DNSTT is faster through the pool in every setup: 1.7 to 1.8 times DNSTT on its first resolver without a rate limit, 6.5 times through three limited resolvers and 1.4 times with one of them dead; on one limited resolver the two are level. MasterDNS through the pool is ahead of every other way to run it in six setups of eight: 40 times MasterDNS alone on one resolver 10 ms away (the copies keep the tunnel's window full), 1.5 times its own balancer with uneven latency, 1.3 times with lossy resolvers (where its uploads are 7 times faster: the own balancer spreads queries over the lossy resolvers too), 1.2 times on one unlimited resolver, and level with it on three unlimited ones. Through three limited resolvers and with one dead it is a tenth to a sixth behind its own balancer, while 9 times MasterDNS alone: a resolver that drops past its rate shows a drop only after a timeout, and the pool's share of them is open. Rounds on the loopback vary by a fifth or more, so the table's smaller gaps are not differences. MasterDNS's own balancer sends every packet over two resolvers (packet_duplication); the pool does the same with duplicate, over resolvers without a rate limit, which is worth 20 times on uneven latency, where MasterDNS otherwise keeps about one query in flight and waits out each answer. Results on the loopback vary by about a fifth between runs, so the table's smaller gaps are not differences. The full table, with uploads and query rates, comes from running the script; the pool's own benchmark, without a tunnel, is go run ./cmd/hmrdbench bench in hmrd_multi_resolver_dns. - The pool listens on 127.0.0.1 only, on a port chosen at start, and closes with the outbound.

docs.title: sslip.io names in the hosts server
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

A name under sslip.io carries its own IP address, such as 1-2-3-4.sslip.io for 1.2.3.4. Hiddify's hosts DNS server ("type": "hosts" in the dns.servers list) reads the address from such a name and answers with it, without asking any DNS server. There is no new field: every hosts server does this.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• A server has no domain, but the client needs one, for example for a TLS server name or a certificate issued for an sslip.io name.
  • On a filtered network, a DNS query for the name can fail or get a false answer. Reading the address from the name needs no query at all.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: No DNS query leaves the device for these names, so DNS blocking or poisoning cannot affect them. The connection itself still goes to the IP address in the name, which a filter can block.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The hosts server first looks in predefined, then in its hosts files. Only when neither has the name does it read the address from the name.
  • An IPv4 address is written with dots or dashes: 1.2.3.4.sslip.io and 1-2-3-4.sslip.io both mean 1.2.3.4. A prefix before the address is allowed: www.1.2.3.4.sslip.io and app-1-2-3-4.sslip.io also mean 1.2.3.4.
  • An IPv6 address is written with dashes for colons: 2a01-4f8-c17-b8f--2.sslip.io means 2a01:4f8:c17:b8f::2, and --1.sslip.io means ::1.
  • The answer has a TTL of 10 minutes. An A query gets only an IPv4 address and an AAAA query only an IPv6 address; the other gets an empty answer.
  • A name that does not hold a valid address, such as foo.sslip.io, gets "no such name", like any other name the hosts server does not know.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The hosts server answers only the names it knows, so send only sslip.io names to it with a DNS rule:

{
"dns": {
"servers": [
{ "type": "hosts", "tag": "hosts" },
{ "type": "https", "tag": "remote", "server": "1.1.1.1" }
],
"rules": [
{ "domain_suffix": ["sslip.io"], "server": "hosts" }
],
"final": "remote"
}
}

The hosts server fields (path, predefined) work as in upstream sing-box.

docs.title: Balancer
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

The balancer is an outbound group that spreads connections over its members. It picks a member for each connection, using the test results from Hiddify's monitoring. It is an outbound: "type": "balancer" in the outbounds list.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• Spread traffic over several servers instead of loading one.
  • Keep each site, or each device and site, on the same server, so logins and sessions do not break.
  • Always use the fastest server, without the URL test group's own test schedule.

The Hiddify app uses it for its "lowest delay" and "load balance" groups.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: It does not. It only chooses among outbounds that do. It helps when some of your servers are blocked: members that fail their test are left out.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The monitoring tests every outbound and reports the results to the group. For each member, the balancer uses the delay from the last test:

  • A member that failed its test, or has no test result yet, counts as dead.
  • A result loaded from the cache at start, not yet tested again, gets 20,000 ms added. A fresh test always wins over an old one.
  • The acceptable delay is the fastest member's delay (at least 100 ms) times delay_acceptable_ratio. It always stays below the timeout value, so a dead member is never acceptable. A member whose delay is not above the acceptable delay counts as alive.

For UDP connections, the group uses only the members that support UDP, when there are any.

When a connection through a member fails to open, that member is tested again at once. The connection is not retried on another member.

docs.title: Which connections are closed
docs.text:
Every connection is tracked under the member it went through. A member that becomes faster only takes the new connections: nothing is closed for speed, so a call or a download through a working server goes on. Connections are closed in two cases only:

  • A member whose test fails has its connections closed; those of the other members stay.
  • Once after start: the first tests may move the selection several times while the connections opened on the provisional choice are still on it. 30 seconds after start, when some member has a result of this run, the connections of the members the group no longer uses (not selected for lowest-delay, outside the acceptable delay otherwise) are closed once. Until a result of this run exists, this waits for the next update.

interrupt_exist_connections says whether the connections that came in from inbounds are closed too in these cases; connections opened inside sing-box always are.

docs.title: During a test cycle
docs.text:
The results of a regular test cycle arrive one by one. lowest-delay and round-robin do not take each as it comes: while a cycle runs, they keep the members they use as long as these answer in this run, and choose again with all the results when the cycle ends. A member in use that fails, or that has no result of this run yet (at start, the cached or the first member), is replaced at once by the best member known so far, until the cycle ends and the best of all is chosen. lowest-delay holds only until the cycle has tested the member in use: from then on a faster member takes the selection at once, as outside a cycle. Holding for the whole cycle kept a member chosen while the fast one did not answer (a failed test) long after the fast one answered again. Tests outside a cycle, such as a test the user asks for, apply at once.

The first cycle after start, and one after a network change, are not held: there is no selection worth keeping yet, and each result is taken as it comes, after the debounce of the group events.

hiddify-core shows a round-robin group in the app as its fastest member, and keeps that member until another one is faster by more than the larger of 50 ms and a tenth of its delay, or it stops answering; during a regular cycle, until it stops answering.

docs.title: Strategies
docs.text:
• round-robin (default): members are sorted by delay, and connections take turns among the alive ones. Until the first test results arrive, all members take turns in config order.
  • lowest-delay: every connection uses the member with the lowest delay. At start it uses the member that was fastest in the cached results, or the first member when there are none. It keeps that member while it answers: another member takes the selection only when it is faster by more than tolerance and by more than tolerance_ratio of the selected member's delay, whichever is larger, so the jitter between two close servers does not move the group. A member that failed its test is left at once for the fastest live one; when no member is live, the selection stays. A member that took the selection with a real ping stays for 30 s while it answers, whatever faster result comes in, then the best known takes it: the first cycle's results arrive one by one, and the selection hopped at each faster one. A ping cached from the previous run decides nothing and is not shown: it only orders the members until the real pings arrive (the first choice at start, and the order the cycle tests them in). A cached pick is left for a better cached one and for the first real ping that works, however slow; a cached ping never takes a member whose real ping answers.
  • consistent-hashing: the member is chosen from the destination: its registrable domain (for example example.com for www.example.com) or its IP address. The same destination always gets the same member while that member is alive. If it is dead, the group tries up to max_retry other picks from the hash, then the first alive member in the list. If none is alive, it uses the hashed member anyway.
  • sticky-sessions: the member is chosen from what sticky_hash names, the source address and the destination unless set. A new key gets a random member, and the group remembers it, for up to 1,000 keys, for ttl. A remembered member that is dead is replaced with another alive member, picked the same way as above.
  • pool: a fixed number of slots (pool, 3 by default, at most the number of members), each held by a working member. A connection goes to the slot picked by a hash of what sticky_hash names, so the same app or site keeps its member.
  • A member keeps its slot while it answers, so the connections of the other slots never move.
  • A dead member is replaced in its slot by a working member outside the pool. While there is none, the slot is skipped: its connections spread over the working slots, the same way each time, and come back when the member answers again.
  • With tolerance unset, the slots keep the first working members in config order. With it, a member outside replaces a slot member only when it is faster by more than tolerance and tolerance_ratio of the slot member's delay, as for lowest-delay.
  • sticky_hash is a list of process, domain (the registrable domain), source_ip, dest_ip and dest_port; the pool's default is ["process", "domain"]. ["none"] sends connections round-robin over the working slots.
  • Refilling a slot does not interrupt connections.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"type": "balancer",
"tag": "balance",
"outbounds": ["server-a", "server-b", "server-c"],
"strategy": "round-robin",
"delay_acceptable_ratio": 2
}
Field Type Default Meaning outbounds list of strings required Tags of the members. strategy string "round-robin" round-robin, lowest-delay, consistent-hashing, sticky-sessions or pool. pool int 3 For pool: the number of slots. sticky_hash list of strings pool ["process", "domain"], sticky-sessions ["source_ip", "domain"] For pool and sticky-sessions: what a connection sticks to its member by. ["none"] turns sticking off. delay_acceptable_ratio number 2 How much slower than the fastest member a member may be and still be used. 2 means up to twice the fastest delay. Unset or 0 is 2. max_retry int 0 For consistent-hashing and sticky-sessions: how many other hash picks to try before going down the list. ttl duration 0 (no expiry) For sticky-sessions: how long a pair keeps its member. interrupt_exist_connections bool false When a member dies, or at the one move after start, also close the connections that came in from inbounds. Without it, only connections opened inside sing-box are closed. tolerance int 50 For lowest-delay: how much faster, in milliseconds, another member must be to take the selection. tolerance_ratio number 0.1 For lowest-delay: how much faster, as a share of the selected member's delay, another member must be to take the selection. The larger of the two tolerances applies.

docs.title: Fallback
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

The fallback group tries its members in order and uses the first one that connects. A member that fails is set aside for a while, so a dead server does not slow down every connection. It is an outbound: "type": "fallback" in the outbounds list.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• You have a main server and one or more backups, and want the backup used only when the main one fails.
  • You want the switch to happen on the connection that fails, not after the next URL test.

It only sees failures to open a connection. Some outbounds report a connection as open before the server has answered, and fail later. Those failures are not caught: use a balancer or a URL test group for them, which test the server itself.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: It does not. It only chooses among outbounds that do.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• For each connection, the group tries the members in config order and uses the first that opens the connection. It works the same way for TCP and UDP.
  • A member that fails is skipped for blacklist_timeout. It moves to the end of the order, and is tried only after all the others fail. So a dead member costs one failed attempt per timeout, not one per connection.
  • When a member opens a connection, it is taken off the skip list.
  • If the connection is canceled while a member is trying, the group stops and does not try the next one.
  • If every member fails, the connection fails with the error of each member.
  • The group reports the member that last opened a connection as its current choice.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"type": "fallback",
"tag": "fallback",
"outbounds": ["main", "backup"],
"blacklist_timeout": "1m"
}
Field Type Default Meaning outbounds list of strings required Tags of the members, in the order to try them. blacklist_timeout duration 1m How long a member that failed is skipped.

Ported from sing-box-extended.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Balancer
  • Monitoring

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

Monitoring tests every outbound and endpoint in the background: it measures the delay through each one and finds the IP address and country it exits from. Groups such as the balancer choose members from these results, and the app shows them. It is always on. Its settings are the monitoring field of the experimental block.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• Groups that use it share one test schedule for the whole config.
  • You see the exit IP address, country and provider of each server, not only its delay.
  • Tests run only while you use the connection, so an idle device does not keep testing.
  • Results are saved, so groups can make a choice right after start, before new tests finish.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: It does not. It finds out which outbounds work, so groups can avoid the blocked ones.

docs.title: What is tested
docs.text:
• Every outbound and endpoint is tested, except groups. A test opens the URL test address through the outbound and measures the delay, as the URL test group does. A test that fails or takes longer than url_test_timeout marks the outbound as failed.
  • A group's result is the result of its selected member. When it has none, it is the best result among its members.
  • After a successful test, monitoring asks an IP information service, through the same outbound, for the exit IP address, country, region, city and network. It does this when the outbound has no IP information yet, or only information loaded from the cache. If that request is faster than the URL test, its time becomes the delay.
  • An outbound that dials through a detour is tested, for its delay and its IP, only once the outbound the detour leads to (for a group, its selected member) has a result of this run and is not being tested again. Before that, its test would fail or measure a path that is about to change.

docs.title: When tests run
docs.text:
• Tests start with sing-box. First, the outbound each group's selection leads to (a selector's pick, a balancer's current member, through nested groups) is tested ahead of everything else: the ping the user looks at shows at once. Then tests run in cycles every interval. Each cycle tests the outbounds whose result is older than interval or marked for testing, fastest first (by the last result, cached or not), then the untested ones, workers at a time. So the first cycle tests last run's fastest member first, and a group on that member confirms it before the others arrive.
  • When no connection has gone through sing-box for idle_timeout, testing stops. The next connection starts it again.
  • An outbound that is not ready yet, for example Psiphon still connecting, or whose detour has no result yet, is skipped and tried again 3 seconds later. After 10 tries it is tested anyway.
  • When an outbound works after failing, the outbounds already tested through it are tested again.
  • Some events test at once: a connection that fails through a balancer member, a selector that switches to another outbound (the new selection is tested, and so are the outbounds that depend on the selector), or an outbound that finished connecting, such as Psiphon or DNSTT. Such a test runs right away, beside the cycle's tests, not behind them: it does not wait for one of the workers, which a cycle of timeouts can hold for seconds. Its result reaches the groups' subscribers at once, past debounce_window.
  • A test asked for runs in stages, on_demand_timeouts (1 s, 3 s and 10 s unless set). The first attempt starts at once. When it fails, or has not answered by the first mark, the outbound shows as unavailable for now. A failed attempt is tried again at the next mark, and so at every mark but the last, which is the deadline of them all; an attempt still running at a mark is left to answer, so a proxy is pinged once unless its ping failed. The answer shows at once, however late: an answer at 1.5 s replaces the miss shown at 1 s. When the last attempt has failed and no mark is left to try at, it is over without waiting for the deadline. A test asked for while a test of the same outbound runs (the cycle's, or an earlier tap) joins it and takes its result: one ping at a time per outbound. Two at once pinged the proxy twice, and the one that ended last wrote the result, so a late failure replaced a fresh answer. A group's new selection is not tested again when it was measured in the last 15 s: under load, that second ping read 2549 ms for a 59 ms member and the group moved on.
  • The log says why every test runs and what every lowest-delay group decides: lines prefixed MONITORING (test, result, cycle, the stages of a staged test) and LOWEST (the member kept or taken, with the fastest one and the reason), at the info level. The first mark is for an outbound nothing is known of yet: no result of this run, or only the one cached from the previous run. An outbound that worked in this run keeps its result past it, instead of showing as unavailable after one slow answer, and its stages start at the second mark (3 s, then the 10 s deadline). Groups never see the miss, only the last confirmed result, so a balancer does not take a slow member for dead, move away from it and cut its connections, on a miss its next attempt answers.
  • A test's delay is published as soon as the URL test answers. The IP lookup that follows it, which can take as long again, brings the IP information when it is done.
  • When the network changes, every outbound is tested again 2 seconds after the last change. A test broken by the network reset runs again.
  • A test that has not returned after three times url_test_timeout plus 2 seconds (an outbound whose dial ignores its deadline, as one into a native library may) counts as failed, and its worker goes on. Otherwise a few such outbounds would hold every worker, and the cycle, for good, and nothing would be tested again.

docs.title: URLs
docs.text: The tests use the first address in urls. If a whole cycle has no successful test, the cycle runs again with the next address, until one works or the list ends. The address that worked is used from then on.

docs.title: Saved results
docs.text:
Results are saved in the cache file and loaded at the next start. A loaded result is marked as "from cache" until the outbound is tested again. The balancer adds 20,000 ms to such results, so a fresh test wins.

The IP information is loaded too, so the app can show the last run's exit IP and country before any test. It stays marked as from the cache (IpInfoFromCache) until an IP lookup of this run succeeds; a failed test does not change it. The exit IP of WARP, Psiphon or a rotating proxy can change between runs, so the app should show such an IP as not confirmed yet.

A failed test keeps its error in the result (Error), so the app can say why the proxy failed: a refused handshake, a timeout, a DNS failure. A test that answers clears it. An outbound that is not ready is not tested, so it has no test error; WARP and MASQUE say why they are not ready through adapter.StatusError instead (a refused registration, a tunnel that does not connect).

Groups that subscribe to monitoring get one update for a burst of results, after debounce_window.

docs.title: IP information services
docs.text:
If ipinfo_url is set, it is tried first. It must return JSON like ipapi.co's, with fields such as ip, country_code, region, city, asn and org. If it fails, these services are tried in turn, starting from a random one:

  • ipapi.co
  • ip-api.com
  • ipinfo.io
  • api.ip.sb
  • ipwho.is
  • api.country.is
  • api.my-ip.io

When every one of them fails, as they do on a busy network where they rate-limit or time out, Cloudflare's own cloudflare.com/cdn-cgi/trace is asked, along with api.country.is and api.my-ip.io: it answers the address and the country only, with no rate limit.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"experimental": {
"monitoring": {
"interval": "5m",
"urls": [
"https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204",
"https://cp.cloudflare.com"
],
"url_test_timeout": "5s",
"on_demand_timeouts": ["1s", "3s", "10s"],
"idle_timeout": "10m"
}
}
}
Field Type Default Meaning interval duration 5m How often outbounds are tested. urls list of strings ["https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204"] Test addresses, in order of preference. ipinfo_url string "" An IP information service to try first, for example from your subscription. verify_ipv6 bool false After each outbound's URL test, the same URL is fetched once more over the host's IPv6 address through it, once per run, to learn whether the outbound carries IPv6; see IPv6 by outbound. ipv6_declared object, tag to bool Outbounds whose IPv6 the link declared (ipv6=1, ipv6=0); known from the start. ipv6_probe Retired, no effect. workers int 10 Tests that run at once. url_test_timeout duration 5s Longest time for one test of the cycle, and for one IP information request. on_demand_timeouts list of durations ["1s", "3s", "10s"] The marks of a test asked for: unavailable for now at the first with no answer, a failed attempt tried again at each but the last, which is the deadline. The first mark is skipped for an outbound that worked in this run. idle_timeout duration 10m Stop testing after this long with no connections. debounce_window duration 500ms How long to collect results before groups get an update.

The IP information services see a request from the exit IP address of each outbound.

docs.text:
• Balancer
  • Fallback
  • Psiphon
  • DNSTT

docs.title: Unified delay
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

With unified delay, a URL test measures one HTTP round trip over a connection that is already open, instead of the time to open the connection and get the first answer. It is a switch in the experimental block: "unified_delay": {"enabled": true}.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
A normal URL test includes the handshakes: TCP, the proxy protocol, and TLS to the test site. Protocols with longer handshakes look slower even when they carry traffic just as fast, and the numbers jump with the cost of each new connection.

With unified delay, every outbound is measured the same way, on an open connection. The numbers are lower, steadier and easier to compare between protocols. Turn it off when you care about the time to open a new connection, for example for many short connections.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: It does not. It only changes how delay is measured.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The test opens the connection and sends its HEAD request, as usual.
  • After the answer, it sends the same request again on the same connection, and reports the time of this second request only.
  • If either request fails, the test fails.
  • It applies to every URL test that sing-box runs: URL test groups, monitoring (and with it the balancer), and the tests the app asks for. The delay test of the Clash API is not affected.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"experimental": {
"unified_delay": {
"enabled": true
}
}
}
Field Type Default Meaning unified_delay.enabled bool false Report the time of a second request on the open connection.

The test site must keep the connection open after the first answer. Common test addresses such as https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204 do.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Monitoring
  • Balancer

docs.title: URL test: Hiddify additions
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

The URL test group ("type": "urltest") tests its members and sends traffic through the fastest. Hiddify adds more test URLs, a failover mode, and a reaction to failed connections, after sing-box-lx.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• One test URL can be blocked on some networks. With several, a working member is not marked dead because of it.
  • Upstream reacts only to tests: when the selected member dies, connections fail until the next test, up to interval later. Hiddify moves to another member on the first failed connection.
  • failover keeps one member for as long as it works, so your exit address does not change every few minutes, and it tests one member per interval instead of all of them.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: It does not. It chooses among outbounds that do, and notices sooner when one is blocked.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Test URLs. Each member is tested with url and every entry of urls at once. The first URL that answers gives the delay. A member is down only when none answers.

Failed connections. When a connection through a member fails because the path is dead (a timeout, or an unreachable network or host):

  • The member gets a penalty.
  • The group tries the connection once more, through the best other member. When that works, the group selects it. Live connections are not closed.
  • If the second try fails too, the first error goes back to the app, but the selection has already moved, so the app's own retry goes another way.

A refused or reset connection gives no penalty and no second try: the destination refused it, and another member would meet the same answer. A connection the app canceled gives none either.

A penalty is cleared only by proof that the member works: a connection or a test through it that succeeds. It does not expire with time.

When the fastest member has 3 penalties, members are ranked by penalties first, then by delay. When every member that has a test result has 3 penalties, all members are tested at once, at most once every 2 minutes, counted from the end of the last such test.

failover mode.

  • The first choice is the fastest member.
  • Each interval, only the selected member is tested (the TCP one, and the UDP one when it differs). While it answers, it stays selected, even when another member is faster.
  • Unless it slowed down: when it is more than 2 times slower than the fastest other member (by their last results), it is tested once more. If it is still that slow, all members are tested, and the group moves when one is more than 1.5 times faster.
  • When it fails, all members are tested and the fastest is selected.
  • A manual test tests all members and selects the fastest.
  • tolerance does not apply.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"type": "urltest",
"tag": "auto",
"outbounds": ["proxy-a", "proxy-b", "proxy-c"],
"url": "https://www.gstatic.com/generate_204",
"urls": ["https://cp.cloudflare.com/", "http://connectivitycheck.platform.hicloud.com/generate_204"],
"mode": "failover",
"interval": "3m"
}
Field Type Default Meaning urls list of strings More URLs to test. A member is up when any of url and urls answers. mode string "" failover keeps the selected member until it fails. Empty selects the fastest at every test.

The other fields are upstream's: outbounds, url, interval, tolerance, idle_timeout, interrupt_exist_connections. Penalties apply in both modes and need no option.

lx's round_robin mode is not included: the balancer group covers it.

docs.title: AmneziaWG
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

AmneziaWG is WireGuard with obfuscation added. It sends junk packets before the handshake, pads the handshake messages with random bytes and replaces the fixed WireGuard message types with your own numbers, so the traffic no longer matches the WireGuard pattern. In a config it is the endpoint "type": "awg".

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text: Plain WireGuard is easy to detect and block, and many networks do that. If a WireGuard server is blocked but an AmneziaWG server with the same keys and peers is reachable, use this endpoint. The server must run AmneziaWG with the same obfuscation values. A plain WireGuard server does not understand the changed packets.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
DPI recognizes WireGuard by its first packet: a 148-byte handshake initiation that starts with the message type 1, answered by a 92-byte response with type 2. AmneziaWG breaks each part of that pattern:

  • Junk packets of random size go out before each handshake, so the first packet of the flow is not the handshake.
  • Random bytes before the initiation and response change their sizes.
  • Custom message types (h1–h4) replace the values 1–4.
  • Optional special packets (i1–i5) let the first packets imitate another protocol, such as a QUIC or DNS packet you captured.

It does not hide that the traffic is UDP to one server, and it does not help when all UDP is blocked or throttled. The encryption is the same as in WireGuard.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The endpoint is a full WireGuard device, built on the AmneziaWG Go library through Hiddify's fork (github.com/hiddifydeveloper/amneziawg-go).
  • Before each handshake initiation it sends the i1–i5 packets (when set), then jc junk packets with random sizes between jmin and jmax bytes.
  • The initiation gets s1 random bytes in front of it and the response gets s2. The four message types are written as h1–h4.
  • Both sides must use the same s1, s2 and h1–h4, or they cannot read each other's packets. jc, jmin, jmax and i1–i5 only affect what one side sends.
  • The endpoint can dial out (a client with one peer) and accept peers (set listen_port). Connections from a peer are routed like any inbound connection.
  • When the endpoint has started, Hiddify runs a URL test on it right away.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"endpoints": [
{
"type": "awg",
"tag": "awg-out",
"private_key": "<base64 private key>",
"address": ["10.8.0.2/32"],
"mtu": 1408,
"awg": {
"jc": 4,
"jmin": 40,
"jmax": 70,
"s1": 15,
"s2": 18,
"h1": "1111111",
"h2": "2222222",
"h3": "3333333",
"h4": "4444444"
},
"peers": [
{
"address": "203.0.113.10",
"port": 51820,
"public_key": "<base64 server public key>",
"allowed_ips": ["0.0.0.0/0", "::/0"],
"persistent_keepalive_interval": 25
}
]
}
]
}

docs.title: Endpoint fields
docs.text: Field Type Default Meaning private_key string required Your WireGuard private key, base64. address list of prefixes required Addresses of this side inside the tunnel, such as 10.8.0.2/32. mtu number 1408 MTU of the tunnel. listen_port number random UDP port to listen on. Set it when peers connect to you. useIntegratedTun bool false Create a real system TUN interface for the tunnel instead of the built-in user-space network stack. awg object none Obfuscation values. See below. peers list none The peers. See below. mtu_discovery bool true Find the MTU that gets through the network and the detour, as the WireGuard endpoint does: ICMP echo requests of every size through the tunnel, the largest answered becomes the MTU. false keeps mtu. Not with useIntegratedTun. fallback_address list of IPs none Other addresses of the only peer, on its port, tried in turn when the one in use gets no handshake, as in the WireGuard endpoint. Needs a single peer given by an IP address. Dialer fields The usual outbound dialer fields, such as detour and bind_interface.

docs.title: Obfuscation fields (awg)
docs.text:
All values must match the server where noted. A value of 0 or "" leaves that part as in plain WireGuard.

Field Type Default Meaning jc number 0 How many junk packets to send before each handshake. jmin number 0 Smallest junk packet, in bytes. jmax number 0 Largest junk packet, in bytes. Must not be smaller than jmin. s1 number 0 Random bytes in front of the handshake initiation. Must match the server. s2 number 0 Random bytes in front of the handshake response. Must match the server. 148 + s1 must differ from 92 + s2. s3 number 0 Random bytes in front of the cookie reply. Must match the server. s4 number 0 Random bytes in front of each data packet. Must match the server. h1 string "" Message type of the handshake initiation: a number, or a range "min-max" from which each packet takes a random value. Must match the server. h2 string "" Message type of the handshake response. Must match the server. h3 string "" Message type of the cookie reply. Must match the server. h4 string "" Message type of data packets. Must match the server. i1 … i5 string "" Special packets sent before each handshake, in order. Each is built from tags, see below.

The four h values must be different from each other, and their ranges must not overlap. Each is a number from 5 to 4294967295, or a range of them.

AmneziaWG 3.x adds these settings. A range is a number or "min-max"; each use takes a random value from it.

Field Type Default Meaning header_protection_key string "" 64 hex digits. Encrypts the message headers, so the message types cannot be read. Each of s1–s4 must then be at least 12. Must match the server. content_padding_addition range Random bytes added to each data packet. rekey_after_time range Seconds before a new handshake. rekey_timeout range Seconds to wait for a handshake response before trying again. reject_after_time range Seconds after which keys are no longer used. keepalive_timeout range Seconds without a packet before a keepalive is sent. max_handshake_attempts range Handshake attempts before giving up. random_trailers bool false Adds random bytes at the end of packets. disable_cookies bool false Turns off cookie replies under load.

Empty values keep amneziawg-go's defaults, which match WireGuard's timings.

Each i packet is a list of tags joined together, for example <b 0xc0ffee><r 16><t>:

Tag Adds <b 0x…> These bytes, in hex. <r N> N random bytes (at most 1000). <t> The current Unix time, 8 bytes. <c> A packet counter, 8 bytes. <wt N> No bytes; waits N milliseconds (at most 5000) before the packet is sent.

docs.title: Masquerade (ip, id, ib)
docs.text:
Instead of writing i1 by hand, the first decoy packet can be generated. With "ip": "quic", i1 becomes a QUIC v1 client Initial for the domain in id: a real, decryptable TLS 1.3 ClientHello for that domain with ALPN h3, as a browser opening an HTTP/3 connection sends. It is built afresh before every handshake, with new connection IDs, random and key share, so a censor never sees the same blob twice.

"awg": { "jc": 4, "jmin": 40, "jmax": 70, "ip": "quic", "id": "www.google.com" }
Field Type Default Meaning ip string "" The protocol to look like: quic, or the name of a noise preset such as sip, dns, stun, random or quic-mimic. id string "" The domain in the decoy. Required with quic; a preset has its own. ib string "" The client profile: chrome, firefox or curl, accepted for configs written for sing-box-lx. This build sends one browser-like ClientHello for all of them.

Any other ip names a noise preset: its packets fill i1, i2, … and its junk fills jc, jmin and jmax when they are not set, so "awg": { "ip": "sip" } alone looks like a VoIP call setup.

ip, id and ib replace i1: a config with both fails to start. i2–i5 still apply. The server needs no change: it ignores the decoy, as it ignores every i packet.

docs.title: Peer fields (peers)
docs.text: Field Type Default Meaning address string none Server IP address or domain. A domain is resolved once at start with the system resolver. port number none Server UDP port. public_key string required The peer's public key, base64. preshared_key string none Optional preshared key, base64. allowed_ips list of prefixes none Addresses routed to this peer, and accepted from it. persistent_keepalive_interval number 0 Seconds between keepalive packets. 0 turns them off. name string none User name for connections from this peer. Stats and auth_user rules see this name. reserved 3 bytes none Written into bytes 1–3 of each message, where WireGuard has them; Cloudflare WARP reads them as the client id. Write it as [124, 245, 25] or base64. It needs s1–s4 at 0, no header_protection_key, h1–h4 from 1 to 255, and one peer. Received messages have the bytes cleared.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The endpoint needs the with_awg build tag. Hiddify's builds include it. Without it, starting the config fails with "Awg is not included in this build, rebuild with -tags with_awg".
  • Each AmneziaWG endpoint has its own values, so endpoints in one config can talk to servers with different settings.
  • If a value is invalid (for example jmax smaller than jmin, or two h values the same), the endpoint fails to start and the log names the value.
  • WireGuard UDP packets from this endpoint may be fragmented by the system, as with official WireGuard. Set "udp_fragment": false to turn that off.
  • The warp endpoint uses this endpoint when its awg block has any value set. It then talks to Cloudflare WARP with junk packets and the other values you give. Cloudflare's servers run plain WireGuard, so changed s1–s4, h1–h4 or a header_protection_key make the handshake fail. For WARP, set only the values that change what the client sends: jc, jmin, jmax and i1–i5.

docs.title: Bond
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

Bond splits every connection over several connections at once, called legs, and joins them again on the server. The legs can be any outbounds: different protocols, servers, ports or networks. It is the outbound and inbound "type": "bond", and it needs the with_bond build tag.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• One connection is throttled to a low speed, but several in parallel are not: bond adds them up.
  • You want each part of the traffic to take a different path, so no single connection carries the whole stream.

It does not make a connection more reliable: when one leg fails, the bonded connection fails.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: Each leg is an ordinary connection of its own protocol (VLESS, Trojan…), so each looks like that protocol. A censor that reads one leg sees only part of the data. Bond adds no obfuscation of its own; the legs' protocols and transports do that.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• For each connection, the client opens one connection through every leg at once and sends a short header on each: a connection ID, the leg's number, the number of legs, the ratios and the destination.
  • The server waits for all legs of a connection (up to the connect timeout; legs that never all arrive are closed), then routes the joined connection to the destination.
  • Data goes in frames of at most 64 KiB. Each frame is split over the legs by the ratios: with upload ratios 60 and 40, the first leg carries 60% of each frame.
  • UDP travels over TCP (UDP over TCP) inside the bonded connection.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Outbound:

{
"type": "bond",
"tag": "bond",
"outbounds": [
{ "outbound": { "type": "vless", "server": "a.example.com", "server_port": 443, "uuid": "…" },
"download_ratio": 30, "upload_ratio": 60 },
{ "outbound": { "type": "vless", "server": "b.example.com", "server_port": 443, "uuid": "…" },
"download_ratio": 70, "upload_ratio": 40, "count": 1 }
]
}
Field Type Default Meaning outbounds list required The legs. outbounds[].outbound outbound required A full outbound, written inline as in outbounds. outbounds[].download_ratio number 0 Percent of the download this leg carries. outbounds[].upload_ratio number 0 Percent of the upload this leg carries. outbounds[].count number 1 How many legs of this outbound to open; each gets the ratios above.

The download ratios of all legs must add up to 100, and so must the upload ratios, counting each leg made by count. At most 255 legs.

Inbound:

{
"type": "bond",
"tag": "bond-in",
"inbounds": [
{ "type": "vless", "listen": "::", "listen_port": 443, "users": [{ "uuid": "…" }] },
{ "type": "vless", "listen": "::", "listen_port": 8443, "users": [{ "uuid": "…" }] }
]
}
Field Type Default Meaning inbounds list of inbounds required The inbounds the legs arrive on, written inline. Other connections on them are routed as usual.

Route rules see bonded connections as coming from the bond inbound's tag. Ported from sing-box-extended, with fixes: writes larger than 64 KiB, ratio totals, legs that never all arrive.

docs.title: Call tunnel
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

The call tunnel carries proxy traffic inside a video call on a public conferencing service: VK Calls, Yandex Telemost, Dion, WB Stream or Bitrix24. One side runs the inbound "type": "call" and the other side runs the outbound "type": "call". Both join the same call, and the data travels as the call's video frames or WebRTC data channels. It was ported from sing-box-extended.

Not tested end to end in Hiddify. Testing needs accounts on these services, so only the data-channel code has been checked on its own. Expect to debug it yourself.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• The network allows only a short list of domestic services, and video calls on one of them still work.
  • Every other proxy is blocked, and you accept low speed and an unstable link to get through.

Choose a normal proxy whenever one works. This tunnel is slower, depends on someone else's service, and needs a real account on it.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
The client never connects to your server. It connects only to the call service's own web, signaling and media servers, the same way a browser does when it joins a call. To the filter, the traffic is a video call to a service that it allows. The data inside the call is encrypted and, in video mode, packed into frames that start like VP8 video.

Limits:

  • Account bans. The server side uses your own account. The service can see a call that runs all day with a non-human video stream and can block the account.
  • Speed limits. The service limits the bitrate of video and data channels, so the tunnel is much slower than a direct proxy. The speed has not been measured in Hiddify.
  • Service changes. The code imitates each service's web client: hard-coded API versions, a Chrome user agent, and, for Telemost, values scraped from the web page. When a service changes its client or API, the tunnel stops working until the code is updated.
  • Captcha on VK. The VK client side joins as an anonymous guest. VK may ask for a captcha. The log then shows "vk-auth: solve the captcha to continue: http://127.0.0.1:PORT/". Open that address in a browser on the same device within 5 minutes, or the connection fails.
  • The link is the key. The encryption key comes from the call link. Anyone who has the link, including the service, can read the tunnel and use your server as a proxy. Keep the link private.
  • It does not help when the service itself is blocked or when the filter limits video calls.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Server side (inbound). It logs in to the service with your account and creates a call, or joins the call in join_link. If it creates the call, it writes the link to the log, for example "call[vk]: join_link=…". Connections that arrive through the call go to the router like those of any other inbound. The inbound does not listen on a port.
  • Client side (outbound). It joins the call in join_link as a guest, without an account. It carries TCP and UDP.
  • Data path. Each connection is a numbered stream inside one tunnel. The tunnel uses one of two carriers:
  • Video: data is encrypted with XChaCha20-Poly1305 and sent as frames of a VP8 video track, and on some services also a screen-share track.
  • Data channel: data is sent over the call's WebRTC data channel.
  • Start-up. Both sides connect when sing-box starts. A try gives up after 60 seconds. When a try fails, the side logs the error and tries again after 5 seconds, then 10 seconds, then 30 seconds, then every minute until sing-box stops. Connections to the outbound wait for its first try. While it is not connected, they fail with "call: not connected to the call yet".
  • Reconnects. When the call reconnects, connections that arrive through it still go to the router, so route rules keep working.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Needs the with_call build tag. Without it, a config with "type": "call" fails with "Call is not included in this build, rebuild with -tags with_call".

Server (inbound):

{
"type": "call",
"tag": "call-in",
"platform": "vk",
"join_link": "https://vk.ru/call/join/AbCdEf123",
"cookies": [
{ "name": "<cookie name>", "value": "<cookie value>" },
{ "name": "<cookie name>", "value": "<cookie value>" }
]
}

Client (outbound):

{
"type": "call",
"tag": "call-out",
"platform": "vk",
"join_link": "https://vk.ru/call/join/AbCdEf123"
}

The link and the cookies above are placeholders. Use the link of a call you created, and the cookies of your own logged-in browser session.

Field Type Default Meaning platform string none, required The service: vk, telemost, dion, wbstream or bitrix. It is not guessed from the link. join_link string "" The call to join. Required on the outbound. On the inbound, leave it empty to create a new call and read its link from the log. mode string see below How data is carried, for wbstream and bitrix only: dc (data channel) or video. Both sides must use the same mode. cookies list of {name, value} [] Inbound only. The cookies of your logged-in session on the service. email string "" Inbound, dion only. With password, logs in without cookies, or again when the refresh cookie is missing or expired. password string "" Inbound, dion only. Goes with email. read_buffer number 32768 Read buffer size, in bytes, for data-channel tunnels.

The usual dial fields (detour, bind_interface and the rest) also work. The tunnel uses them to reach the call service.

docs.title: Platforms
docs.text: platform Service Inbound join_link mode vk VK Calls yes A VK call link. The last part of the path is the call token. not used, video telemost Yandex Telemost yes A Telemost conference link. not used, video dion Dion yes https://dion.vc/event/<slug>, dion://<slug> or the slug alone. not used, video wbstream WB Stream yes https://stream.wb.ru/room/<id>, wbstream://<id> or the id alone. dc (default) or video bitrix Bitrix24 no https://<portal>/video/<alias> video (default) or dc

docs.title: Cookies
docs.text:
cookies is a JSON list of {"name": …, "value": …} objects, the format that browser cookie export extensions produce. Other fields in those objects are ignored. Entries without a name are skipped. Copy the cookies of a browser where you are logged in to the service. What each service needs, as far as the code shows:

  • vk: your vk.ru login cookies. The code sends them to login.vk.ru to get a token.
  • telemost: your Yandex login cookies. The code sends them to the Telemost API.
  • dion: the code reads vc-refresh-token and vc-access-token. If vc-refresh-token is missing or rejected and email and password are set, it logs in with them instead. With email and password, the list can be empty. Without them, it must not be.
  • wbstream: must include __wb_device_id. Of the rest, only wbx-refresh, x_wbaas_token, _wbauid and wbx-validation-key are sent.

The cookies and the password are as powerful as your account login. Anyone who reads your config can use your account.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• bitrix works only as an outbound. An inbound with "platform": "bitrix" fails with "call: unsupported platform bitrix", so a Hiddify server cannot be the other side.
  • The outbound accepts cookies, but they are not used: the client always joins as a guest.
  • max_buffered_amount and memory_limit are accepted and have no effect.
  • On wbstream, a mode other than dc or video makes the config fail to load with "call: unknown wbstream mode …, use dc or video".
  • On telemost, when the relay fails to start, the error is logged and sing-box keeps running.
  • On vk, the log does not show the call's join token, which is part of the tunnel key.
  • When the server side creates a new call, the link changes each time it connects. Set join_link on the inbound to keep it the same.

docs.text:
