docs.title: DNSTT
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

DNSTT carries your traffic inside DNS queries and answers. The client sends queries for names under a domain you control, through public DNS resolvers, and your DNSTT server answers them. It is an outbound: "type": "dnstt" in the outbounds list. The client is built on VayDNS, a DNSTT fork, and can also talk to original DNSTT servers.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• It works on networks where almost everything is blocked but DNS through public or local resolvers still works.
  • It finds working resolvers by itself from a built-in list, and remembers which ones worked.

It is slow: each query carries only a little data, and resolvers limit how many queries they take. Use it when nothing else gets through, not as your everyday connection.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
The filter sees only DNS queries to a resolver, for names under your domain. The resolver forwards them to your server, because your server is the authority for that domain. The data in the queries is encrypted with the Noise protocol, so the resolver and the filter cannot read it. Queries to a resolver can also go over DNS over HTTPS (DoH) or DNS over TLS (DoT), with a browser TLS fingerprint (utls).

It does not help when DNS to every outside resolver is blocked or rewritten, or when the resolvers you can reach drop long or unusual queries.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Finding resolvers. After start, the outbound checks each resolver in resolvers, up to 100 at a time. A check sends a normal DNS query (pretest-domain, pretest-record-type), then opens a real tunnel through that resolver within 5 seconds. Each resolver that passes joins the pool, and checking stops adding once more than 10 are in use. The outbound is ready as soon as the first resolver passes.
  • History. Each resolver gets a score from -10 to 10, saved in the cache file. Within the built-in list and within your own entries, resolvers with a better score are checked first.
  • Tunnel. By default one tunnel spreads its queries over every resolver in the pool. With single-resolver, each resolver gets its own tunnel, and each connection uses one picked at random; a tunnel that fails is closed and rebuilt. With smart_pool, queries go to a local resolver pool that spreads them over the working resolvers, slows down for a resolver that rate-limits, and skips one that stops answering (see Smart resolver pool).
  • Inside the tunnel. The data runs over KCP for reliability, Noise for encryption, and smux so that many connections share one tunnel.
  • Destination. The outbound does not choose where a connection goes. Every connection reaches your DNSTT server, which forwards it to the one service it is set up for, usually a SOCKS or SSH server. To use it, put that kind of outbound in front with detour.

TCP only. UDP is not supported.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The DNSTT server forwards to a SOCKS server, so a socks outbound runs through the dnstt outbound. The socks server address is not used, because the DNSTT server decides where the connection goes.

{
"outbounds": [
{
"type": "dnstt",
"tag": "dnstt-out",
"domain": "t.example.com",
"pubkey": "<server public key, hex>",
"resolvers": ["auto", "8.8.8.8:53", "https://dns.google/dns-query"]
},
{
"type": "socks",
"tag": "proxy",
"server": "127.0.0.1",
"server_port": 1080,
"detour": "dnstt-out"
}
]
}
Field Type Default Meaning domain string required The tunnel domain your DNSTT server is the authority for. pubkey string required The server's Noise public key, in hex. resolvers list of strings required Resolvers to use. "1.1.1.1:53" is plain DNS over UDP, "https://..." is DoH, "dot://host:853" is DoT. "auto" (or an empty string) adds the built-in list of about 58,000 public resolvers. At least one is needed. pretest-domain string "www.google.com" Name queried to check that a resolver answers. pretest-record-type string "a" Record type of that query: a, aaaa, cname, mx, ns, ptr, soa, srv or txt. record-type string "txt" Record type of the answers that carry data back from the server: txt, cname, a, aaaa, mx, ns or srv. It must match the server. Another value uses TXT. Each record type keeps its own saved resolver history. utls string "" TLS fingerprint for DoH and DoT, for example "Chrome", "Firefox", "iOS" or "random". Empty uses Go's own TLS. single-resolver bool false One tunnel per resolver instead of one tunnel over all of them. smart_pool bool or object false; on by itself with several resolvers Send queries through the outbound's own resolver pool, as described above: true, or an object with load_balance, deadline, per_attempt, probe_interval, down_after and duplicate (see Smart resolver pool). A tunnel runs over one resolver, so with more than one the pool is on whatever this says. dnstt-compat bool false Use the original DNSTT wire format, for an original DNSTT server. clientid-size int 2 Client ID size in bytes. Ignored with dnstt-compat, which uses 8. Must match the server. max-qname-len int 101 (253 with dnstt-compat) Longest query name to send. max-num-labels int 0 (no limit) Most data labels in a query name. rps number 0 (no limit) Most queries per second. mtu int computed Packet size inside the tunnel. When unset, it is computed from the domain and the two limits above. idle-timeout duration 60s (2m with dnstt-compat) Close the session after this long with no answer. keepalive duration 10s Interval between keep-alive messages. open-stream-timeout duration 10s How long opening a connection in the tunnel may take. max-streams int 0 (no limit) Most connections at once in one tunnel. reconnect-min duration 1s Shortest wait before the tunnel reconnects. reconnect-max duration 30s Longest wait before the tunnel reconnects. session-check-interval duration 20s How often the tunnel checks that its session is alive. handshake-timeout duration 15s How long the Noise handshake may take. udp-timeout duration 500ms For plain UDP resolvers: how long to wait for each answer. udp-workers int 100; with smart_pool: 300 For plain UDP resolvers: queries in flight at once. With smart_pool, toward the pool, each worker keeps one socket. udp-shared-socket bool false For plain UDP resolvers: send every query from one socket instead of one socket per query. udp-accept-errors bool false For plain UDP resolvers: accept answers with an error code instead of dropping them. tunnel-per-resolver int Deprecated and ignored.

The sockets that send the DNS queries use the outbound's socket settings, such as bind_interface and routing_mark, and the platform's socket protection. So on a VPN the queries do not loop back into the tunnel. detour is not supported: the queries go out directly, and the log shows a warning.

dnstt-compat and clientid-size change the wire format, so they must match your server.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Smart resolver pool
  • Monitoring

docs.title: GooseRelay
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

GooseRelay sends your traffic through a Google Apps Script web app to your own server. To the network, your device only talks HTTPS to a Google address with the name www.google.com. It is an outbound: "type": "gooserelay" in the outbounds list. It is the client side of the GooseRelayVPN project.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• It works on networks that block most servers but must leave Google reachable.
  • It carries any TCP connection, not just web pages, because a real server of yours opens the connections.

You need two things set up first: a small server (VPS) running the GooseRelayVPN exit server, and one or more Google Apps Script deployments of the GooseRelayVPN forwarder script. The GooseRelayVPN project explains both. Each deployment has a daily limit on how many requests Google runs for it, so heavy use needs several deployments.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
The outbound connects to a Google address and uses www.google.com (or the names in sni) as the TLS server name. Inside that TLS connection, the requests go to script.google.com. This is called domain fronting: the filter sees a connection to Google, and Google sends the request to your Apps Script. The script passes the data on to your server without reading it.

Everything is encrypted with AES-256-GCM using tunnel_key, which only your device and your server know. Google never has the key.

It does not help when the Google address in google_host is blocked, or when Google stops routing these requests.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• After start, the outbound checks every deployment in script_keys at once. A check confirms that the deployment is public and runs the forwarder, then sends an encrypted probe to check that your server is reachable and the key matches. The outbound is ready when one deployment passes, and fails when all of them fail. Log messages say what is wrong, for example a wrong deployment ID or a key mismatch.
  • Each connection becomes a session. Its data is sent in encrypted batches as HTTPS requests, and answers come back by long polling. Your server opens the real connection to the destination.
  • Requests are spread over the deployments in script_keys, and over the names in sni. Each name gets its own TLS connections.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"type": "gooserelay",
"tag": "goose",
"script_keys": ["<Apps Script deployment ID>"],
"tunnel_key": "<64 hex characters, same as on the server>"
}
Field Type Default Meaning script_keys list of strings required Apps Script deployment IDs. Paste only the ID, not the full URL. tunnel_key string required AES-256 key as 64 hex characters. It must match the server. google_host string "216.239.38.120:443" The Google address and port to connect to. Other Google front addresses also work. sni list of strings ["www.google.com"] TLS server names to use. Several names spread the load. handshake_timeout duration 10s How long the startup check may take. debug_timing bool false Log timing details of the relay. udp_over_tcp object The UDP over TCP setting from sing-box. The outbound accepts only TCP from the router, so routed UDP traffic does not use it.

The carrier makes its own connections to Google, so the dial fields such as detour are not used for them.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Monitoring
  • Fallback

docs.title: MasterDNS
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

MasterDNS carries your TCP connections inside DNS queries and answers, through public DNS resolvers, to a MasterDnsVPN server that you run. It is an outbound: "type": "masterdns" in the outbounds list. The client is the MasterDnsVPN Go client, embedded as a library.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• It works on networks where almost everything is blocked but DNS to public or local resolvers still passes, including the national-intranet mode where only domestic resolvers answer and they forward your queries abroad.
  • Compared with DNSTT, its own protocol has a much smaller header, so each query carries more data; it sends every packet over several resolvers at once (duplication), moves a connection away from a resolver that drops its packets, measures the MTU each resolver passes and keeps testing failed resolvers in the background. The project reports several times the throughput of DNSTT.
  • The server opens the connection to the destination itself, so no SOCKS or SSH outbound is needed behind it (mode: socks5).

It is still a DNS tunnel: slow next to a direct proxy, and limited by how many queries the resolvers accept. Use it when nothing else gets through.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
The filter sees DNS queries to a resolver for names under your tunnel domain, and the resolver forwards them to your server, which is the authority for that domain. The data in the names and in the answers is encrypted with a key only your device and your server know (encryption, key): XOR (light, no extra bytes), ChaCha20 or AES-GCM. Resolvers that alter binary answers can be given base64 answers (base_encode).

It does not help when the resolvers you can reach refuse long names, or when every outside resolver is blocked and the domestic ones do not forward.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Start. The client sends MTU probes to every pair of tunnel domain and resolver in resolvers, mtu_test_parallelism at a time, with mtu_test_retries tries of mtu_test_timeout each. A resolver passes when the server's answers come back through it; the smallest upload and download sizes that passed become the MTU of the tunnel. With auto_remove_low_mtu_resolvers, a few resolvers that would pull the shared MTU down are dropped instead. Then the client opens one session with the server. The outbound is ready once the session is open; a connection made before that waits up to ready_timeout.
  • Resolvers. Each query goes to a resolver chosen by balancing, and is sent packet_duplication times over different resolvers, so one lossy resolver does not lose it. A connection that keeps resending on its resolver moves to another. A resolver that only times out is set aside (auto_disable_timeout_resolvers) and tested again later (recheck_inactive_resolvers).
  • Smart pool. With smart_pool, the client sees one resolver: the outbound's own smart resolver pool, the same code as DNSTT's. Each resolver in resolvers is first sent a plain query (pretest_domain, pretest_record_type), the ones that worked before first, and those that answer join the pool until 10 work; when some go down, the next ones are checked. The pool spreads the tunnel's queries over them, slows down for a resolver that rate-limits, and skips one that stops answering. Resolvers may then also be DoT (dot://host:853), DoH (https://host/dns-query) or auto, the built-in list of public resolvers. Each resolver's score is saved in the cache file. The MasterDnsVPN client's own balancing, duplication and per-resolver MTU then apply to the pool as a whole, so a pool of resolvers with different limits gets the MTU of the smallest; without smart_pool the client does all of this itself, over plain UDP resolvers only.
  • Inside the tunnel. Every connection is a stream with its own reliable delivery (ARQ: acknowledgements, retransmission, a window of arq_window packets). Control messages are packed together, and data can be compressed (upload_compression, download_compression).
  • Destination. In socks5 mode (the server's default) the server connects to the address of each connection, so the outbound carries any TCP connection by itself. In tcp mode the server forwards every connection to the one target it is set up for, and the destination is ignored; put the matching outbound (for example socks or ssh) in front with detour. The MasterDnsVPN server refuses connections to private and loopback addresses.

TCP only. Routed UDP does not use this outbound; udp_over_tcp carries UDP over a stream for servers that support it.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"type": "masterdns",
"tag": "masterdns-out",
"domains": ["v.example.com"],
"resolvers": ["8.8.8.8", "1.1.1.1", "9.9.9.9:53"],
"encryption": "xor",
"key": "<the server's encrypt_key.txt>"
}
Field Type Default Meaning domains list of strings required The tunnel domains the server is the authority for, the server's DOMAIN. All must belong to the same server. resolvers list of strings required Plain DNS resolvers: "8.8.8.8", "1.1.1.1:5353", "10.0.0.0/30", "10.0.0.0/30:5353" or "[2001:db8::1]:53". A range adds every address in it. With smart_pool (no ranges): also "dot://host:853", "https://host/dns-query" and "auto". encryption string "xor" The server's DATA_ENCRYPTION_METHOD: none, xor, chacha20, aes-128-gcm, aes-192-gcm or aes-256-gcm, or its number 0 to 5. key string required unless none The server's key, the content of its encrypt_key.txt. mode string "socks5" The server's PROTOCOL_TYPE: socks5 or tcp, as described above. smart_pool bool or object false Run the outbound's own resolver pool, as described above: true, or an object with load_balance, deadline, per_attempt, probe_interval and down_after (see Smart resolver pool). Needed for DoT, DoH and auto resolvers. pretest_domain string "www.google.com" With smart_pool: the name queried to check that a resolver answers. pretest_record_type string "a" With smart_pool: the record type of that query: a, aaaa, cname, mx, ns, ptr, soa, srv or txt. balancing string "round-robin" How the resolver of each query is chosen: random, round-robin, least-loss, lowest-latency, hybrid, loss-then-latency, least-loss-top-random or least-loss-top-round-robin, or the number 1 to 8 of RESOLVER_BALANCING_STRATEGY. least-loss suits lossy links with many resolvers. packet_duplication int 2 How many times each packet is sent, over different resolvers (1 to 10). More is more reliable and uses more bandwidth. setup_packet_duplication int 2 The same for the packets that open a connection (up to 12). upload_compression string "off" off, zstd, lz4 or zlib. download_compression string "off" off, zstd, lz4 or zlib. base_encode bool false Ask for base64 answers, for resolvers that damage binary records. min_upload_mtu int 38 Smallest accepted upload MTU, in bytes. max_upload_mtu int 150 Largest tried upload MTU. min_download_mtu int 100 Smallest accepted download MTU. max_download_mtu int 500 Largest tried download MTU. Resolvers that pass large answers allow more. mtu_test_timeout duration 2s How long one MTU probe may take. mtu_test_retries int 2 How many times a probe is sent. mtu_test_parallelism int 16 How many resolvers are tested at once. auto_remove_low_mtu_resolvers bool true Drop the few resolvers that would pull the shared MTU down. recheck_inactive_resolvers bool true Test failed resolvers again in the background. auto_disable_timeout_resolvers bool true Stop using a resolver that only times out. workers int 4 UDP read and write workers. process_workers int from the machine Packet processors. arq_window int 600 The reliable delivery window, in packets. ready_timeout duration 30s How long a connection waits for the tunnel to be ready before it fails. connect_timeout duration 30s How long a connection waits for the server to reach the destination. log_level string "info" Level of the MasterDnsVPN client's own messages: debug, info, warn or error. They appear in the sing-box log. udp_over_tcp object The UDP over TCP setting from sing-box, for a server that terminates it.

The sockets that send the DNS queries use the outbound's socket settings, such as bind_interface and routing_mark, and the platform's socket protection, so on a VPN the queries do not loop back into the tunnel. detour is not supported: the queries go out directly, and the log shows a warning.

Every other setting of the MasterDnsVPN client keeps the default of its sample configuration. The client's own resolver finder (client_resolvers.txt with ranges) is replaced by resolvers. hiddify-core's ray2sing reads two links into this outbound: masterdns://, which carries the same fields, and the dnst:// URL of the dnst URL spec (dnst://v.example.com/masterdns/socks?mkey=…&encryption=5), where the socks backend is this outbound alone and any other backend sets mode: tcp with that outbound in front. It also reads the masterdns:// profile link of WhiteDNS (base64url JSON, schema whitedns.profile). A link turns smart_pool on unless it says smart_pool=0 or lists an address range, and a link without resolvers (a dnst:// link names none) uses auto through the pool, or a list of well-known public resolvers without it.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• With many resolvers the start takes longer, because every one is MTU-tested first. Keep a list of resolvers that passed, and put the best ones first.
  • The key and the encryption method must match the server exactly, or the server drops every packet and the client never becomes ready.
  • Share links with the tunnel domain only with people you trust: a published domain is blocked within hours.

docs.text:
• DNSTT
  • Smart resolver pool
  • Monitoring
  • Fallback

docs.title: Mieru
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

Mieru is a proxy protocol from the mieru project. Every byte it sends is encrypted, with random padding, so the traffic has no fixed header or pattern to match. It runs over TCP or UDP. In a config it is the outbound "type": "mieru"; Hiddify also has a mieru inbound for running a server.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text: Use it to connect to a mieru server (the official mita server, or a sing-box mieru inbound). It needs no TLS certificate and no domain, and it can use a range of ports. It is a good choice where TLS-based protocols are blocked by SNI or certificate checks but random-looking traffic still gets through.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
Mieru does not imitate another protocol. Instead it gives a filter nothing to recognize: there is no plain-text handshake, no protocol header and no fixed packet size, because everything, including the first packet, is encrypted and padded. The server answers only clients that have a valid key, so a probe that sends random data gets no useful reply.

This does not help on networks that block traffic they cannot classify, or that allow only known protocols. Such networks often block fully random traffic, so test it on your network.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The encryption key comes from the user name, the password and the current time. The time is rounded to 2-minute steps, so the clocks of the client and the server must be within a few minutes of each other. If they are not, the connection fails.
  • The client connects to one of the server's port bindings, over TCP or UDP as the binding says.
  • Several proxied connections can share one underlying connection (multiplexing).
  • UDP traffic is carried inside the mieru stream, so UDP works on a TCP binding too.
  • With handshake_mode set to HANDSHAKE_NO_WAIT, the client sends the first data together with the connect request (0-RTT). With HANDSHAKE_STANDARD it waits until the server has connected to the destination (1-RTT).

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"outbounds": [
{
"type": "mieru",
"tag": "mieru-out",
"server": "203.0.113.10",
"portBindings": [
{ "protocol": "TCP", "portRange": "2012-2022" }
],
"username": "alice",
"password": "<password>",
"multiplexing": "MULTIPLEXING_LOW"
}
]
}

docs.title: Outbound fields
docs.text: Field Type Default Meaning server string required Server IP address or domain. server_port number none A single server port. If set, portBindings must hold exactly one binding with the same port. Usually leave it out and use portBindings. portBindings list required The server's ports. See below. username string required User name. password string required Password. multiplexing string "" How many connections share one underlying connection: ""/DEFAULT, LOW, MIDDLE (or MEDIUM), HIGH. The MULTIPLEXING_ prefix is optional. handshake_mode string "" ""/DEFAULT, STANDARD or NO_WAIT. The HANDSHAKE_ prefix is optional. network string both tcp, udp, or empty for both. Which kinds of proxied traffic this outbound accepts. Dialer fields The usual outbound dialer fields, such as detour.

docs.title: Port binding fields (portBindings)
docs.text:
Field Type Default Meaning protocol string required TCP or UDP. port number none One port. portRange string none A range of ports, such as "2012-2022".

Each binding must have either port or portRange, not both. Ports are from 1 to 65535.

docs.title: Inbound fields
docs.text:
The mieru inbound runs a mieru server. It takes the usual listen fields and:

Field Type Default Meaning users list required Users, each with username and password. portBindings list required Ports to listen on, same format as above. network string both tcp, udp, or empty for both.

If listen_port is set, portBindings must hold exactly one binding with the same port.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Values are case-insensitive. An unknown multiplexing or handshake_mode value, a missing user name or password, or a bad port binding stops the config from loading with an error that names the problem.
  • Mieru does not use TLS, so the tls block does not apply.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: • All Hiddify features

docs.title: Psiphon
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

The Psiphon outbound connects to the Psiphon network through the official Psiphon tunnel core, built into sing-box. Psiphon runs the servers, so you only need this outbound. It is an outbound: "type": "psiphon" in the outbounds list.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• You get a working proxy with no server of your own and no account.
  • It is a good last resort when your own servers are blocked: Psiphon keeps many servers and many ways to reach them, and updates its server list by itself.
  • You can pick the country the traffic leaves from with egress_region.

Psiphon is shared by many users. It is often slower than your own server, and it carries TCP only.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
Psiphon does the work, not sing-box. The tunnel core knows many Psiphon servers and several obfuscated protocols to reach them. It tries them until one connects, and downloads a signed, updated server list once it is in. When one server or protocol is blocked, it moves to another.

It does not help when the network blocks all traffic to the outside, or when every Psiphon server it knows is blocked and it cannot fetch a new list.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• At start, the outbound builds a Psiphon config (see config below), opens its data store in data_directory, and starts the tunnel core in the background. Startup does not wait for the tunnel.
  • Until the tunnel is up, the outbound shows "Connecting..." and connections through it fail. When the first tunnel is up, the mark goes away, and Hiddify's monitoring tests it at once.
  • The tunnel core makes its own connections to Psiphon servers. These go through this outbound's dial settings (for example detour), through a local SOCKS bridge, so they do not loop back into your VPN. If you set upstream_proxy_url, that proxy is used instead.
  • When the network changes, the outbound tells the tunnel core to reconnect.
  • When the tunnel core stops (it gives up after establish_tunnel_timeout, or fails), it is started again after 5 seconds, then twice as long each time, up to every 5 minutes; a connection resets the wait.
  • Several Psiphon outbounds can run at once, for example one per egress_region. Each keeps its downloads in data_directory/<tag>; what an earlier version kept in data_directory itself is moved there. The tunnel core reports its state without saying which outbound it is about, so next to other Psiphon outbounds each one checks its own tunnel before it shows as connected.
  • Each TCP connection is opened through the Psiphon tunnel to its real destination. UDP is not supported.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"type": "psiphon",
"tag": "psiphon",
"egress_region": "DE"
}
Field Type Default Meaning config string "" A Psiphon config to start from. "hiddify" uses the config built into the Hiddify app, if this build has one; otherwise a warning is logged and the defaults are used. Any other value is the Psiphon JSON config, either encrypted with this build's key or in base64. Empty means the defaults. data_directory string "data/psiphon" Where Psiphon keeps its data: each outbound in a folder named after its tag. egress_region string "" Two-letter country code of the exit server, for example "US" or "DE". Empty lets Psiphon choose. propagation_channel_id string "FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF" Psiphon client identity value. sponsor_id string "FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF" Psiphon client identity value. network_id string "test" Psiphon network ID. client_platform string built-in value Platform string sent to Psiphon. client_version string "" Version string sent to Psiphon. remote_server_list_url string Psiphon's public list URL Where to download the server list. remote_server_list_download_filename string "remote_server_list" File name for the downloaded list. remote_server_list_signature_public_key string Psiphon's public key Key that checks the list's signature. upstream_proxy_url string "" Send Psiphon's own connections through this proxy, for example socks5://127.0.0.1:1080. Empty uses the outbound's dial settings. allow_default_dns_resolver_with_bind_to_device bool true Let Psiphon use the system DNS resolver while bound to a network interface. establish_tunnel_timeout duration 1m How long the tunnel core tries to connect before it gives up. Values under one second count as one second.

The usual dial fields (detour, bind_interface and the rest) also apply, as described above. The network field is accepted but has no effect: the outbound is TCP only.

For each identity and server list field, the order is: the value set in the outbound, then the value in config, then the default.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Monitoring
  • Balancer

docs.title: Soar
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

Soar carries your TCP connections inside DNS queries and answers, through recursive resolvers, to a Soar server that you run as the authority for a delegated zone. It is an outbound: "type": "soar" in the outbounds list. The client is the Soar Go library from the Lantern team (github.com/getlantern/soar), used as it is.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• It works on networks where almost everything is blocked but DNS still passes, like the other DNS tunnels (DNSTT, MasterDNS).
  • It was designed against what censors and resolvers do: every resolver is a path with its own round-trip time, loss record, name and answer size limits and congestion window; losses are found fast at both ends and only the lost packets are sent again; the server holds idle queries and answers the moment it has data. Its project measures it ahead of the other DNS tunnels on lossy, rate-limited and Iran- and Russia-like networks, and it connects in about a second.
  • It finds working resolvers by itself (discovery): from the device's own, a curated list for the country, and public resolvers. A resolver is used only once the server's signed answer came back through it, so hijacking resolvers are left out by the same test.
  • The server connects to the destination itself: no SOCKS or SSH outbound behind it.

It is still a DNS tunnel: slow next to a direct proxy. The reference server only reaches public addresses on ports 80 and 443 unless it is started with -allow-ports.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
The filter sees DNS queries for names under your zone, sent to ordinary resolvers, which forward them to your server. Every session starts with an X25519 key exchange signed by the server's Ed25519 key, so a forged answer cannot authenticate and is ignored; data is sealed with ChaCha20-Poly1305. Names start at 101 characters, which networks that drop long names still pass, and grow only where they go through. Where UDP/53 is intercepted, DNS over TCP is used; where TXT records are refused, AAAA records carry the answers.

It does not help when no resolver you can reach forwards queries for your zone.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Session. The client handshakes at the first connection, then carries every connection as a stream of one session. A session without connections ends after session_idle, and the next connection opens a new one.
  • Resolvers written in the config. They go through the outbound's own smart resolver pool, on unless smart_pool is false: each is first sent a plain query (pretest_domain, pretest_record_type), and the ones that answer join the pool, up to 10 working, more when some go down. The client sees the pool as one resolver, on the loopback. Resolvers may then also be tcp://, DoT (dot://host:853) or DoH (https://host/dns-query). With smart_pool: false, each resolver is a path of the client's own, plain UDP (and TCP, see tcp) only.
  • auto, or no resolvers. The client's own discovery runs, the code of the Soar library: it tries the resolvers it verified on earlier runs (saved in the cache file), then the device's own (where the system lets it read them), the curated list of the country that Soar bundles (Iran, China, Russia), and global public resolvers; with sample_ranges, also addresses of the country's ranges. It keeps want working and looks for more when some stop. Its settings are smart_pool.discovery, the block every DNS tunnel shares; DNSTT and MasterDNS take the same candidates for their auto. These resolvers are paths of the client's own, next to the pool when the config also writes resolvers. hiddify-core sets discovery.country from the app's region when it is empty.
  • Sockets. The queries go out with the outbound's socket settings (bind_interface, routing_mark) and the platform's protection, so on a VPN they do not loop back into the tunnel; queries to the pool on the loopback use a plain socket. detour is not supported.

TCP only. UDP is not carried.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"type": "soar",
"tag": "soar-out",
"domain": "t.example.com",
"public_key": "<soar-server pubkey key>",
"resolvers": ["8.8.8.8", "1.1.1.1", "auto"],
"smart_pool": {
"enabled": true,
"discovery": { "country": "ir" }
}
}
Field Type Default Meaning domain string required The tunnel zone delegated to the server (soar-server -zone). public_key string required The server's Ed25519 public key, as soar-server pubkey prints it (base64; base64url and hex are read too). resolvers list of strings auto Resolvers: "8.8.8.8", "1.1.1.1:5353", or "auto" for Soar's discovery. With the smart pool also tcp://, dot://host:853 and https://host/dns-query. smart_pool bool or object on The smart pool for the resolvers written, as described above; false turns it off. The object takes the pool's settings, among them discovery, which also steers Soar's own discovery: country, sample_ranges, want (default 16 here), concurrency (16), pace (20ms). With the pool off, write {"enabled": false, "discovery": {...}}. pretest_domain string "www.google.com" With the pool: the name queried to check a resolver. pretest_record_type string "a" With the pool: the record type of that query. tcp string "auto" DNS over TCP: auto (for a resolver whose UDP never answers), on, only or off. off with the pool alone. safe_qname int 101 Name length every resolver starts at. max_qname int 253 Longest name a resolver is probed up to. max_answer int 1232 Largest DNS answer probed up to, in bytes. hold duration 500ms How long the server may hold an idle query. max_inflight int 128 Queries outstanding over all resolvers (at most 1024). max_path_window int 32; max_inflight with the pool alone Queries outstanding over one resolver. max_streams int 64 Connections open at once (at most 256). stream_window int 262144 Each connection's receive window, in bytes. send_buffer int 65536 Each connection's send buffer, in bytes. session_idle duration 90s A session without connections ends after this; keep it below the server's 2 minutes. connect_timeout duration 90s How long a connection waits for the session.

docs.title: Links
docs.text:
Soar defines no share link. hiddify-core's ray2sing reads soar:// in two forms:

  • The profile link of WhiteDNS, which exports and imports soar://<base64url JSON> with schema whitedns.profile: the server's domain and public_key, its resolvers and soarSettings (transport, discovery, country, name and answer sizes, windows, timeouts). Discovery on adds auto to the resolvers.
  • A URL: soar://t.example.com?pk=<public key>&resolvers=8.8.8.8,1.1.1.1&country=ir#name, or the key before the host, soar://<public key>@t.example.com?.... The key is written in base64url, or percent-encoded in the query. Every field of the table is a parameter, country, sample_ranges, discovery_want, discovery_concurrency and discovery_pace go into smart_pool.discovery, smart_pool=0 turns the pool off, discovery=1 adds auto to written resolvers; no resolvers means auto. masterdns and dnstt links take the same discovery parameters.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Soar is pre-release: its protocol may still change, and client and server must be of versions that speak the same one.
  • Anyone with the zone and the public key can use the server. Share them only with people you trust: a published zone is soon blocked.
  • The pool is one path for the client, so its per-resolver tuning (name length, answer size, window) applies to the pool as a whole. Without resolvers in the config, or with smart_pool: false, the client tunes every resolver separately.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Smart resolver pool
  • MasterDNS
  • DNSTT

docs.title: SSH: inbound and Hiddify additions
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

Upstream sing-box can only connect to an SSH server. Hiddify adds an SSH server (inbound, "type": "ssh" in the inbounds list), UDP for the SSH outbound through UDP over TCP, and a background connection that keeps the outbound ready. The rest of the SSH outbound works as in upstream sing-box and is documented there. This page covers only the Hiddify parts.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• You want a server that any SSH client can use as a proxy, with port forwarding (ssh -L) or as a SOCKS proxy (ssh -D), without giving users a shell on the machine.
  • You want UDP (for example DNS, QUIC or voice calls) through an SSH outbound. Plain SSH carries only TCP.
  • You want the SSH outbound connected, tested and shown as ready before the first connection goes through it.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
SSH is a common protocol for managing servers, and many networks leave it open. The traffic is encrypted, so a filter cannot see the sites you open.

It does not hide that the traffic is SSH. A filter can see the SSH handshake, and some networks slow down or block long or busy SSH sessions. Use it where SSH is allowed.

docs.title: Inbound
docs.text:
• The server listens on TCP and runs the SSH handshake with its host_key.
  • A user logs in with a password or a public key from users. Both checks look up the user by name.
  • The server accepts only port forwarding requests (direct-tcpip channels). Requests for a shell, a command or a subsystem are rejected. A forward request the server cannot read is refused alone; the SSH connection and its other forwards go on.
  • Each forwarded connection is routed like a connection from any other inbound. The user name is set, so stats and auth_user route rules work. Read and write deadlines work on forwarded connections.
  • A forwarded connection to the UDP over TCP address of sing-box carries UDP. So a Hiddify SSH outbound with udp_over_tcp can send UDP through this server. When network does not list udp, this is turned off.

docs.title: Outbound: UDP over TCP
docs.text:
With udp_over_tcp turned on, the outbound sends each UDP session inside a forwarded TCP connection, in the sing-box UDP over TCP format. The server must understand this format: the Hiddify SSH inbound does, a normal OpenSSH server does not.

Without udp_over_tcp, the outbound does not accept UDP, even when network lists udp. Route UDP to another outbound.

docs.title: Outbound: background connection
docs.text:
• After start, the outbound connects to the server in the background, without waiting for traffic. When the session drops, it connects again, waiting 1 second after a failure, then twice as long after each new failure, up to 1 minute.
  • When it connects, the outbound is tested at once by monitoring.
  • While it is not connected, the app shows it as connecting, and the last connection error as the proxy's error (not in its type). Monitoring skips the outbound until it is connected.
  • When the app does not ask to keep idle connections, the session closes after its last connection ends, and it is not opened again until the next connection.

docs.title: Inbound
docs.text:
{
"inbounds": [
{
"type": "ssh",
"tag": "ssh-in",
"listen": "::",
"listen_port": 2222,
"host_key": [
"-----BEGIN OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----\n...\n-----END OPENSSH PRIVATE KEY-----"
],
"users": [
{ "user": "alice", "password": "<password>" },
{ "user": "bob", "public_key": "ssh-ed25519 AAAA... bob@laptop" }
]
}
]
}
Field Type Default Meaning host_key list of strings required Private keys of the server, in PEM or OpenSSH format. A server without a host key cannot complete a handshake. users list of objects none Users who can log in. users[].user string none User name. users[].password string none Password. Leave it empty to turn off password login for this user. users[].public_key string none One public key, as a line of an authorized_keys file. Leave it empty to turn off key login for this user. server_version string Go SSH default The version string the server sends, such as SSH-2.0-OpenSSH_9.6. Without the SSH-2.0- prefix, it is added. host_key_algorithms list of strings all Host key algorithms the server offers. An RSA key signs only with the listed rsa-sha2-512, rsa-sha2-256 or ssh-rsa. Another key is used only when its type is listed, such as ssh-ed25519. If no host key is left, the config fails to load. network "tcp" or "udp" both Without udp, the server does not carry UDP over TCP. The server always listens on TCP.

The usual listen fields (listen, listen_port and the rest) work as for other inbounds.

docs.title: Outbound
docs.text:
{
"outbounds": [
{
"type": "ssh",
"tag": "ssh-out",
"server": "203.0.113.10",
"server_port": 2222,
"user": "alice",
"password": "<password>",
"udp_over_tcp": true
}
]
}
Field Type Default Meaning udp_over_tcp bool or object off Send UDP inside forwarded TCP connections. true uses version 2. The object form is {"enabled": true, "version": 1} or 2. network "tcp" or "udp" both Networks the outbound accepts. Upstream accepts only TCP. UDP is accepted only when udp_over_tcp is on.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Monitoring
  • PROXY protocol

docs.title: Sudoku
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

Sudoku is an encrypted proxy over TCP that hides its bytes as clues of small sudoku puzzles. You can tune the result to look like plain text or to have a fixed, low randomness instead of looking like random noise. It is the inbound and outbound "type": "sudoku". It carries TCP, and UDP inside the TCP connection. It is the Sudoku protocol of saba-futai/sudoku, which mihomo also supports, ported from sing-box-extended.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• The network blocks traffic that looks fully random, the way plain Shadowsocks or VMess does.
  • You want the traffic to look like plain text (prefer_ascii), or like HTTP from the first byte.
  • You want an HTTP or WebSocket tunnel that can run behind a CDN (stream, poll, ws).

The cost is speed: every byte you upload becomes at least four bytes on the wire.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
Some filters block connections whose bytes look completely random, because a normal protocol shows some structure. Sudoku never sends its encrypted bytes directly. It sends sudoku clues instead, and you choose how those look:

  • prefer_entropy (default): the bytes on the wire follow a fixed bit pattern, so the traffic is less random than encrypted data.
  • prefer_ascii: every byte on the wire is a printable character, so the traffic looks like text.
  • custom_table: you choose which bits of each byte carry the clue, so the pattern differs from other Sudoku servers.

The HTTP mask adds an HTTP request in front of the connection (legacy), or runs the whole connection as real HTTP or WebSocket requests that a CDN can forward (stream, poll, ws, auto).

Limits:

  • A filter can learn the byte pattern of a mode and block it. Tables and the HTTP mask make this harder, not impossible.
  • The legacy mask is one fake HTTP request followed by non-HTTP data. It does not pass a CDN or a filter that reads past the first request.
  • Without the HTTP mask and TLS, there is no TLS handshake, so a filter that allows only TLS blocks it.
  • It does not help when the server's IP address is blocked, unless you put it behind a CDN.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Each byte value has its own 4×4 sudoku grid, picked from the 288 possible grids by the key. The sender sends four clues, each a cell position and its value, that fit only that grid. The receiver finds the grid and gets the byte back. Each byte has many possible sets of clues, and the sender picks one at random and in random order.
  • Each clue is one byte on the wire, so upload traffic grows four times. Random padding bytes are mixed in as well (padding_min to padding_max).
  • Download traffic uses the same encoding by default. With enable_pure_downlink: false, it uses a packed form that is about one and a third times the data, which is faster.
  • Inside the encoding, the data is encrypted with aead_method. The handshake makes fresh session keys with X25519 and rejects replays.
  • The client and server clocks must be within 60 seconds of each other, or the handshake fails.
  • With multiplex: "on", many connections share one Sudoku session.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Needs the with_sudoku build tag. Without it, a config with "type": "sudoku" fails with "Sudoku is not included in this build, rebuild with -tags with_sudoku".

Server:

{
"type": "sudoku",
"tag": "sudoku-in",
"listen": "::",
"listen_port": 8443,
"key": "a long random password",
"table_type": "prefer_ascii"
}

Client:

{
"type": "sudoku",
"tag": "sudoku-out",
"server": "example.com",
"server_port": 8443,
"key": "a long random password",
"table_type": "prefer_ascii"
}

docs.title: Fields on both sides
docs.text:
These must be the same on the client and the server.

Field Type Default Meaning key string required The shared key. Either any password, or a key pair (see below). aead_method string chacha20-poly1305 Encryption of the data: chacha20-poly1305, aes-128-gcm or none. table_type string prefer_entropy How the bytes look on the wire: prefer_entropy, prefer_ascii, up_ascii_down_entropy or up_entropy_down_ascii. "up" is client to server, "down" is server to client. custom_table string "" Eight letters that set which bits of each byte carry what: exactly two x, two p and four v, for example xpxvvpvv. Used only in the entropy direction. custom_tables array of strings [] Several custom_table patterns. The client picks one per connection; the server finds out which one. Replaces custom_table when set. padding_min number 10 Least share of padding, in percent, 0 to 100. padding_max number 30 Most share of padding, in percent, 0 to 100. At least padding_min. enable_pure_downlink boolean true true encodes download traffic the same way as upload. false uses the packed form, which uses less data.

If you set only one of padding_min and padding_max, the other one moves to match it when the defaults would conflict.

When custom_table or custom_tables is set with an entropy upload direction, the server also accepts clients that use the default table, so clients can switch one by one.

docs.title: Server (inbound) fields
docs.text:
The usual listen fields (listen, listen_port, …), plus:

Field Type Default Meaning handshake_timeout number 5 Seconds to wait for the client's handshake. HTTP tunnel modes wait at least 15. disable_http_mask boolean false true turns the HTTP mask off. http_mask_mode string legacy legacy, stream, poll, ws or auto. auto accepts stream, poll and ws clients. path_root string "" A first path segment put before all HTTP mask paths, for example aabbcc gives /aabbcc/session. Letters, digits, _ and - only.

The inbound has no TLS. For HTTPS, put a CDN or a reverse proxy that ends TLS in front of it.

fallback is a host:port. A connection that is not Sudoku, such as a browser or a prober, is passed to it with what it already sent, so the server looks like the site there. It works when the HTTP mask is off (disable_http_mask); a connection that sends more than 64 KiB before failing is closed instead.

docs.title: Client (outbound) fields
docs.text:
The usual server and dial fields (server, server_port, detour, …), plus:

Field Type Default Meaning multiplex string off off, auto or on. on runs many connections over one Sudoku session. auto only reuses HTTP connections in the stream, poll and auto mask modes. http_mask object mask on, legacy The HTTP mask. Without this object the mask is on in legacy mode. http_mask.enabled boolean false Turns the mask on. Once you add http_mask, you must set this to true, or the mask is off. http_mask.mode string legacy legacy, stream, poll, ws or auto. auto tries stream, then poll. http_mask.host string "" Host header and TLS server name for stream, poll, ws and auto. Empty uses server. http_mask.path_root string "" Same as the server's path_root. http_mask.multiplex string "" Overrides multiplex when set. http_mask.tls object none A normal outbound TLS block. Used only by stream, poll, ws and auto.

docs.title: The HTTP mask on both sides
docs.text:
The client turns the mask on by default, and the server's mask follows disable_http_mask, which is also on by default. Keep both sides the same:

  • Client without http_mask, server without disable_http_mask: both use the legacy mask.
  • To turn it off, set "disable_http_mask": true on the server and give the client "http_mask": { "enabled": false }.
  • For a tunnel mode, set the same mode on both sides (or auto on the server), and the same path_root.

A legacy server also accepts clients without the mask. A server with the mask off does not accept masked clients. A server in stream, poll, ws or auto mode does not accept legacy clients.

docs.title: Keys
docs.text:
key is either:

  • A password: the same text on both sides.
  • A key pair: the server gets the public key (64 hex characters), and the client gets a private key (64 or 128 hex characters). The client can also use the public key itself. Several different private keys can belong to one public key, so each user can have their own.

This build has no command to make a key pair.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: A wrong table_type, custom_table, aead_method, padding, mode, multiplex or path_root, or an empty key, stops the config from loading, on both sides.

docs.title: Compatibility
docs.text: Tested only between two Hiddify sing-box instances: without the mask, with the HTTP mask, and with prefer_ascii. It has not been tested against the original Sudoku or mihomo.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Mieru
  • Shadowsocks obfs
  • XHTTP

docs.title: TrustTunnel
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

TrustTunnel is a VPN protocol published at trusttunnel.org. It carries your traffic as HTTP CONNECT requests inside an HTTPS connection, over HTTP/2 on TLS or over HTTP/3 on QUIC. Hiddify uses the sing-trusttunnel library. In a config it is the outbound "type": "trusttunnel", and the inbound of the same type runs a server.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text: Use it to connect to a TrustTunnel server, or run your own server with the trusttunnel inbound. It is a good choice where HTTPS to ordinary sites works but proxy protocols are blocked, and it can switch between TCP (HTTP/2) and UDP (HTTP/3) with one field.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
To a filter, a TrustTunnel connection is an HTTPS connection to your server's domain: a normal TLS handshake, then HTTP/2 or HTTP/3. The proxied traffic is inside the encrypted HTTP streams. The login is a standard Proxy-Authorization header inside that encryption.

The protection depends on your TLS setup. A real domain with a valid certificate looks like any HTTPS site. TLS features such as uTLS fingerprints and ECH come from the tls block. It does not help when the server's IP address or domain is blocked, and QUIC mode does not help where UDP or QUIC is blocked.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The client opens one TLS (or QUIC) connection to the server and sends each proxied TCP connection as an HTTP CONNECT request on its own stream. Many connections share the one connection.
  • UDP traffic goes through one CONNECT request to a special address (_udp2), with the packets framed inside the stream.
  • With health_check on, the client sends a small check request when the connection has been idle for 7 seconds, so a dead connection is found early.
  • When the network changes, the client drops its connections and opens new ones.
  • The server checks the user name and password of each request and refuses unknown users.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"outbounds": [
{
"type": "trusttunnel",
"tag": "trusttunnel-out",
"server": "vpn.example.com",
"server_port": 443,
"username": "alice",
"password": "<password>",
"tls": {
"enabled": true,
"server_name": "vpn.example.com"
}
}
]
}

docs.title: Outbound fields
docs.text: Field Type Default Meaning server string required Server address. server_port number required Server port. username string required User name. password string required Password. tls object required Outbound TLS settings. enabled must be true. quic bool false Use HTTP/3 over QUIC instead of HTTP/2 over TLS. quic_congestion_control string "bbr" QUIC congestion control: bbr, cubic or reno. An unknown value means bbr. health_check bool false Check the connection when it has been idle for 7 seconds. Dialer fields The usual outbound dialer fields, such as detour.

docs.title: Inbound fields
docs.text: Field Type Default Meaning users list required Users, each with username and password. network string both tcp (HTTP/2), udp (HTTP/3), or empty for both. quic_congestion_control string "bbr" Congestion control for HTTP/3 clients: bbr, cubic or reno. tls object Inbound TLS settings. Required when network includes udp. Listen fields The usual inbound listen fields, such as listen and listen_port.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• QUIC needs the with_quic build tag. Hiddify's builds include it. Without it, quic: true fails with a "QUIC is not included" error.
  • Without TLS, or without a user name and password, the outbound fails to load. The inbound fails to load without at least one user.
  • Each user name must have a password.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: • All Hiddify features

docs.title: Tunnel (reverse tunnel)
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

The tunnel endpoints connect several sing-box instances through one public server, so that a machine without a public address (behind NAT or a firewall) can still be reached. The server runs the endpoint "type": "tunnel_server" and each other machine runs "type": "tunnel_client". Each client keeps connections open to the server, and the server sends traffic for that client back down those connections. Every party has a UUID, and route rules choose the party that traffic goes to.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• Reach a home or office machine that has no public IP address, through a server that has one.
  • Connect two clients that cannot reach each other directly, through the server.
  • Use any proxy protocol between the clients and the server, for example VLESS with REALITY, so the tunnel gets that protocol's protection.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: The tunnel adds no obfuscation of its own. Its traffic travels inside the outbound you give the client and the inbound you give the server, so it looks exactly like that protocol. Choose a protocol that works on your network. Because the client always dials out to the server, it also works where incoming connections to the client are blocked.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Identities. Each client has a uuid (its public name, used in route rules) and a key (a secret, also in UUID format). The server has its own uuid and a list of users, each with the uuid and key of one client.
  • Standby connections. After start, each client opens 5 connections to the server through its outbound and keeps them ready. The server keeps up to 10 per client and closes the oldest when a new one arrives. If a connection fails, the client waits 5 seconds and tries again.
  • Control address. Tunnel connections go to the address sp.tunnel.sing-box.arpa:444 inside the outbound protocol. The server's inbound handles them. Other connections that reach that inbound are routed as usual, so the same inbound can also serve normal proxy users.
  • Sending traffic. A connection routed to the tunnel_client endpoint is sent to the server with the UUID of the party it is for (its tunnel destination). On the server it is routed again, with tunnel_source set to the sending client and tunnel_destination set to the target:
  • If the target is the server's own uuid, the server routes it like any other connection (for example to the internet).
  • If the target is another client, a rule sends it to the tunnel_server endpoint, which hands it to that client over one of its standby connections. The target client routes it with tunnel_source set to the sender.
  • Only TCP is carried. UDP is refused.
  • A connection whose destination is the sender itself is refused as a routing loop.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Server:

{
"endpoints": [
{
"type": "tunnel_server",
"tag": "tunnel",
"uuid": "00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001",
"users": [
{
"uuid": "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111",
"key": "aaaaaaaa-aaaa-aaaa-aaaa-aaaaaaaaaaaa"
},
{
"uuid": "22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222",
"key": "bbbbbbbb-bbbb-bbbb-bbbb-bbbbbbbbbbbb"
}
],
"inbound": {
"type": "vless",
"tag": "tunnel-in",
"listen": "::",
"listen_port": 443,
"users": [{ "uuid": "cccccccc-cccc-cccc-cccc-cccccccccccc" }]
}
}
],
"route": {
"rules": [
{
"tunnel_destination": ["22222222-2222-2222-2222-222222222222"],
"outbound": "tunnel"
}
]
}
}

Client:

{
"endpoints": [
{
"type": "tunnel_client",
"tag": "tunnel",
"uuid": "11111111-1111-1111-1111-111111111111",
"key": "aaaaaaaa-aaaa-aaaa-aaaa-aaaaaaaaaaaa",
"outbound": {
"type": "vless",
"tag": "tunnel-out",
"server": "203.0.113.10",
"server_port": 443,
"uuid": "cccccccc-cccc-cccc-cccc-cccccccccccc"
}
}
]
}

docs.title: tunnel_client fields
docs.text: Field Type Default Meaning uuid string required This client's UUID. Others use it as a tunnel destination. key string required This client's secret, in UUID format. It must match a user key on the server. outbound object required A full outbound (with type, tag and its fields) that reaches the server's inbound.

docs.title: tunnel_server fields
docs.text: Field Type Default Meaning uuid string required The server's UUID. Traffic for this UUID leaves through the server. users list none The clients, each with uuid and key. inbound object required A full inbound (with type, tag and its fields) that the clients connect to. connect_timeout duration 5s How long to wait for a free standby connection of the target client.

docs.title: Route rule fields
docs.text: Field Where Meaning tunnel_source route and DNS rules, rule sets Matches the UUID of the party that sent the connection. tunnel_destination route and DNS rules, rule sets Matches the UUID the connection is for. override_tunnel_destination route and route-options actions Sets the UUID a connection is for.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• A new connection gets its tunnel destination from the override_tunnel_destination of a route or route-options action. Both endpoints refuse a connection without one ("tunnel destination not set").
  • An unknown client key, or a target UUID that is not a user, is refused and logged.
  • All UUIDs and keys must be valid UUIDs, or the config fails to load.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: • All Hiddify features

docs.title: VLESS encryption
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

VLESS encryption is Xray's encryption layer for VLESS, mlkem768x25519plus. It encrypts the VLESS stream with keys agreed through a hybrid post-quantum handshake (ML-KEM-768 and X25519), so VLESS can run safely without TLS, or inside any transport. It is the encryption field of a VLESS outbound and the decryption field of a VLESS inbound. The strings are the same as Xray's.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• To connect to Xray servers that require VLESS encryption.
  • To run VLESS without TLS, or behind a CDN or proxy that ends TLS, and still have the content encrypted end to end between client and server.
  • To add Vision (xtls-rprx-vision) on top of the encryption when there is no TLS.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
With the random mode, everything on the wire, including the handshake, looks like random bytes, with no protocol header for a filter to match. xorpub hides only the public keys in the handshake; native sends the handshake as is. Padding settings in the string change the sizes of the first packets.

Random-looking traffic is itself blocked on some networks. In those places, use encryption inside a transport that looks like normal web traffic (such as XHTTP or WebSocket with TLS) rather than bare.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The client string lists the server's public keys; the server string has the matching private keys. Several keys in a row form a chain, and both sides must list the same number in the same order.
  • 1rtt does the full handshake on every connection. 0rtt reuses a ticket from the server, so later connections send data at once. The server decides how long tickets last.
  • The encryption runs inside TLS and the transport, right under VLESS, so it works with every transport. On a server, kTLS is turned off when decryption is set.
  • If the handshake fails or the connection's context ends first, the connection is closed.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Client:

{
"outbounds": [
{
"type": "vless",
"server": "203.0.113.1",
"server_port": 8443,
"uuid": "bf000d23-0752-40b4-affe-68f7707a9661",
"encryption": "mlkem768x25519plus.random.0rtt.<server public key>"
}
]
}

Server:

{
"inbounds": [
{
"type": "vless",
"listen": "::",
"listen_port": 8443,
"users": [{ "uuid": "bf000d23-0752-40b4-affe-68f7707a9661" }],
"decryption": "mlkem768x25519plus.random.600s.<server private key>"
}
]
}
Field Type Default Meaning encryption (outbound) string "" none or empty: no encryption. Otherwise mlkem768x25519plus.<mode>.<rtt>[.<padding>…].<key>[.<key>…]. decryption (inbound) string "" none or empty: no encryption. Otherwise mlkem768x25519plus.<mode>.<seconds>[.<padding>…].<key>[.<key>…].

Parts of the string, separated by dots:

Part Values Meaning <mode> native, xorpub, random native: plain handshake. xorpub: the public keys in the handshake are hidden. random: all bytes look random. Both sides must use the same mode. <rtt> (client) 0rtt, 1rtt Reuse server tickets, or do the full handshake every time. <seconds> (server) such as 600s or 300-600s How long a ticket stays valid. <padding> Xray padding segments Optional; sizes and delays of padding on the first packets, as in Xray. <key> (client) base64url X25519 public key (32 bytes) or ML-KEM-768 encapsulation key (1184 bytes). <key> (server) base64url X25519 private key (32 bytes) or ML-KEM-768 seed (64 bytes).

Keys and complete strings can be made with Xray's xray vlessenc command. A string with a wrong prefix, mode, RTT value or key length is a configuration error.

Vision: in Hiddify, flow: "xtls-rprx-vision" on the outbound also works over VLESS encryption with no TLS or REALITY; it needs one of the two. With random mode Vision does not splice (copy directly between sockets). When multiplex is enabled, the flow is turned off, since Vision cannot run over a multiplexed connection.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• REALITY in Hiddify
  • XHTTP transport

docs.title: WARP over MASQUE
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

WARP over MASQUE connects you to Cloudflare's free WARP VPN with MASQUE, the protocol the official WARP apps now use. Your IP packets travel inside an HTTP CONNECT-IP request, over HTTP/3 (QUIC) or HTTP/2 (TLS over TCP). It is an outbound, "type": "masque" in the outbounds list, and runs a device enrolled elsewhere: it registers none.

This page is about MASQUE to WARP. The same tunnel runs in two places:

  • The warp endpoint with masque set (recommended): one endpoint that registers the device, looks up endpoints, and runs WireGuard, AmneziaWG or MASQUE. Its display type is WARP · MASQUE. See WARP.
  • The masque outbound, described here, which runs the device it is given (device) and registers none.

For your own MASQUE server, use the masque-client and masque-server types from upstream sing-box (RFC 9484 CONNECT-IP, with a path, a username and password, and the usual TLS settings). They are documented there.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• It works where WireGuard is blocked: the tunnel looks like HTTPS traffic to Cloudflare.
  • With vhttp set to auto, it falls back to HTTP/2 over TCP when UDP or QUIC is blocked.
  • Like WARP, it needs no server of your own.

Choose WARP when WireGuard works on your network. It has less overhead.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
The tunnel is a TLS connection to Cloudflare with the server name consumer-masque.cloudflareclient.com, over QUIC or over TCP. To a filter it looks like any other HTTPS connection to Cloudflare. Over HTTP/2, the tls block can also split the ClientHello (fragment, record_fragment).

When HTTP/3 is blocked, auto moves to HTTP/2. When an address or port is blocked, the scanner finds another one that answers.

Limits: a filter that blocks Cloudflare's MASQUE addresses (162.159.198.0/24 and 2606:4700:103::/64) blocks this outbound. The server name is fixed by Cloudflare, so a filter that blocks that name also blocks it, unless you change server_name to one Cloudflare still accepts.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Device. The outbound needs device: a device Cloudflare enrolled for MASQUE (its key, its tunnel addresses and the endpoints), as masque:// share links carry it. It never reaches Cloudflare's API and never registers a device. A config without device fails to load with "masque outbound needs a device (an enrolled MASQUE key); to register a WARP device, use the warp endpoint with mode masque".

When Cloudflare refuses the device (a key that was never enrolled, or a device that was deleted), the tunnel keeps trying, and the outbound reports the refusal as why it is not ready. It does not register a replacement. The warp endpoint with mode masque takes such a device as masque.device and, once Cloudflare refuses it, goes on with its saved or newly registered devices; see WARP.

masque:// links. hiddify-core reads a masque:// link to Cloudflare's WARP (an endpoint in WARP's ranges or under cloudflareclient.com, or Cloudflare's server name, or none) as a warp endpoint with mode masque, with the link's key as masque.device, or with none when the link has no key. Only a link to another MASQUE server becomes this outbound, and it needs its key.

HTTP version. vhttp chooses how the tunnel connects:

  • h3: HTTP/3 over QUIC only.
  • h2: HTTP/2 over TLS and TCP only.
  • auto: HTTP/3 starts first. HTTP/2 starts too after 3 seconds, or at once if HTTP/3 fails. The first to connect wins, and a late success of the other is closed. Some networks drop QUIC without an error, so HTTP/3 would only stall; this keeps the wait short.

In auto, an HTTP/2 win is remembered so the next connects go straight to HTTP/2. It is remembered for 1 second, then 10 seconds, 30 seconds, 5 minutes and 10 minutes, one step longer for each HTTP/2 win in a row. An HTTP/3 win starts over. This way a short HTTP/3 refusal doesn't keep the tunnel on HTTP/2 for good. If the remembered HTTP/2 fails, the next connect tries HTTP/3 first again.

Endpoints. Without the scanner, the tunnel uses the profile's HTTP/3 endpoint and 162.159.198.2 for HTTP/2, on port 443, or on the port a device endpoint was given with.

Scanner. With scanner.enabled, the outbound looks for an endpoint that answers before it connects. The scanner works as in WARP, with these differences:

  • A probe is the handshake the tunnel starts with: a QUIC handshake for HTTP/3, or a TLS handshake over TCP for HTTP/2. It uses the tunnel's TLS settings and the outbound's dialer.
  • HTTP/3 and HTTP/2 endpoints are different servers, so they are scored apart. In auto, both are scanned.
  • The default ranges are what Cloudflare serves. Over QUIC only 162.159.198.1, 162.159.198.2, 2606:4700:103::1 and 2606:4700:103::2 answer. Over HTTP/2 all of 162.159.198.0/24 and 2606:4700:103::/64 answer, except the first address. The default ports are 443, 500, 1701, 4443, 4500, 8095 and 8443. UDP 443 is often blocked, so the HTTP/3 scan mostly searches the ports.
  • With use_ipv6, only IPv6 endpoints are scanned.

Failover. Each connect of the tunnel counts for its endpoint: a success adds to its score, a failure takes from it. After two failed connects in a row on one HTTP version, the tunnel scans for the best other endpoint of that version and switches to it. If none answers, it keeps the current one.

Network change. After a network change, the outbound names the new network (for the scores) and drops the tunnel connection. The next use connects again.

Connected state. The outbound counts as connected (no "Connecting...") only while it has a connection to Cloudflare's server, not as soon as it is set up; when the connection drops, through a detour or otherwise, it shows as connecting until it reconnects. Its display type is WARP · MASQUE, with the scanner status after it as for WARP.

Group detour. When detour is a group, the tunnel reconnects when the group moves to another member.

Through a proxy. QUIC reads each packet into a buffer of about one packet. A proxy that decrypts in place, like Shadowsocks, needs more room, so each packet is read whole from a proxy's packet connection and then copied. Before, a full packet was cut off and the HTTP/3 tunnel never connected through Shadowsocks, VLESS or Trojan.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"outbounds": [
{
"type": "masque",
"tag": "warp-masque",
"vhttp": "auto",
"device": {
"private_key": "MHcCAQEEI...",
"ipv4": "172.16.0.2",
"endpoint_v4": "162.159.198.2:443"
},
"scanner": {
"enabled": true
}
}
],
"route": {
"final": "warp-masque"
}
}
Field Type Default Meaning device object required A device already enrolled for MASQUE, used as is: no call to Cloudflare's API. See below. vhttp string auto h3, h2 or auto. Empty means auto, or h2 when use_http2 is on. use_http2 bool false Older way to choose HTTP/2. vhttp takes priority. server_name string consumer-masque.cloudflareclient.com TLS server name. use_ipv6 bool false Connect to Cloudflare over IPv6. The profile has no IPv6 HTTP/2 endpoint, so auto uses HTTP/2 only when the scanner finds one and otherwise stays on HTTP/3; h2 needs the scanner. scanner object off Endpoint scanner and failover. Same fields as in WARP. tls object TLS settings. See below. udp_timeout duration sing-box default Idle timeout of UDP sessions in the tunnel. udp_keepalive_period duration 30s QUIC keepalive period. udp_initial_packet_size number QUIC default QUIC initial packet size. When set, path MTU discovery is off. mtu number 1280 MTU of the tunnel, 1280 to 9000. Over HTTP/3, a packet larger than the path carries gets an ICMP "packet too big" back, so TCP adjusts to it. reconnect_delay duration 0 Wait between failed connects of the tunnel. unique_identifier string the tag Key of the scanner scores in the cache file.

Dial fields (detour, bind_interface and the rest) apply to the tunnel, the scanner probes and the network name check.

docs.title: device
docs.text:
A device enrolled elsewhere, as masque:// share links carry it. Cloudflare's API is not reached, so it works where the API is blocked; the keys must belong to a device that Cloudflare enrolled for MASQUE.

Field Type Default Meaning private_key string The device's ECDSA key: base64 (standard or URL) of SEC 1 or PKCS #8 DER. endpoint_public_key string the edge's The endpoint's key: PEM, or base64 of PKIX DER. Cloudflare's MASQUE edge presents one fixed certificate on every endpoint and port, and its key is built in, so links that carry no key (MahsaNG's) still pin the endpoint. ipv4, ipv6 string Tunnel addresses. At least one. endpoint_v4, endpoint_v6 string HTTP/3 endpoints, an IP or ip:port; the port of the first one given is used, 443 without one. At least one. endpoint_h2_v4, endpoint_h2_v6 string Cloudflare's HTTP/2 endpoints. id, license string The device's ID and license, for information.

A device that cannot work (a key that does not parse, no address, no endpoint) fails the config. A device Cloudflare refuses is not replaced; see "How it works". profile is no longer read: the outbound registers no device.

docs.title: scanner defaults for MASQUE
docs.text:
Field Default ports 443, 500, 1701, 4443, 4500, 8095, 8443 cidrs HTTP/3: 162.159.198.1/32, 162.159.198.2/32, 2606:4700:103::1/128, 2606:4700:103::2/128. HTTP/2: 162.159.198.0/24, 2606:4700:103::/64.

The other scanner fields and their defaults are the same as in WARP.

docs.title: tls
docs.text:
Field Type Default Meaning insecure bool false Don't check that the server's key is the one in the profile. certificate_public_key_sha256 list of strings Check the server by the SHA-256 (hex) of its certificate's public key instead, one of these; Xray's pinnedPeerPublicKeySha256. cipher_suites list of strings TLS cipher suites to offer. curve_preferences list of strings Key exchange curves to offer. fragment bool false Split the ClientHello into TCP segments (HTTP/2). fragment_fallback_delay duration As in a TLS block's fragment_fallback_delay. record_fragment bool false Split the ClientHello into TLS records (HTTP/2). kernel_tx, kernel_rx bool false Use kernel TLS. Linux only.

Notes:

  • The outbound needs the with_masque build tag. It is in the default tags of the Makefile. Without it, the config fails to load with "MASQUE outbound is not included in this build".
  • The scanner scores live in the cache file, under unique_identifier or the tag. Without cache_file, the scanner starts with no history.
  • The tunnel starts in the background. Connections wait for the first start to finish. If it failed, they fail with "tunnel not initialized".
  • When a connect fails, the tunnel logs the error and tries again after reconnect_delay.
