docs.text: • WARP

docs.title: WARP scanner and noise
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

How a WARP endpoint finds a way through a network that blocks it: the endpoint scanner looks for a Cloudflare address and port that answers, noise sends a few decoy packets before each WireGuard handshake, the noise search tries ready-made noises when the configured one gets no answer, and auto mode races WireGuard, AmneziaWG and MASQUE. This page explains how they work together. The fields are listed on the WARP page.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• Many filters block WARP by the first packets of a flow: a WireGuard handshake initiation is easy to recognise (fixed size, fixed first bytes). Noise changes what the flow starts with.
  • Filters block some Cloudflare addresses or ports and not others; the scanner finds one that works and remembers it for each network.
  • A noise that works on one network can fail on another. The noise search finds one that works on the network you are on, and remembers it too.
  • Auto mode does the same for the tunnel: on a network where UDP is throttled MASQUE may win, elsewhere WireGuard.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
A filter that classifies a UDP flow by its first packets sees something else first:

Noise What the filter sees first random (default) short packets that start like a QUIC long header, then random bytes raw random bytes of random sizes, no structure at all quic a real QUIC version 1 Initial, with a TLS ClientHello for www.google.com packets whatever the templates build: a DNS query, a SIP request, a QUIC packet

The WireGuard handshake follows in the same flow. A filter that only looks at the start lets it through; one that keeps watching the whole flow can still find WireGuard, and then MASQUE (HTTPS to Cloudflare) is the way out.

docs.title: Noise modes
docs.text:
The noise of the wireguard and warp endpoints (noise.fake_packet) is sent before each handshake initiation, count packets with a random delay between them:

  • Default mode (no mode): each packet is one byte from header (or none), the bytes 00 00 00 01 08, 8 random bytes, 00 00 44 D0, then size random bytes. This came from GFW-knocker; it starts like a QUIC long header.
  • raw: size random bytes, nothing else. This is Xray's WARP noise (wnoise=random) and AmneziaWG's junk packets.
  • quic: real QUIC Initials for sni (www.google.com by default): the first carries the ClientHello, the others PING frames, as QUIC retransmissions would.
  • packets: templates sent first, in order, in the AmneziaWG i1–i5 syntax: <b 0xHEX> bytes, <r N> random bytes, <rc N> random letters and digits, <rd N> random digits, <t> the Unix time (4 bytes), <qi SNI> a QUIC Initial. Then the count packets of the mode.

With awg, AmneziaWG sends its own noise instead: i1–i5, then jc junk packets of jmin to jmax bytes. Cloudflare only accepts standard WireGuard messages, so for WARP the AmneziaWG headers h1–h4 stay 1–4 and s1–s4 stay 0: only the packets before the handshake change.

docs.title: Noise presets
docs.text:
Taken from WARP configs that work (Xray links and AmneziaWG "WG Mimic" configs). Each works as WireGuard noise and as AmneziaWG settings.

Preset Sends before the handshake Looks like xray-random 5 random packets of 5 to 10 bytes, 2 to 5 ms apart nothing in particular: tiny packets break a size-based fingerprint quic 2 to 4 QUIC Initials for www.google.com the start of an HTTP/3 connection to Google dns-google 3 DNS queries for google.com (A, AAAA, HTTPS), each with a random id, then 6 junk packets of 56 to 160 bytes DNS traffic dns-cloudflare 2 DNS queries for cloudflare.com (A, AAAA), then 9 junk packets of 81 to 224 bytes DNS traffic to Cloudflare dns-www-cloudflare 2 DNS queries for www.cloudflare.com (A, AAAA), then 6 junk packets of 43 to 109 bytes DNS traffic to Cloudflare quic-mimic a recorded QUIC Initial (1,210 bytes: 276 recorded, 934 random) and a short-header packet, then 4 junk packets of 60 to 199 bytes a QUIC connection sip a SIP INVITE and its 100 Trying answer, then 10 junk packets of 42 to 224 bytes a VoIP call setup stun 2 STUN Binding Requests, each with a random transaction id, then 4 junk packets of 40 to 120 bytes a video call or WebRTC client checking its address

As AmneziaWG settings, a preset's templates become i1, i2, … and its junk jc, jmin, jmax; quic becomes <qi www.google.com> packets. awg mode without awg settings uses dns-google.

The presets are not only for WARP: any WireGuard endpoint takes one as its noise mode ("mode": "sip"), and any AmneziaWG endpoint as its ip ("ip": "sip"). dns and random are short for dns-google and xray-random.

docs.title: Endpoint scanner
docs.text:
With scanner.enabled, before it connects WARP probes endpoints (address and port) with a real WireGuard handshake made with the device's own key, after the same noise the tunnel will send, through the endpoint's dialer (so detour applies). Endpoints are tried in this order: the ones that worked on this network, by score; then ones that scored well elsewhere; then random addresses in cidrs on ports; the lowest scores last. The scan stops when an endpoint with a score of 3 or more answers, or 4 have answered, and the best is used. Scores (-10 to 10 per endpoint and network) are kept in the cache file; a network is named by its interface type, country and public address range. After a network change, and when traffic goes out with no handshake for 3 minutes, the endpoint in use is probed again and replaced when it no longer answers.

For MASQUE the scanner probes with a TLS handshake to the MASQUE endpoints, over HTTP/3 and HTTP/2 apart.

docs.title: Noise search
docs.text:
With scanner.search_noise, the scanner also looks for a noise:

  1. It scans with the noise that got through on this network before, if any.
  2. If no endpoint answers, with the configured noise (noise, or the awg settings).
  3. If still none, with each preset of noise_presets (all, in the order above, by default), on at most 16 endpoints each: the endpoints known to answer come first, so a few are enough to tell.
  4. The first noise that gets an answer is used: the tunnel starts with it, and it is saved for the network and tried first there next time.

The probe always sends what the tunnel sends, so a noise that gets the probe through gets the tunnel through. Each search costs at most the number of presets times 16 probes, run 8 at once.

docs.title: Auto mode
docs.text:
With "mode": "auto", WARP has a WireGuard, an AmneziaWG and a MASQUE device of its own, and starts by racing the three tunnels:

  1. One handshake with each at once, to the device's own endpoint: WireGuard with the endpoint's noise, AmneziaWG with its awg settings (or dns-google), MASQUE with a TLS handshake. Two tries each, within 5 seconds.
  2. The fastest that answered becomes the inner tunnel. WARP · Auto 🔍 Searching... shows during the race, then WARP · WG, WARP · AWG or WARP · MASQUE.
  3. The chosen tunnel then runs as in its own mode: the scanner and the noise search apply to it (the WireGuard scanner for WireGuard and AmneziaWG, the MASQUE scanner for MASQUE).
  4. The chosen tunnel has 20 seconds to connect. An answer to one handshake does not prove that the tunnel carries traffic: when it does not connect, the race runs again without it, and when every tunnel failed it starts over.
  5. When none answered, WireGuard is used, so the scanner and the noise search can still look for an endpoint and a noise.
  6. When a group detour moves to another member, the race runs again: the new proxy may carry another tunnel better, or only one (a proxy without UDP, such as SOCKS4, carries MASQUE over HTTP/2 only). After a selector the user moved, at once; after a group that moved by itself (a URL test, a balancer), at most every 30 seconds, through a new tunnel next to the one in use that replaces it only once it connects (see group detour). A network change forgets which tunnels failed.
  7. While the endpoint has not been connected for 3 minutes, it races again, at most every 10 minutes, and moves to another tunnel that answers.

The race uses the configured noise, not the presets: the noise search runs inside the tunnel that was chosen.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Search endpoints and noise, with auto mode:

{
"experimental": {
"cache_file": { "enabled": true, "store_warp_config": true }
},
"endpoints": [
{
"type": "warp",
"tag": "warp",
"mode": "auto",
"noise": {
"fake_packet": { "enabled": true, "mode": "quic", "count": "2-4", "delay": "10-30" }
},
"scanner": { "enabled": true, "search_noise": true }
}
]
}

Only some presets, in this order:

"scanner": { "enabled": true, "search_noise": true, "noise_presets": ["dns-google", "sip", "quic-mimic"] }

A DNS-looking noise for plain WireGuard, written by hand:

"noise": {
"fake_packet": {
"enabled": true,
"packets": ["<r 2><b 0x0100000100000000000106676f6f676c6503636f6d00000100010000291000000000000000>"],
"mode": "raw",
"count": "6",
"size": "56-160"
}
}
Field Where Meaning scanner.enabled warp Scan for an endpoint that answers, and fail over. scanner.search_noise warp Also look for a noise preset that gets through. scanner.noise_presets warp The presets to try, in order; all when empty. An unknown name is a config error. noise.fake_packet.mode warp, wireguard "", raw or quic. noise.fake_packet.packets warp, wireguard Templates sent first, in the AmneziaWG i1–i5 syntax. mode warp wg, awg, masque or auto.

The other scanner fields (ports, cidrs, max_rtt, timeout, count, concurrency) are on the WARP page.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The scores and the noise found are kept in the cache file; without cache_file, every start scans from nothing.
  • The scanner is off when server is set.
  • Noise does not help against a filter that blocks all UDP, or all of Cloudflare's WARP ranges: then auto mode, or masque with vhttp auto (HTTP/2 over TCP), is the way.

docs.text:

docs.title: WARP
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

WARP connects you to Cloudflare's free WARP VPN over WireGuard, over AmneziaWG when you set awg, or over MASQUE (HTTP/3 or HTTP/2) when you set masque. It registers a free WARP account by itself, so you don't need a key or a server. It can also send fake packets before each handshake, look for a Cloudflare address that answers, and switch to another one when the address in use stops working. It is an endpoint: "type": "warp" in the endpoints list.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• You get a working VPN with no server of your own and no account setup.
  • The traffic leaves from a Cloudflare address, which many sites trust more than a VPS address.
  • The scanner finds an address and port that work on your current network, and remembers them per network. When you move from home Wi-Fi to mobile data, it starts from what worked there before.

If your network blocks UDP, or blocks WireGuard even with noise, set masque: the tunnel then runs over HTTP/3, or HTTP/2 on TCP. See WARP over MASQUE for how MASQUE gets past filtering.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
• Noise. Before each WireGuard handshake, WARP can send a few fake packets. Some filters only look at the first packets of a UDP flow, and a flow that starts with something else is not seen as WireGuard. In quic mode the fake packets are real QUIC version 1 Initial packets with a TLS ClientHello for a well-known name (www.google.com by default). A filter that decrypts QUIC Initials sees the start of a normal QUIC connection to that site.
  • Other addresses and ports. Cloudflare serves WARP on many addresses and ports. When the default one is blocked, the scanner finds one that is not.
  • A new source port. When handshakes keep failing, the WireGuard device opens a new socket on a new source port. This helps when a filter has flagged one connection, or when a NAT mapping expired while the device slept.

Limits: noise does not help against a filter that blocks all UDP, or all traffic to Cloudflare's WARP ranges. The traffic is still WireGuard after the noise, so a filter that checks the whole flow can still find it.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Devices. WARP needs a device registered with Cloudflare for each tunnel: a WireGuard one, an AmneziaWG one (a WireGuard device of its own) and a MASQUE one (a device given a MASQUE key). In awg mode alone, a saved WireGuard device is taken when there is no AmneziaWG one, so the device of an earlier version keeps working. Every device registered is kept in one pool in the cache file (key warp-profiles) unless cache_file.store_warp_config is false (it is on by default), shared by all warp endpoints. Each endpoint leases its own devices: two endpoints on one device would push each other off Cloudflare. It takes, in order:

  1. A profile written in the config itself (private_key, interface, peers), for WireGuard; for MASQUE, masque.device, a device enrolled elsewhere (a masque:// link's). When Cloudflare refuses that device (its key was never enrolled, or the device was deleted), WARP remembers it in the cache file, goes on with 2 and 3, and does not try it again while the config carries it.
  2. A device of the kind from the pool that is not retired nor leased by another endpoint: the one this endpoint (by unique_identifier, or the tag) used before, else any free one. Not with profile.recreate (then each start registers a new one). A closed endpoint gives its devices back.
  3. A new device, registered with Cloudflare's API. With profile.id and profile.auth_token, that device is taken instead, until it is retired. With profile.license, the license (for example a WARP+ key) is applied to a new WireGuard device. The requests go through profile.detour when set; if that fails, WARP tries again through each outbound in turn. A failed registration is tried again after 1 s, then after twice as long each time, up to every 30 s, until it works or the endpoint closes.

Devices saved by earlier versions (one per key) are taken into the list.

When a device is given up. A network that blocks WARP is not a reason for a new device: a new one would be blocked the same way, and Cloudflare limits registrations. When WARP has not been connected for 3 minutes, it asks Cloudflare about the device in use, at most every 10 minutes. Only when Cloudflare answers that the device is gone (HTTP 401, 403, 404 or 410), disabled, or that its account used up its quota, is the device retired: WARP starts again with the next saved device, or registers a new one. When the API cannot be reached, or it says the device is fine, the device stays in use. A device in the config is never retired.

Tunnel. mode picks the tunnel:

  • wg: WireGuard, the default.
  • awg: AmneziaWG, with the awg settings, or without them those of the dns-google noise preset. An awg block without mode means awg too.
  • masque: MASQUE, over HTTP/3 or HTTP/2. A masque block (any setting, or enabled) without mode means masque too. The scanner then looks for MASQUE endpoints. server and server_port set the MASQUE server.
  • auto: WARP gets a WireGuard, an AmneziaWG and a MASQUE device, then makes one handshake with each tunnel at once (WireGuard with the endpoint's noise, AmneziaWG with its awg settings, MASQUE with its masque settings), two tries each within 5 seconds, and runs the fastest that answered. Each tunnel has its own device, so the handshakes do not share a key, and they are handshakes rather than whole tunnels so the race costs nothing once it is over. When none answers it uses WireGuard, so the scanner and the port rotation can still find a way. While it has not been connected for 3 minutes it races again (at most every 10 minutes) and moves to another tunnel that answers. server and server_port apply to the WireGuard peer only. Until it has chosen, the display type is WARP · Auto, with 🔍 Searching... during the race.

Without mode, awg and masque together are a config error. When the first start fails (AmneziaWG fails at once when its detour does not work yet), it is tried again in the same way as registration.

Peer. The tunnel uses the profile's IPv4 peer address (its IPv6 one when there is no IPv4 one) and one of its ports, chosen at random. server and server_port replace them. Without the scanner and without server_port, a port that completes no handshake within 10 seconds is replaced by the profile's next port; "rotate_ports": false turns this off. fallback_address lists other WARP addresses to try, on the same port, when the one in use gets no handshake in 15 seconds (the WireGuard fallback_address). For every warp endpoint behind a detour (the extra security hop, WARP in WARP) hiddify-core turns the rotation off and gives an IPv6 WARP address here, so it tries only the profile's IPv4 address, which needs smaller packets and works through proxies without IPv6, and then that IPv6 address.

Connected state. The peer gets a keepalive every 25 seconds, as in the WARP apps, so the handshake stays fresh while the path works. WARP counts as connected (no "Connecting...") only while the last handshake is less than 3 minutes old; through a detour that stops working, it shows as connecting again. Over MASQUE, it counts as connected while it has a connection to the server.

Status and display type. The type shown for the endpoint names the tunnel: WARP · WG, WARP · AWG or WARP · MASQUE; then, once the scanner has chosen, · 🔍 <address:port> or · 🔍 Not found. The status is not in the type; the app shows it from the status the core sends, as for every outbound and endpoint:

Status When registering A device is being registered. searching The scanner looks for an endpoint that answers. connecting It has not connected yet. reconnecting It was connected and the peer stopped answering. failed The config cannot work (a profile without peers, MASQUE not in the build); the type then ends with why, : <error>. ready It carries traffic.

For example WARP · MASQUE · 🔍 162.159.198.1:443, or, failed, WARP · WG: <error>.

Group detour. When detour is a group (a selector, URL test or balancer), WARP follows the member it resolves to, through nested groups. The WireGuard or AmneziaWG socket, or the MASQUE connection, would otherwise stay on the member the group left. How WARP moves depends on who moved the group:

  • The user moved a selector: WARP reconnects through the new member at once, and in auto mode races the tunnels again.
  • The group moved by itself (a URL test, a balancer, a fallback): WARP moves at most every 30 seconds, and joins the moves in between; a group that comes back to its member before then changes nothing. It moves at once when the member it left had failed its last test, or when WARP is not connected. Then it opens a new tunnel through the new member next to the one in use (in auto mode, after a new race), and moves traffic to it only once it connects, within 25 seconds; when it does not connect, the old tunnel stays.

The standalone masque outbound follows the same rules, and reconnects its tunnel.

Noise. Before each handshake initiation, the device sends count fake packets, with a random delay between them. In the default mode each packet is a short header and size random bytes. In quic mode the first packet carries the ClientHello for sni, and the others carry PING frames, as QUIC retransmissions would. Noise applies to the WireGuard mode. With awg, AmneziaWG's own junk settings are used instead.

Handshake recovery. After 3 unanswered handshake initiations, when there is no working session, the device reopens its socket on a new source port. It also does this when it gives up on a handshake. This happens at most once every 90 seconds. A set listen_port is kept.

Scanner. With scanner.enabled, WARP looks for an endpoint (address and port) that answers before it connects:

  • Each probe is a real WireGuard handshake made with the profile's keys, sent after the configured noise, through the endpoint's own dialer. detour and interface binding apply.
  • Endpoints are tried in this order: the endpoints known on this network, by score; then endpoints that scored well on other networks; then random addresses in cidrs on ports; then endpoints at the lowest score (-10) last.
  • An endpoint that answers slower than max_rtt counts as a failure.
  • The scan ends when an endpoint with a score of 3 or more answers, or when 4 endpoints have answered. Among the answers, the higher score wins, then the lower round-trip time.
  • IPv4 and IPv6 ranges are both scanned when the network has a global address of that family. When one family is unreachable, it is skipped for the rest of the scan.
  • If no endpoint answers, WARP uses the profile's endpoint.
  • The scanner is off when server is set.

Scores. Each endpoint has a score from -10 to 10 on each network:

  • An answer adds 1, up to 10. An answer from a negative score sets it to 1.
  • A failure takes 1, at most once an hour, so one outage costs one point.
  • An endpoint that answered in the last 7 days never drops below -5.

Scores are kept in the cache file when cache_file is enabled. A network not seen for 90 days is forgotten, and each network keeps its best 64 endpoints.

Network names. A network is named by the type of the default interface (Wi-Fi, cellular, ethernet), plus the country and the /16 (IPv4) or /32 (IPv6) of the public address. The public address comes from https://www.cloudflare.com/cdn-cgi/trace, or from https://www.speedtest.net/cdn-cgi/trace when the first does not answer. The request goes through the endpoint's dialer. This keeps a carrier's address pool, or an ISP that changes your address, as one network. The Wi-Fi name is not used, because reading it needs a location permission. When neither trace answers, the interface type alone names the network.

Failover. With the scanner on, WARP checks the endpoint in use:

  • after a network change (it waits 2 seconds, then names the new network), and
  • every minute, when traffic goes out but no handshake has completed for 3 minutes.

The check probes the endpoint in use twice. If it answers, its score goes up. If not, its score goes down, and WARP scans again without it. It starts a new inner WireGuard endpoint on the best answer, switches traffic to it, and then closes the old one. If the scan finds nothing, WARP keeps the current endpoint. The first handshake of each endpoint also counts as an answer.

docs.title: Endpoint fields
docs.text:
Field Type Default Meaning profile object How to get the WARP account. See below. unique_identifier string the tag Key of the saved profile and scores in the cache file. server string profile's peer Peer address to use instead of the profile's. Turns the scanner off. server_port number a profile port Peer port to use instead of the profile's. noise object off Fake packets before each handshake. See below. awg object AmneziaWG settings (jc, jmin, jmax, s1–s4, h1–h4, i1–i5). When any is set, the tunnel uses AmneziaWG instead of WireGuard. mode string from the blocks wg, awg, masque, or auto (the fastest that answers). See How it works. masque object MASQUE settings. When any is set, or enabled, the tunnel uses MASQUE instead of WireGuard. See below. Needs the with_masque build tag. scanner object off Endpoint scanner and failover. See below. mtu number WireGuard default Tunnel MTU. mtu_discovery bool true MTU discovery of the WireGuard or AmneziaWG tunnel. false keeps mtu. rotate_ports bool true Without the scanner and server_port, try the profile's next port when the one in use gets no handshake. fallback_address list of IPs none Other WARP addresses, tried in turn on the same port when the one in use gets no handshake (WireGuard and AmneziaWG). system bool false Use a system interface, as in the wireguard endpoint. name string Interface name when system is on. listen_port number random Local UDP port. udp_timeout duration UDP NAT timeout, as in the wireguard endpoint. workers number WireGuard worker count, as in the wireguard endpoint. private_key, interface, peers A complete WARP profile in Cloudflare's format. When given, no account is registered.

Dial fields (detour, bind_interface and the rest) apply to the tunnel, the scanner probes and the network name check.

docs.title: profile
docs.text: Field Type Default Meaning private_key string random WireGuard private key for the new account. license string WARP license key to apply to the new account (for example WARP+). id, auth_token string An existing device. With both, the device is fetched instead of registered, and private_key is required: it must be the device's own key. detour string direct Outbound tag used to reach Cloudflare's API for registration. recreate bool false Register a new device at each start instead of taking a saved one.

docs.title: masque
docs.text:
An empty masque object is dropped when the config is read, so write "masque": {"enabled": true} to use MASQUE with every default.

Field Type Default Meaning enabled bool false Use MASQUE with every default. vhttp string auto h3, h2, or auto (HTTP/3, falling back to HTTP/2). server_name string consumer-masque.cloudflareclient.com TLS server name. use_ipv6 bool false Use the IPv6 endpoint. tls object insecure, cipher_suites, curve_preferences, fragment, fragment_fallback_delay, record_fragment, kernel_tx, kernel_rx, ech. ech takes enabled, config and query_server_name: the ClientHello then carries an encrypted config list. WARP publishes no config of its own and rejects the public one, so a rejection falls back to a plain handshake, which the pinned peer key still verifies. udp_keepalive_period duration 30s QUIC keepalive. udp_initial_packet_size number First QUIC packet size. reconnect_delay duration Wait between connect attempts. device object A device enrolled elsewhere, used before the saved devices and registering: the fields of the masque outbound's device. A device that cannot work (a key that does not parse, no address) fails the config. See "Devices" above for a device Cloudflare refuses.

The endpoint's mtu (1280 to 9000 over MASQUE), udp_timeout, scanner, server, server_port and dialer fields apply too. noise, listen_port, workers, system and name are WireGuard settings and are not used.

docs.title: noise.fake_packet
docs.text:
Ranges take a number (5), a string ("5-10") or an object ({"from": 5, "to": 10}).

Field Type Default Meaning enabled bool false Send fake packets. count range Number of packets before each handshake. Nothing is sent when it is 0. delay range Wait between packets, in milliseconds. mode string "" quic sends real QUIC Initial packets. raw sends size random bytes with no header, as Xray's random noise and AmneziaWG's junk. Empty sends random packets after a short header. packets list of strings Sent first, in order, as they are: templates in the AmneziaWG i1–i5 syntax (<b 0xHEX> bytes, <r N> random bytes, <rc N> random letters and digits, <rd N> random digits, <t> the Unix time, <qi SNI> a QUIC Initial). A template that cannot be built fails the config. sni string www.google.com Server name in the QUIC ClientHello. Only for quic mode. size range Random bytes in each packet. Needed in the default mode. Not used in quic mode. header bytes (base64) Bytes to pick the first byte of each packet from. Not used in quic mode. no_modify bool false Send packets as they are, without the changes the WireGuard connection makes to its packets. quic mode always sends them as they are.

docs.title: scanner
docs.text:
Field Type Default Meaning enabled bool false Scan for an endpoint that answers, and fail over. ports list of numbers profile's ports, or a built-in list of WARP ports Ports to try on random addresses. cidrs list of prefixes Cloudflare's WARP ranges Ranges to pick random addresses from. max_rtt duration 1s Slowest handshake accepted. timeout duration 2s How long one probe waits for an answer. count number 64 Most endpoints tried in one scan. Known endpoints are always tried. concurrency number 8 Probes run at once. search_noise bool false Also look for noise that gets through. See below. noise_presets list of strings all presets The presets search_noise tries, in order.

Noise search. With search_noise, when no endpoint answers with the configured noise, the scan is tried again with each noise preset, on at most 16 endpoints each, and the first preset that gets an answer is used: as the WireGuard noise, or with awg as the junk and special packets (jc, jmin, jmax, i1–i5; the other awg settings are kept). The preset is remembered for the network in the cache file and tried first there next time. The presets come from WARP configs that work:

Preset What it sends before the handshake xray-random 5 random packets of 5 to 10 bytes, 2 to 5 ms apart, as Xray's WARP noise quic 2 to 4 QUIC Initials for www.google.com dns-google DNS queries for google.com (A, AAAA, HTTPS), then 6 junk packets of 56 to 160 bytes dns-cloudflare DNS queries for cloudflare.com (A, AAAA), then 9 junk packets of 81 to 224 bytes dns-www-cloudflare DNS queries for www.cloudflare.com (A, AAAA), then 6 junk packets of 43 to 109 bytes quic-mimic a QUIC Initial and a short-header packet, then 4 junk packets of 60 to 199 bytes sip a SIP INVITE and its 100 Trying, then 10 junk packets of 42 to 224 bytes stun 2 STUN Binding Requests, then 4 junk packets of 40 to 120 bytes

The probe sends what the device sends: the configured noise, or with awg its junk and special packets.

The default ranges are 162.159.192.0/24, 162.159.193.0/24, 162.159.195.0/24, 188.114.96.0/24 to 188.114.99.0/24, 2606:4700:d0::/64 and 2606:4700:d1::/64.

Notes:

  • The endpoint needs the with_wireguard build tag, and awg needs with_awg. Both are in the default tags.
  • The profile and the scores live in the cache file. Without cache_file, each start registers a new account and the scanner starts with no history.
  • The tunnel starts in the background. Connections wait for the first start to finish. If it failed, they fail with "endpoint not initialized".
  • If registration or the first start fails, the error is logged and it is tried again until it works or the endpoint closes.

docs.title: WireGuard: Hiddify additions
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

Hiddify adds a few things to the upstream WireGuard endpoint ("type": "wireguard"): fake "noise" packets before each handshake, a user name per peer, automatic recovery when the UDP socket stops working, and UDP fragmentation turned on by default. Everything else in the endpoint works as in upstream sing-box and is documented there. This page covers only the Hiddify parts.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• Noise helps when a network blocks WireGuard by its first packet. It works with any normal WireGuard server, because the server simply drops the fake packets.
  • Peer user names give per-user stats and auth_user route rules when you run WireGuard as a server.
  • Recovery brings the tunnel back on its own after the device sleeps, the NAT mapping expires or the network drops the flow, instead of waiting for a network change.
  • UDP fragmentation keeps WireGuard working inside another tunnel with a smaller MTU.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
Many filters look only at the first few packets of a UDP flow. If those do not look like a WireGuard handshake, the flow is let through or classified as something else. With noise turned on, the client sends a few fake packets to the server before every handshake initiation:

  • In the default mode the packets are random bytes with a header that looks like the start of a QUIC packet.
  • In quic mode the packets are real QUIC version 1 Initial packets to the name you set in sni. A filter that decrypts QUIC Initials (anyone can, the keys come from the packet itself) finds a valid TLS 1.3 ClientHello for that name with ALPN h3. The flow then looks like the start of an HTTP/3 connection.

Noise does not change the WireGuard packets themselves. A filter that reads the whole flow can still find the handshake after the noise. For that case, use AmneziaWG. Noise also does not help when UDP is blocked.

docs.title: Noise
docs.text:
• Before each handshake initiation, including retries, the client sends count fake packets, waiting delay milliseconds between them. Then it sends the handshake.
  • In the default mode each packet is: one byte picked at random from header (if set), the bytes 00 00 00 01 08, 8 random bytes, the bytes 00 00 44 D0, then size random bytes.
  • In quic mode the first packet carries the ClientHello and the rest carry PING frames, as QUIC retransmissions would. Each packet is padded to at least 1200 bytes. size and header are not used.
  • In raw mode each packet is size random bytes, with no header, as Xray's random noise and AmneziaWG's junk packets.
  • packets are sent first, as they are: templates in the AmneziaWG i1–i5 syntax, such as a DNS query (<r 2><b 0x0100…>) or a SIP INVITE, so the special packets of AmneziaWG configs work as plain WireGuard noise too.
  • A mode that names a noise preset (sip, dns, stun, random, quic-mimic, dns-cloudflare, ...) sends that preset: its packets, then its junk. count, size, delay and sni set next to it win, and packets follow the preset's. quic without a count sends 2 to 4 Initials, as the quic preset.
  • For a peer given by domain, the noise goes to every resolved address of that domain.
  • A noise packet that fails to send is logged and skipped; it never stops the handshake.

docs.title: Peer user names
docs.text: WireGuard accepts a packet from a peer only when its source address is in that peer's allowed_ips. So the source address of a connection tells which peer sent it. When a peer has a name, connections from its addresses get that user name, the same as a user of a VLESS or Trojan inbound. When allowed_ips of named peers overlap, the most specific prefix wins.

docs.title: Recovery (Hiddify's wireguard-go)
docs.text:
The endpoint runs on Hiddify's copy of wireguard-go (replace/wireguard-go), which adds:

  • New port after failed handshakes. A handshake that keeps failing from the same socket rarely recovers. After 3 unanswered initiations (about 15 seconds) while the peer has no valid session, or when a handshake cycle gives up, the socket is reopened on a new random port, which gives a new UDP flow. A configured listen_port is kept. This happens at most once every 90 seconds.
  • Reopen when receiving fails. If the socket returns a permanent error, or ten errors in a row, the socket is reopened one second later. Before, the tunnel stopped receiving until the network changed.
  • IPv4 kept without IPv6. When the endpoint opens its own sockets (no detour) and the IPv6 socket cannot be opened (IPv6 off, or no IPv6 on the bound interface), the endpoint keeps working on IPv4. Before, it did not start.
  • Bounded waits. Dialing the UDP connection through a detour gives up after 15 seconds and is retried, so a hung detour does not block the tunnel. TCP connections through the tunnel give up after 15 seconds instead of about a minute.

docs.title: Fallback addresses
docs.text: A peer can often be reached at more than one address (WARP at IPv4 and IPv6 ones), and the path may carry only some of them: a network or proxy without IPv6, or a tunnel too small for IPv6's larger packets. With fallback_address, when packets went out but no handshake came back in 15 seconds, the endpoint sends to the next address, and so on in turn; an idle endpoint is left alone. When the path changes (the detour's connection is made again, the network changes), it starts again from the peer's own address, the preferred one. It works with or without a detour. hiddify-core puts an IPv6 WARP exit hop on an IPv4 address and keeps the IPv6 one here.

docs.title: UDP fragmentation
docs.text: The endpoint now lets the system fragment its UDP packets, as official WireGuard does. Before, the "don't fragment" flag was set, so a packet larger than the path MTU (for example WireGuard inside another tunnel) was dropped. Set "udp_fragment": false to get the old behavior.

docs.title: MTU discovery
docs.text:
An endpoint works only when every layer under it carries its packets: the network, and the detour when there is one (WARP in WARP, or WireGuard through a proxy). A packet too large for one of them is lost without a word, and connections stall on their first full-size packet.

  • When the endpoint starts, and whenever its path may have changed (the network changed, or its connection through the detour was made again because the detour's selector switched or the socket was recovered), it sends ICMP echo requests through the tunnel to 1.1.1.1 (2606:4700:4700::1111 without an IPv4 address): one of each size from 576 (1280 for IPv6) to mtu, in steps of 16, all at once. Each goes out as one tunnel packet of that size. The largest size answered becomes the tunnel's MTU, usually within a second.
  • On a new path it first drops its session keys and starts a handshake, as WireGuard does when a peer's endpoint changes. Otherwise the server keeps sending to the old path for about 15 seconds.
  • When the MTU is lowered, the TCP connections made through the endpoint before are closed, so apps reconnect with packets that fit: the server side of such a connection would keep sending packets that are lost. A packet larger than the MTU is answered with ICMP "packet too big", as a router on the path does.
  • When even the smallest request has no answer (a server that drops ICMP, or no route to the target), the MTU stays as configured. Discovery never raises the MTU above mtu, so set mtu to the largest value the first layer can carry.
  • It is on by default, with or without a detour; "mtu_discovery": false turns it off. It does not run with "system": true.

docs.text:

{

{
"address": "203.0.113.10",
"port": 51820,
"public_key": "<base64 server public key>",
"allowed_ips": ["0.0.0.0/0", "::/0"]
}

docs.title: Noise fields (noise.fake_packet)
docs.text:
Field Type Default Meaning enabled bool false Send fake packets before each handshake. count range none How many packets to send. Nothing is sent while this is 0. size range none Random bytes per packet, in the default mode. Nothing is sent in the default mode while this is 0. delay range 0 Milliseconds to wait between two fake packets. mode string "" "" for random packets after a short header, "raw" for random packets with no header, "quic" for real QUIC Initial packets, or the name of a noise preset: "sip", "dns", "stun", "random", "quic-mimic", "dns-cloudflare", "dns-www-cloudflare". packets list of strings none Templates sent first, in order, in the AmneziaWG i1–i5 syntax: <b 0xHEX>, <r N>, <rc N>, <rd N>, <t>, <qi SNI>. A template that cannot be built fails the config. sni string "www.google.com" Server name in the QUIC ClientHello. Only used with "mode": "quic". header list of bytes none Default mode only: each packet starts with one of these bytes, picked at random. Write it as numbers, such as [192, 193, 194], or as a base64 string. no_modify bool false Default mode only: send the packets exactly as built, without writing the peer's reserved bytes into them. quic mode always does this.

A range is written as a number (3), a string ("2-4" or "3"), or an object ({"from": 2, "to": 4}). Both ends are included, and each packet gets a new random value. from must not be larger than to.

docs.title: Peer field
docs.text: Field Type Default Meaning name string none User name for connections from this peer. Stats and auth_user route rules see this name.

docs.title: Dialer field default
docs.text: Field Type Default Meaning udp_fragment bool true Let the system fragment WireGuard UDP packets. Upstream's default for this endpoint is false.

docs.title: Endpoint field
docs.text: Field Type Default Meaning mtu_discovery bool true Find the MTU that gets through the layers under the tunnel (see MTU discovery). false keeps mtu. fallback_address list of IPs none Other addresses of the only peer, on its port, tried in turn when the address in use gets no handshake (see Fallback addresses). Needs a single peer given by an IP address.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The warp endpoint takes the same noise block and passes it to its WireGuard connection.
  • A wireguard endpoint with an awg block fails to start: use the awg endpoint for AmneziaWG obfuscation, or the awg block of a warp endpoint.
  • Noise works with any WireGuard server. The server needs no change.

docs.title: WireGuard outbound (legacy format)
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

Upstream sing-box removed the WireGuard outbound in version 1.13; WireGuard is now an endpoint. Hiddify brings the outbound back under a new type name, so configs written in the old format keep working. It is an outbound: "type": "wireguard_legacy" in the outbounds list. The fields are those of the old wireguard outbound.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• You have a config or a converter that writes the old WireGuard outbound, and you do not want to rewrite it as an endpoint.

For new configs, use the WireGuard endpoint. It has the Hiddify additions (noise packets, recovery, peer names), and this outbound does not.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: It does not. It is plain WireGuard, which a filter can recognize by its handshake. For obfuscation, use the WireGuard endpoint with noise, or AmneziaWG.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• It runs the same WireGuard engine as the endpoint, with a user-space network stack, or with a system interface when system_interface is set.
  • With peers, each peer has its own address, keys and allowed IPs. Without peers, the top-level server, server_port, peer_public_key, pre_shared_key and reserved make one peer that receives all traffic (0.0.0.0/0 and ::/0).
  • A domain as destination is resolved with the default DNS rules, then the connection goes through the tunnel. A peer given by domain is resolved the same way.
  • TCP, UDP and ping go through the tunnel. network limits TCP and UDP; ping is always offered.
  • The type is still reported as wireguard, so the app shows it as WireGuard.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"outbounds": [
{
"type": "wireguard_legacy",
"tag": "wg-out",
"server": "203.0.113.10",
"server_port": 51820,
"local_address": ["10.8.0.2/32"],
"private_key": "<base64 private key>",
"peer_public_key": "<base64 server public key>"
}
]
}
Field Type Default Meaning local_address list of prefixes required Addresses of this side of the tunnel. private_key string required Private key, base64. server string none Server address, when peers is empty. server_port int none Server port, when peers is empty. peer_public_key string none Server public key, base64, when peers is empty. pre_shared_key string none Pre-shared key, base64, when peers is empty. reserved list of 3 bytes none Reserved bytes for the peer, when peers is empty. Cloudflare WARP uses them. peers list of objects none Several peers. Each has server, server_port, public_key, pre_shared_key, allowed_ips (required) and reserved. mtu int 1408 MTU of the tunnel. workers int number of CPUs WireGuard worker count. system_interface bool false Use a system network interface instead of the user-space stack. interface_name string none Name of the system interface. network "tcp" or "udp" both Networks the outbound accepts, as in upstream's old outbound. Ping is always accepted. gso bool false Accepted for old configs, but not used. It cannot be used with detour.

The dial fields (detour, bind_interface and the rest) work as for other outbounds. There is no keepalive option, as in upstream's old outbound.

docs.title: finalmask
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

finalmask applies Xray-core's finalmask masks to the connections an outbound opens. A mask changes the bytes on the wire: it splits them, adds noise packets, adds headers, or wraps them in another protocol (DNS, ICMP, a Minecraft-like stream and more). It is the finalmask field of the dial fields, so you can set it on any outbound that dials (and on DNS servers and other places that take dial fields). The JSON is the same as Xray's streamSettings.finalmask.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• To use an Xray server that is set up with finalmask masks: the client must apply the same masks, or the server cannot read the traffic.
  • To change how a connection looks on the wire without changing the protocol: split the TLS ClientHello (fragment), send junk UDP packets before a WireGuard or QUIC handshake (noise), or obfuscate UDP with a password (salamander).

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
Filters match on the first bytes and packets of a connection, their sizes and their timing. Masks change exactly that. fragment cuts the ClientHello into small pieces so a filter that does not reassemble them cannot read the SNI. noise sends random packets first, so the real handshake does not start the flow. Header and wrapping masks make the traffic look like another protocol, or like random bytes.

Masks that only change sizes and timing (fragment, merge, oob, mirage, noise) work with any server. Masks that change the content (headers, salamander, sudoku, xdns, xicmp, xmc, mkcp-legacy, realm) need the same mask on the server, which means an Xray server configured for it. udphop needs a server that listens on every port it hops to. A mask does not help when the filter blocks the server's IP address, except xdns: it reaches the server through public DNS resolvers, so the server's own address is never contacted.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• tcp masks wrap every TCP connection the outbound opens, and udp masks every UDP socket and connected UDP connection.
  • Masks run in list order: the first mask gets the bytes the outbound writes, and the last mask's output goes on the wire. Replies pass through them in reverse.
  • The masks sit under the protocol and its TLS layer, so they see exactly what would go on the wire. With detour, they wrap the connection made through the detour outbound.
  • The connection is dialed through the masks, as in Xray. A mask that opens sockets of its own (xdns to its resolvers, udphop to each new port) opens them with the outbound's dialer, so they take the same detour, interface and routing mark as the connection. xdns, xicmp and udphop replace the socket to the server: they must be the last udp mask.
  • Only the client side is implemented: inbounds do not take finalmask.
  • The masks are Xray-core's own code (from Xray-core v26.10.31), except merge and oob, which come from patterniha's Xray-core; their behavior and settings follow Xray's documentation for finalmask. Xray's inbound-only filter mask is not available.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
A VLESS outbound whose ClientHello is fragmented, and a WireGuard endpoint that sends noise before each handshake:

{
"outbounds": [
{
"type": "vless",
"server": "example.com",
"server_port": 443,
"uuid": "bf000d23-0752-40b4-affe-68f7707a9661",
"tls": { "enabled": true, "server_name": "example.com" },
"finalmask": {
"tcp": [
{ "type": "fragment", "settings": { "packets": "tlshello", "length": "100-200", "delay": "10-20" } }
]
}
}
],
"endpoints": [
{
"type": "wireguard",
"tag": "wg",
"address": ["10.0.0.2/32"],
"private_key": "...",
"peers": [{ "address": "203.0.113.1", "port": 51820, "public_key": "...", "allowed_ips": ["0.0.0.0/0"] }],
"finalmask": {
"udp": [
{ "type": "noise", "settings": { "noise": [{ "rand": "10-50", "delay": "5-10" }] } }
]
}
}
]
}
Field Type Default Meaning finalmask.tcp array — Masks for TCP connections, in order. finalmask.udp array — Masks for UDP, in order. finalmask.quicParams object — Accepted so Xray configs load; not used. QUIC protocols have their own options in sing-box. …[].type string — Mask type (see below). Case does not matter. …[].settings object {} The mask's settings, exactly as in Xray.

Supported mask types:

Type tcp udp What it does Main settings fragment yes — Splits the first writes (or the TLS ClientHello) into small pieces with delays. see below merge yes — Holds quick writes and sends them as one, for the first writes of the connection. From patterniha's Xray-core. see below oob yes — Sends each of the first writes with one more byte as TCP urgent (out-of-band) data, which the server drops and a filter may misread. Xray's (patterniha's) dialMode oob.<bytes>. see below mirage yes — Splits the TLS ClientHello into two TLS records, written on their own or in one write, so a filter cannot match the server name. PoriyaVali's Mirage library. offset, layout header-custom yes yes Adds custom bytes the server expects (a fake protocol header). TCP: clients, servers, errors; UDP: mode, client, server sudoku yes yes Sudoku obfuscation, keyed by a password. password, ascii, customTable, customTables, paddingMin, paddingMax xmc yes — Makes the stream look like a Minecraft connection. hostname, profiles, password noise — yes Sends random or fixed packets before the real ones; a type exp packet is built from an expression. noise (list of rand, randRange, type, packet, delay), reset, script salamander — yes Hysteria2's Salamander obfuscation; with packetSize, the Gecko variant that also changes packet sizes. password, packetSize (at most 2048) mkcp-legacy — yes mKCP's old packet headers (dns, dtls, srtp, utp, wechat, wireguard) or its AES-GCM layer. header, value xdns — yes Carries UDP in DNS queries to the server's domain, through DNS resolvers over UDP, TCP or DoH. see below xicmp — yes Carries UDP in ICMP echo packets. ips, dgram realm — yes Connects to the peer through NAT hole punching, using STUN servers and a rendezvous URL. url (realm:// or realm+http://), stunServers, tlsConfig udphop — yes Port hopping: moves the UDP flow to another server port, and another local socket, every few seconds or per connection. see below

An unknown type, a TCP-only type in udp (or the other way round) or bad settings is a configuration error that names the mask, such as finalmask.tcp[0] fragment.

fragment settings:

Field Type Default Meaning packets string — tlshello splits the TLS ClientHello; a range such as "1-3" splits those writes of the connection. length range — Size of each piece in bytes. delay range 0 Wait between pieces in milliseconds. lengths range list — One length per piece, in place of length. delays range list — One delay per piece, in place of delay. maxSplit range — Largest number of pieces.

A range is "from-to" or a number; a range list is an array of them, or a single one.

noise with "type": "exp" takes packet as an expression of segments: <b 0x1700> fixed bytes in hex, <r 10-20> random bytes, <rc 8> random letters, <rd 4> random digits, <t> a timestamp, <c> a counter, <n> a nonce. script is the path of a local .lua file that makes the packets instead of noise (Xray has turned inline scripts off for now).

xdns settings, for the client:

Field Type Default Meaning domains[].names string list — The server's domains; queries go to their subdomains. Required. domains[].types number list [16] DNS record types to ask for: 1 (A), 5 (CNAME), 16 (TXT), 28 (AAAA). domains[].edns0 number 0 EDNS0 UDP size to announce. The same value on the server lets a reply carry more: without it a reply holds about 500 bytes, too few for mKCP segments. domains[].lenLimit, labelLimit number 255, 63 Longest query name and label. resolvers[].addrs string list — Resolvers: 8.8.8.8 or udp://8.8.8.8:53, tcp://9.9.9.9:53, https://1.1.1.1/dns-query. Required. resolvers[].worker number 32 Queries in flight per resolver. resolvers[].tlsConfig object — TLS of a DoH resolver, as Xray's tlsSettings: serverName, alpn (["h3"] for DoH over QUIC), fingerprint, pinnedPeerCertSha256, verifyPeerCertByName, echConfigList and the like. Required for https://. resolvers[].quicConfig object — QUIC settings of a DoH resolver over h3, as Xray's quicParams. extraPoll number 0 Extra empty queries per write, 0 to 3, so replies come back sooner.

The settings of earlier Xray versions still load: "resolvers": ["t.example.com+udp://8.8.8.8:53"] becomes the domain t.example.com with the resolver udp://8.8.8.8:53, and {"name": ...} and {"type": ..., "addr": ...} become names and addrs.

udphop settings:

Field Type Default Meaning mode string — Comma separated: intervalLocal changes the local socket, intervalRemote the server port on a timer, perConnRemote picks a server port per connection. Required. interval range 30 Seconds between hops, at least 5. remotePorts port list — Server ports to hop between: "20000-20100,443". remoteIPs string list — Server addresses or prefixes to hop between as well.

merge settings:

Field Type Default Meaning times number 0 How many merged writes to send; then writes pass through. 0 or less merges for the whole connection. delayMs number 30 A held write goes out when no new one comes for this many milliseconds. maxBytes number 16384 Held bytes go out at once when they reach this size.

oob settings:

Field Type Default Meaning bytes number list — One byte (0 to 255) per write: write i is sent with bytes[i] as urgent data. Required.

mirage settings:

Field Type Default Meaning offset number 5 Size of the first record's handshake bytes (1 to 16383). Safe sizes depend on the network: 1, 2, 4 and 5 passed in Iran in 2026, 3 and 6 or more were dropped. layout string separate separate writes each record on its own (what MCI and Irancell let through in September 2026); single writes both in one write (what Iran let through in August 2026).

mirage only changes the first write when it is one complete ClientHello with a server name; any other first write goes out unchanged. Put it last in tcp, or after the masks that need the plain ClientHello. A bad offset can make the filter drop the whole connection, even for an allowed name.

oob works on the socket, so put it last in tcp; a share link's dialMode=oob.0,32 becomes {"type": "oob", "settings": {"bytes": [0, 32]}} after the link's other masks. It needs a real TCP socket: through a detour it does nothing.

Related options: the outbound's tls_fragment is added as the first fragment mask. tls_tricks changes the ClientHello itself and is not a mask. tls_fragment cannot be used with tcp_fast_open.

docs.title: Custom gRPC paths
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

The gRPC transport's service_name can be a full custom path, as in Xray. A name that starts with / is read as /<service>/<stream>, so /my/path/Tun sends requests to the path /my/path/Tun. Any other name works as before and gives the path /<service_name>/Tun. This is the service_name field of a "type": "grpc" transport, on clients and servers.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• To connect to Xray servers that use a custom gRPC path. Before, sing-box always sent /<service_name>/Tun and could not reach them.
  • To let Xray clients with a custom path connect to a sing-box server.
  • To pick a path that fits the site behind a CDN or reverse proxy, instead of one that ends in /Tun.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: It does not change how gRPC looks; it only lets you choose the request path. A path that matches the decoy site makes the traffic less distinct for a filter that inspects decrypted traffic (a CDN or a reverse proxy that routes by path). It does not help against a filter that cannot see inside TLS.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• /<service>/<stream>: everything between the first / and the last / is the service, and the part after the last / is the stream. /my/path/Tun is service my/path, stream Tun.
  • Xray's server form /<service>/<stream>|<multi stream> also names the stream of Xray's multi mode, which sing-box does not use; the part after | is ignored. So a server can use the same value as an Xray server, such as /my/path/Tun|TunMulti.
  • Each path segment is URL-escaped, as in Xray.
  • A name without a leading / is the service and the stream is Tun, as before.
  • Both gRPC implementations read the name the same way: the full gRPC one (in builds with the with_grpc tag) and the built-in gRPC-lite one.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"outbounds": [
{
"type": "vless",
"server": "example.com",
"server_port": 443,
"uuid": "bf000d23-0752-40b4-affe-68f7707a9661",
"tls": { "enabled": true, "server_name": "example.com", "alpn": ["h2"] },
"transport": { "type": "grpc", "service_name": "/my/path/Tun" }
}
]
}
Field Type Default Meaning service_name string "" A plain name (the path is /<name>/Tun), or a custom path /<service>/<stream>, optionally followed by \|<multi stream> (ignored).

Client and server must give the same path. Tested in both directions, with both implementations, against Xray 26.10.21 and 26.3.27.

docs.text: • XHTTP transport

docs.title: mKCP transport
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

mKCP carries a proxy protocol (VLESS, VMess, Trojan…) over UDP with KCP, a reliable protocol that resends lost packets fast. It is the V2Ray transport "type": "mkcp" (or "kcp") of an outbound or inbound, and it is the same mKCP as in Xray 26.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• The network drops or throttles TCP but lets UDP through.
  • The link loses many packets: KCP resends sooner than TCP and keeps the speed up, at the cost of more traffic.
  • You connect to an Xray server that offers mKCP.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
On its own, mKCP is plain UDP with a recognizable header. To hide it, give the outbound a finalmask UDP mask, as Xray does since mKCP's header and seed moved there:

  • mkcp-legacy with value encrypts every packet with AES-GCM (the old seed).
  • mkcp-legacy with header (dns, dtls, srtp, utp, wechat, wireguard) makes each packet look like that protocol (the old header).
  • Other UDP masks (noise, salamander, …) work as well.

The server must use the same masks. TLS can run inside mKCP with the outbound's tls block.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The client opens one UDP socket per connection and runs one KCP session on it.
  • The server reads all sessions from the inbound's UDP port and tells them apart by the sender and the session number.
  • There is no handshake of its own: the proxy protocol inside starts at once.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
Needs the with_kcp build tag. Without it, a config with mKCP fails with "mKCP is not included in this build".

{
"type": "vless",
"server": "example.com",
"server_port": 4443,
"uuid": "b831381d-6324-4d53-ad4f-8cda48b30811",
"transport": { "type": "mkcp", "uplink_capacity": 20, "downlink_capacity": 100 },
"finalmask": { "udp": [{ "type": "mkcp-legacy", "settings": { "value": "a password" } }] }
}
Field Type Default Meaning mtu number 1350 Largest packet, in bytes. At least 21. tti number 50 Update interval in milliseconds, 10 to 1000. Lower is faster and uses more traffic. uplink_capacity number 5 Upload speed to aim for, in MB/s. downlink_capacity number 20 Download speed to aim for, in MB/s. cwnd_multiplier number 1 Scales the congestion window. max_sending_window number 2097152 Largest send buffer, in bytes. At least mtu.

The fields and defaults are Xray 26's kcpSettings. Tested in both directions against Xray 26.10.21 and 26.3.27, plain and with the aes128gcm and wechat masks. Xray 26.3 names these masks mkcp-aes128gcm and header-wechat; they are the same on the wire.

Inbounds do not take finalmask, so a Hiddify mKCP server works only without masks.

docs.title: Raw transport
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

raw is a V2Ray transport that adds nothing: the protocol runs straight over TCP, or over TLS when the tls block is enabled. It is the same as having no transport block, and matches Xray's raw (formerly tcp) network. Set it with "transport": {"type": "raw"} on a VLESS, VMess or Trojan inbound or outbound.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text: It lets configs converted from Xray, or written by tools that always fill in a transport, load without change. A node whose Xray network is raw or tcp can be written as "type": "raw". You never need it in a config you write by hand.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: It does not. It adds no framing or disguise; what the filter sees is the protocol itself and its TLS or REALITY layer.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Client: dials the server over TCP, does the TLS handshake if TLS is enabled, and hands the connection to the protocol.
  • Server: accepts TCP connections, does the TLS handshake if TLS is enabled, and hands each one to the protocol. It does not listen on UDP.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"outbounds": [
{
"type": "vless",
"server": "example.com",
"server_port": 443,
"uuid": "bf000d23-0752-40b4-affe-68f7707a9661",
"tls": { "enabled": true, "server_name": "example.com" },
"transport": { "type": "raw" }
}
]
}
Field Type Default Meaning type string — raw. The transport has no other fields.

docs.title: See also
docs.text: • XHTTP transport

docs.title: rmux multiplexing
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

rmux is one more protocol for sing-box multiplexing: "multiplex": {"protocol": "rmux"} on an outbound. Like smux, yamux and h2mux, it carries many connections inside one connection to the server. It comes from sing-box-extended (github.com/shtorm-7/rmux).

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• Fewer connections to the server: each new connection opens a stream in a session that already exists, with no new handshake, so it starts faster and shows fewer connections to the network.
  • You want a multiplexer other than the usual ones; rmux is newer and less common on the wire.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text: It does not on its own. It runs inside the outbound's protocol and transport, which are what the network sees.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Data travels in frames of at most 32 KiB, each tagged with its stream.
  • A stream can be closed for writing while it still reads, as with h2mux.
  • Sessions are kept and reused as for the other protocols; keepalive frames are off, as sing-box manages idle sessions itself.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"type": "vless",
"server": "example.com",
"server_port": 443,
"uuid": "b831381d-6324-4d53-ad4f-8cda48b30811",
"multiplex": { "enabled": true, "protocol": "rmux", "max_connections": 4 }
}

The server's inbound needs "multiplex": {"enabled": true} and Hiddify's sing-box: it accepts rmux like the other protocols, and an upstream sing-box server refuses it. The other multiplex fields work as for the other protocols. No build tag is needed.

docs.text: • Bond

docs.title: Shadowsocks simple-obfs server and fallback
docs.text:
All Hiddify features

The Shadowsocks inbound can run the server side of simple-obfs (obfs-server), so clients using the obfs-local plugin in http or tls mode can connect to sing-box directly. It can also pass every connection that is not a valid client to a decoy server, so a probe sees a real website instead of a closed connection. These are the obfs_mode and obfs_fallback fields of a "type": "shadowsocks" inbound, and they work with one user, many users (users) and relay (destinations) inbounds.

docs.title: Why use it
docs.text:
• To serve Shadowsocks clients that use obfs-local (Shadowsocks apps, and sing-box's own Shadowsocks outbound with "plugin": "obfs-local") without running a separate obfs-server.
  • To make the server look like an ordinary web server to anyone who connects to it without the right password.

docs.title: How it gets past filtering
docs.text:
• simple-obfs wraps the start of each connection in an HTTP WebSocket upgrade request (http) or a TLS ClientHello (tls), so plain Shadowsocks traffic, which looks random, starts like web traffic.
  • Filters often probe suspected servers: they connect and send their own data, or replay a recorded client request, and watch the reply. With obfs_fallback, such a probe is connected to the decoy, for example a real website on the same port, and gets its normal answer.

simple-obfs is old and its HTTP and TLS forms are easy to recognize for a filter that checks them closely; the TLS form is not real TLS. Use it for clients that cannot use anything else.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• With obfs_mode set, the inbound reads the client's first request. For http, it must be a GET with Upgrade: websocket; for tls, a ClientHello with simple-obfs' exact layout. The server replies with an HTTP 101 or a TLS ServerHello, and the Shadowsocks data inside is passed on.
  • With obfs_fallback set, the inbound keeps a copy of what the client sent (up to 16 KB) until Shadowsocks has authenticated the client. If anything fails before that, the connection and the copied bytes go to the fallback address. This covers:
  • connections that are not simple-obfs, such as a browser or a scanner (like obfs-server --failover);
  • connections that pass obfs but fail Shadowsocks: an unknown user, a wrong password or a replayed request. So a probe that copies a real client's obfs request also gets the decoy.
  • After authentication, nothing more is recorded, and a later error closes the connection.
  • The fallback connection is routed like any other connection from the inbound, with the fallback address as its destination, so your route rules decide which outbound reaches it (usually direct).
  • obfs applies to TCP only. Shadowsocks UDP is not changed.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
{
"inbounds": [
{
"type": "shadowsocks",
"listen": "::",
"listen_port": 443,
"method": "2022-blake3-aes-128-gcm",
"password": "8JCsPssfgS8tiRwiMlhARg==",
"users": [{ "name": "alice", "password": "PCD2Z4o12bKUoFa3cC97Hw==" }],
"obfs_mode": "tls",
"obfs_fallback": { "server": "www.example.com", "server_port": 443 }
}
]
}

A matching client:

{
"outbounds": [
{
"type": "shadowsocks",
"server": "203.0.113.1",
"server_port": 443,
"method": "2022-blake3-aes-128-gcm",
"password": "8JCsPssfgS8tiRwiMlhARg==:PCD2Z4o12bKUoFa3cC97Hw==",
"plugin": "obfs-local",
"plugin_opts": "obfs=tls;obfs-host=www.example.com"
}
]
}
Field Type Default Meaning obfs_mode string "" http or tls: run the simple-obfs server. Empty: no obfs. obfs_fallback object — Decoy server for connections that fail obfs or Shadowsocks authentication: server and server_port. Needs obfs_mode. obfs_host string "" Hosts the client may use, comma-separated. When set, a client whose HTTP Host or TLS server name is not listed is treated as not simple-obfs: it goes to obfs_fallback, or is closed. Empty allows any host. Needs obfs_mode.

Errors: an obfs_mode other than http or tls, obfs_fallback without obfs_mode, or a fallback without a valid address and port is a configuration error. Without obfs_fallback, a failed connection is closed.
